1.open: Think of a plant or tree you have seen thriving somewhere unlikely, or one you have managed to keep alive. What do you think made the difference?
questions: Verse 1 describes someone who does not "walk in the counsel of the wicked," or "set foot on the path of sinners," or "sit in the seat of mockers." Walking, then standing, then sitting is how many readers see a slow slide. Where have you seen influence creep in gradually, in your own life or someone else's?
Who are the voices that shape you most right now: friends, family, news, social media, coworkers? What do they tend to say about what matters?
Verse 2 says "his delight is in the Law of the LORD." The word here means instruction, not just rules. What would it look like to enjoy God's teaching instead of treating it as a chore?
The person in verse 2 "meditates day and night." What helps you keep a verse or an idea turning over in your mind, and what gets in the way?
Verse 3 pictures a tree "planted by streams of water" whose leaf "does not wither." What are the dry seasons in your life, and what has kept you going through them, even a little?

The verse says this person "prospers in all he does" (v. 3). Christians read that differently: some see visible success, others a deeper flourishing that may not show outwardly. How do you read it, given what you have seen in real life?
The wicked are "like chaff driven off by the wind" (v. 4). Why might Scripture picture a life without roots as weightless rather than just bad? When have you felt blown about?
Verse 6 says "the LORD guards the path of the righteous." If you are not sure you feel guarded or rooted right now, what would you honestly say about where you are?
1.life: This week, pick one input that shapes you, such as a feed, a show or a habit of conversation, and notice how it leaves you feeling. Then set aside five minutes a day to read one short passage of Scripture slowly and let a single line stay with you.
1.prayer: Ask God to be the deep water your life draws from. Pray for anyone in the group who feels dry or blown about right now.
1.tip: Verse 3 can sound like a promise that good people never struggle, which will sting for anyone who is hurting. Gently say that Christians read it differently, and remind the group that the tree is described by its roots, not by how easy its weather has been.

2.open: When you were a kid, what rule did you most want to break free from, and did you ever try?
questions: The psalm opens with a question: "Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?" (v. 1). What do you think drives people to push against any authority over them, even a good one?
The rulers say, "Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords" (v. 3). When have you felt that way about God, or about anyone who had a claim on your life?
In verse 4, "The One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord taunts them." What picture of God does that give you, and does it comfort you, unsettle you, or a bit of both?
In verse 6 God says, "I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain." Why might it matter that God's answer to the uproar is simply to point to the king he has already chosen?
In verse 7 the king hears, "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father." Christians read this as pointing to Jesus. What does it tell you about the kind of king God chose?
The psalm ends with a warning, "be wise, O kings" (v. 10), and an invitation, "Blessed are all who take refuge in Him" (v. 12). Which one speaks to you more tonight, and why?

Verse 11 says, "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling." Fear and joy sit side by side here. What does it mean for you to hold both? If you honestly struggle to trust God as king, what makes it hard?
Verses 8 and 9 use very strong pictures of the king's victory. How do you take that language, and how does it sit with what you know of Jesus?
2.life: Pick one area where you tend to resist being led, whether by God, a boss, a parent or a habit of doing things your own way. This week, stop and ask honestly whether you are resisting something unjust or something you would be better off trusting, and tell God what you find.
2.prayer: Thank God that he is not anxious or threatened, and that his chosen King offers refuge. Ask for honesty about where you are pulling against him, and for the trust to run to him rather than away.
2.tip: The language in verses 8 and 9 about breaking and shattering can feel harsh, and the Hebrew in verse 12 is unclear. Don't rush to explain it away. Say that Christians also differ on whether the psalm first described David's line or was a direct prophecy of the Messiah, then bring the group back to the final line, which offers refuge to all who come.

3.open: What is something that keeps you awake at night, or something that helps you finally fall asleep?
questions: The heading says David wrote this while running from his own son Absalom. What do you think it felt like to be hunted by family, and why might that hurt more than an attack from a stranger?
David begins by telling God plainly, "how my foes have increased!" (v. 1). Why do you think he starts with the problem instead of with praise? What does that say about how we can talk to God?
Many were saying, "God will not deliver him" (v. 2). When have you heard a voice, from others or in your own head, telling you that God has given up on you?
David answers with "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head" (v. 3). Which of those three pictures speaks to you most right now, and why?

God answers "from His holy mountain" (v. 4), the city David had just been forced to leave. What might it mean that David trusted God was still near even when he was away from the place God was thought to live?

David says, "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me" (v. 5). What helps you rest when life feels stacked against you? And if rest isn't coming for you right now, what is that like?
In verse 7 David asks God to "break the teeth of the wicked." It is a violent image. How do you feel reading a prayer like that, and what do you think it shows about being honest with God?
The psalm ends with "may Your blessing be on Your people" (v. 8), not only on David. What difference does it make to pray for others when you are the one in trouble?
3.life: Before bed each night this week, name one worry out loud to God, then pray verse 5 in your own words: "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me." Notice what changes, even if it is small.
3.prayer: Tell God honestly about whatever feels like it is closing in on you. Thank Him that He is "a shield around me" (v. 3), and ask for trust enough to rest tonight.
3.tip: Verse 7 may make some people uncomfortable, and others may want to skip past it. Say that the psalms let people be raw with God, and that David hands his anger to God instead of acting on it himself. Note too that the Hebrew can be read as a request or as something God has already done. Don't push the group to resolve it, and let the quiet ones know it is fine to say the verse bothers them.

4.open: What helps you fall asleep on a night when your mind will not slow down?
questions: David begins, "Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness!" (v. 1). What does it say about him that he asks this so directly? When do you find it easy or hard to speak to God that plainly?
In verse 2 he asks, "How long, O men, will my honor be maligned?" Think of a time your name or reputation was dragged through the mud, or you saw it happen to someone else. What did that feel like?
Verse 3 says, "the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself." David may be speaking to people with power over him. Why might that truth matter most to someone who feels powerless?

Verse 4 says, "Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still." What do you usually do with anger at night, and what might it look like to be honest with God about it without acting on it?
Verse 5 says to "trust in the LORD." Trust is easy to say and hard to do. What makes it harder for you when someone has wronged you and nothing is settled?
In verse 6 David notes that many people are asking who can show them the good. Where do people around us look for good, and what do they hope it will give them? Where do you look, if you are honest?
David says God has given him more joy "than when grain and new wine abound" (v. 7). What is a good thing in your life that you still do not want to depend on for your joy?

Verse 8 says, "I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety." Nothing in the psalm says David's problems are gone. If you cannot say this yet, what is getting in the way? That is a fair answer here.
4.life: For the next few nights, spend a minute before bed telling God plainly what is weighing on you, including any anger. Then read verse 8 slowly and hand the rest over until morning.
4.prayer: Ask God to hear you when you call, as David did. Pray for anyone in the group who is carrying an unresolved hurt or struggling to sleep, and ask for the kind of peace that rests on God and not on circumstances.
4.tip: Verse 4 can lead people to feel guilty about being angry. Point out that the verse does not say anger is the sin; it says not to let it lead you into sin. Also, some in your group may find verse 8 hard to say tonight. Let them be honest about that, and treat it as a place to begin, not a test they failed.

5.open: What is your morning routine like, and is there one part of it you would never skip?
questions: David asks God to "consider my groaning" (v. 1). What does it say about God that a prayer can be just a groan? When did you last pray without finding the right words?
He prays "in the morning" and then waits "in expectation" (v. 3). What would it look like for you to bring something to God and then actually watch for an answer?
Verses 4 to 6 say God is not a God who "delights in wickedness." Why might it matter to David, who is being lied about, that God takes evil seriously?
Verse 5 says "You hate all workers of iniquity." That is a hard line to read. What goes through your mind when you hear it, and what questions does it raise for you?
David says he can enter God's house "by the abundance of Your loving devotion" (v. 7). How does it change things to come to God because of his love and not because of our record?
In verse 9 David says of his enemies, "not a word they speak can be trusted." Have you ever been hurt by someone's words, whether lies, gossip or flattery? How did you handle it?

In verse 10 David asks God to "declare them guilty." Christians read this differently: some hear an honest cry for justice, others read it alongside Jesus' call to love and pray for enemies. How do you hold those together?
The psalm ends with God's favor as "the shield" around the righteous (v. 12). If you are honest, do you feel sheltered right now, or exposed? What would help?
5.life: Pick one time each morning this week, even just two minutes, to tell God plainly what is weighing on you. Then pause and wait before you start your day. If someone has wronged you, say honestly to God what you feel about it.
5.prayer: Thank God that he hears even our groaning. Ask him to lead you and to shelter anyone in the group who feels under attack, and for honesty to bring him what you really feel.
5.tip: Verses 5 and 10 may stir strong reactions, and some people may feel uneasy or even angry. Say plainly that Christians read these lines differently, avoid settling it, and note that the psalm shows it is acceptable to bring raw feelings to God. Leave space for someone who finds the passage troubling to say so.

6.open: When was the last time you were so tired that you could hardly think straight? What did you do about it?
questions: David begins, "O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger" (v. 1). Why do you think he is afraid God is angry with him? Have you ever felt that way when things went wrong?
He says, "I am frail" and "my bones are in agony" (v. 2). Why might it matter that he brings his body's pain to God and not only his spiritual troubles?
In verse 3 he cries, "How long, O LORD, how long?" and the sentence just stops. What do you think is going on when someone can't finish a prayer?
In verse 4 he asks to be saved "because of Your loving devotion," not because of anything he has done. What difference does it make to ask for help on that basis?
Verse 5 says, "There is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?" What does this tell us about how Israel thought of death, and how does it compare with what you have been taught?
Verse 6 describes nights of weeping, with a bed flooded with tears. What would it look like for us to bring our unfiltered, honest sorrow to God? What makes that hard?

Then the mood turns: "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy" (v. 9). Nothing has visibly changed yet. If you have ever felt that kind of shift, or are still waiting for it, how would you describe where you are today?
Verse 10 hopes that his enemies will be "ashamed and dismayed." How do you handle honest anger or a wish for justice in prayer, and where does grace come in?
6.life: Set aside five minutes this week, perhaps at night, to pray as honestly as David does here. Name what hurts, even if you only manage a few words or end with "how long?"
6.prayer: Thank God that he hears weeping as well as praise. Invite people to name quietly what is weighing on them, and ask God for mercy and strength for each one.
6.tip: Verse 9 can sound like instant relief, and someone who is still hurting may feel left behind. Say plainly that scholars are unsure why the mood changes, and that it is fine to stay in the first half of the psalm for a while. Also note that Christians disagree on whether this is a prayer of repentance, since it never confesses a sin, and leave that open.

7.open: Think of a time you were blamed for something you didn't do. What did you wish someone would say or do for you?
questions: The psalm opens with "I take refuge in You" (v. 1). When you feel under attack, where do you usually run first? What does it look like to run to God instead, or as well?
The speaker fears being torn apart "with no one to rescue me" (v. 2). What was it like for him to be so alone, and when have you felt that kind of aloneness?
In verses 3 to 5 he says, "if injustice is on my hands," then let the enemy catch him. What was he doing there, and how is that different from claiming to be perfect?
He asks God to "Arise" and "Awake" (v. 6), as if God were asleep. Have you ever felt that way about God? What do you make of the Bible letting a person pray so boldly?
Verse 9 speaks of "O righteous God who searches hearts and minds." Is it comforting or uncomfortable to think God sees what no one else can? Why?
Verse 11 says God "feels indignation each day," and verses 12 and 13 picture a sword and bow. How do you picture God's anger, and how does it sit alongside his mercy?

In verses 14 to 16 the one who digs a pit "has fallen into a pit of his own making." Where have you seen harm come back around on the person who caused it? What should we make of that, and what should we avoid assuming?
The psalm ends with "I will thank the LORD for His righteousness" (v. 17). If you are honestly not at that place yet, what would you say to God instead?
7.life: Think of someone who has wronged you. This week, pray the way this psalm does: tell God exactly what happened, ask him to set things right, and leave the outcome with him. Notice whether you are asking for justice or for them to suffer.
7.prayer: Thank God that he is a fair judge who sees what is hidden. Bring him one hurt or false accusation, and ask for the trust to leave it in his hands.
7.tip: The talk of enemies, swords and arrows can lead people to either skip the anger or use it against someone they know. Say plainly that the psalm hands the case to God rather than taking revenge, and that verse 12 is read differently by Christians. Then keep the group on honest prayer rather than settling that question.

8.open: When was the last time you looked up at a night sky, and what did you notice?
questions: The psalm begins and ends with the same line: "how majestic is Your name in all the earth!" (vv. 1, 9). Why might the writer wrap the whole song in that sentence? What do you notice about everything in between?

Verse 2 says God has ordained praise "from the mouths of children and infants." Scholars are not sure of the exact sense of this verse, but it seems to say God can use the weakest voices. When have you seen something small or simple say more about God than something impressive?
The writer looks at "the moon and the stars" and calls them "the work of Your fingers" (v. 3). What does it say about God that the whole night sky is described that casually?
Verse 4 asks, "what is man that You are mindful of him?" Put that question in your own words. When do you feel small, and when do you feel noticed?

Verse 5 says God "crowned him with glory and honor." Those are words usually used of kings. What does it mean that ordinary people are given that kind of dignity? How might it change the way we treat each other?
In verse 6 humans are made "ruler of the works of Your hands," with animals, birds and fish under their care. What do you think it looks like to take care of creation well, as opposed to using it up?

Christians read verses 4 to 8 in different ways: some see them mainly as describing humanity's place in the world, others as a prophecy fulfilled in Jesus. Which reading helps you more right now, and why?
If you are honest, do you find it easier to believe God is great or that God cares about you personally? Say whatever is true for you, including doubts.
8.life: Spend ten minutes this week outside under the night sky, with your phone away. Read verses 3 and 4 slowly, then tell God what you feel, whether small, noticed, or both.
8.prayer: Praise God for being majestic in all the earth. Thank him for noticing and caring for small people like us, and ask for help to treat people and creation with the honor he has given them.
8.tip: Verses 5 to 8 can slide into debates about dominion, the environment or angels versus God in verse 5. Name briefly that translations differ and Christians read these lines differently, then steer back to the wonder at the heart of the psalm. Give quiet people time to answer the last question without pressure.

9.open: When you were growing up, who did you go to when something felt unfair?
questions: David begins, "I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart" (v. 1). What would it look like for you to thank God with your whole heart rather than just a part of it?
He promises to "recount all Your wonders" (v. 1). What is one thing God has done, in your life or someone else's, that you could tell this group about?
In verse 4 David says God sits on his throne as a righteous judge. What did it mean for people then to picture God as a judge, and why might that have been good news to the wronged?
Verses 5 and 6 speak openly about enemies being destroyed and even their memory vanishing. How do you react to language that strong in a psalm? What do you think David is feeling?
Verse 9 says, "The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble." When have you needed a place of safety, and what did you reach for first?

Verse 12 says God "does not ignore the cry of the afflicted." If you have ever felt unheard or forgotten, what is it like to read that? Be as honest as you want, including if it is hard to believe right now.
In verse 15 the nations fall "into a pit of their making." Where have you seen people's own schemes or choices turn back on them, and what should we do with that thought about ourselves?
Verse 18 says "the needy will not always be forgotten." Who around us feels forgotten right now, and what could our group do to remember them?
9.life: Pick one person who is overlooked or struggling, a neighbor, coworker or someone in your church. Reach out this week with a call, a note or a meal, and pray for them by name each day.
9.prayer: Thank God that he is a refuge for the oppressed and does not forget the needy. Bring to him anyone who feels unseen, including yourself, and ask him to be their stronghold.
9.tip: The strong language about destroying enemies in verses 5 and 6 and 19 and 20 may make some people uncomfortable. Let them say so. Point out that the psalm is a prayer handed to God, not a plan for revenge, and that it comes from people who were truly wronged and had nowhere else to turn.

10.open: When was the last time you felt like you were waiting a long time for someone to show up or step in?
questions: The psalm opens, "Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?" (v. 1). Does it surprise you that a prayer in the Bible starts with a complaint? What does that tell you about how we can talk to God?
The psalmist describes the wicked man as proud, someone who "boasts in the cravings of his heart" (v. 3). What do you notice about how he thinks and talks, and what does that look like today?

In verse 4 we read, "in all his schemes there is no God." The note on this passage suggests this is less about arguing against God and more about living as if he will never have to answer to anyone. Where do you see that way of living around us?
Verses 8 and 9 picture an ambusher, a lion and a hunter with a net. Why do you think the writer uses such vivid images of the helpless being caught?

The wicked man tells himself, "God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees" (v. 11). Have you ever been afraid that was true, even a little? You can answer as honestly as you like, including if you still wonder about it.
In verse 12 the psalmist prays, "Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand, O God!" Why might it matter that this raw, angry plea is in the Bible rather than a tidied-up one?
Verse 14 says, "You have regarded trouble and grief," and that God is "the helper of the fatherless." What does it mean to you that God sees what the powerful think no one notices?
The psalm ends with "The LORD is King forever and ever" (v. 16), though nothing in the situation has visibly changed. How do you hold on to that kind of trust while you are still waiting?
10.life: Think of one person who is being overlooked or treated unfairly, in your community or in the news. This week, pray for them by name each day, and ask God if there is one small way you could help or stand with them.
10.prayer: Tell God honestly where he seems far away right now. Ask him to defend those who are being hurt, and to strengthen the hearts of the humble, as verse 17 says he will.
10.tip: Verses 2 and 15 ask God to catch and break the wicked, which can feel harsh to some people. Help the group see these as honest cries for justice from people who have been hurt, not permission to take revenge. Also leave room for anyone who feels God is far away to say so without being hurried toward a tidy answer.

11.open: When you were a kid, where did you go when you wanted to hide or feel safe?
questions: David begins, "In the LORD I take refuge" (v. 1). What does taking refuge in someone look like in everyday life, and how is it different from simply feeling calm?
The advice in verse 1 is, "Flee like a bird to your mountain!" Why might that advice sound sensible, and what do you think is behind it: fear, concern, or something else?
Verse 3 asks, "If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?" When have you felt that something solid in your life or in the world was giving way?
Verse 4 says, "The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne." How does picturing God on his throne change the way you see the danger in verses 1 to 3?
We read that "His eyes are watching closely" (v. 4). Does being seen by God feel comforting, uncomfortable, or both for you? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 5 says, "The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked." Why might God test people, and what have hard seasons shown you about what you really trust?
Verse 6 pictures fiery judgment, and verse 5 says God hates "the lover of violence." How do you take that? What does it say about how God feels toward injustice and the people who are hurt by it?
The psalm ends with "The upright will see His face" (v. 7). What does that hope mean to you, especially if you are tired, afraid, or unsure what you believe right now?
11.life: This week, when you feel the urge to run, give up, or panic about something, stop and say verse 1 aloud: "In the LORD I take refuge." Then ask yourself honestly whether this is a moment to stay and trust or a moment to get help or step away, and talk it over with God and one trusted person.
11.prayer: Tell God about one thing that feels like it is shaking right now. Ask him to be your refuge and to help you see clearly when to stand and when to seek safety.
11.tip: Verse 1 can sound like it says never leave a dangerous situation. It does not. Make clear that trusting God and wisely getting out of harm, such as an abusive home or workplace, can go together. Also, verse 6 is hard for many people, so let them say so. Keep the focus on verse 7, that God loves justice, and do not push anyone to feel comfortable about judgment.

12.open: Think of a time someone told you what you wanted to hear instead of what was true. How did you feel when you found out?
questions: David opens with "Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more" (v. 1). Why do you think he goes straight to God instead of first trying to fix things himself?
Verse 2 says people "speak with flattering lips and a double heart." What does flattery look like today, at work, at church, or online, and why is it so easy to fall for?
The proud say, "We own our lips" (v. 4). What do you think it looks like when people believe their words answer to no one?
In verse 5 God says he will "arise" for "the oppressed" and "the needy." What does it tell you about God that he answers for the people with the least power?
Verse 6 says the LORD's words are "flawless, like silver refined in a furnace." When have you found God's word to be solid when other voices let you down?

The psalm ends with "The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men" (v. 8), even after God's promise. If you are honest, how do you hold hope when things around you still look the same? Doubts and mixed feelings are welcome here.
Verse 7 says "You, O LORD, will keep us." What would it look like for us to be people whose words can be trusted, especially toward those with less power?
12.life: This week, pay attention to your own words. Once a day, choose to say the plain, kind, true thing instead of the flattering or convenient one. Also take a few minutes to read a short passage of Scripture slowly.
12.prayer: Bring God the places where you feel surrounded by empty or false words. Thank him that his words are "flawless," and ask him to make your own words honest and trustworthy.
12.tip: Verse 8 may leave people feeling the psalm ends on a downer. Don't rush to tidy it up. Point out that the poet admits the trouble is not over while still trusting God's promise, and let quieter members say where that feels true for them. Also, verses 3 and 5 can be read as a prayer or a promise; you can mention that lightly, but don't spend long on it.

13.open: What is something you have waited a long time for, and how did you pass the time?
questions: David asks "How long, O LORD?" and "Will You forget me forever?" (v. 1). What do you notice about how bluntly he speaks to God? How does that compare to how you talk to God?
He says he must "wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day" (v. 2). What does it feel like when a hard thing does not let up, even for a day?
In verse 1 he feels God is hiding His face. Why might someone who loves God still feel that way? What does it say that this psalm is in the Bible?
In verses 3 and 4 he asks God to "Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death" and fears his enemy will gloat. What is he really asking God for, and what is he afraid of?
Verse 5 begins with "But I have trusted in Your loving devotion." Nothing in the psalm says his situation has changed. What do you make of that turn?

In verse 6 he says, "He has been good to me." Some readers think he is remembering past help, and others think he is speaking of rescue as already done. What difference does it make to you which one it is?
If you wrote your own honest "how long?" prayer tonight, what would it say? You can answer in general terms, or simply say it is hard to pray at all right now.
David sings even before he sees an answer. What helps you hold on to trust, or to a small bit of hope, when things stay hard?
13.life: This week, pray one honest "how long?" to God in your own words, without tidying it up. Then write down one way God has been good to you in the past, and read it over when things feel heavy.
13.prayer: Thank God that we are free to bring Him our real complaints and tears. Ask Him to be near anyone in the group who is waiting or worn down, and to help each person trust His loving devotion.
13.tip: Do not hurry to verse 5 or tidy the sorrow into a happy ending. Let verses 1 to 4 sit and give people room to say that waiting is hard. If someone says to just trust God, remind the group that David voices his pain and his trust in the same prayer.

14.open: When you were a kid, what did you do differently when you thought nobody was watching?
questions: Verse 1 says the fool "says in his heart" that there is no God. The word for fool here means morally reckless, not unintelligent. Why might this psalm place the problem in the heart rather than in the head?
Think of someone who lives as if nobody will ever hold them to account. What do you think changes in how they treat people weaker than themselves?
Verse 2 says the LORD "looks down from heaven" to see "if any seek God." What do you picture when you imagine God looking at us like this? Does it feel comforting, uncomfortable, or something else?

Verse 3 says, "there is no one who does good, not even one." Christians read this in different ways. Some take it as a description of every human being, as Paul does in Romans, and others see it as describing the oppressors in this psalm, set against the righteous poor. Which reading makes more sense to you, and why?
Verse 4 says evildoers "devour my people like bread." What are some modern ways people are used up and brushed aside without anyone seeming to notice?
Verse 5 says the wicked are "overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous." What does it mean to you that God is present with people who are being crushed?

Verse 7 says, "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!" The psalmist longs for God to step in and set things right. What is one situation you wish God would put right, and how honest can you be about the waiting?
Be honest here, there is no wrong answer. Are there times when God feels absent or silent to you, and what do you do with that feeling?
14.life: This week, notice one moment when you are tempted to act as if no one is watching, such as a shortcut, a harsh word, or ignoring someone who needs help. Pause and tell God about it. Then do one small thing for someone with less power or fewer options than you.
14.prayer: Thank God that he sees everyone, including those who are overlooked, and is a shelter to the oppressed. Ask him to show you where you have lived as if he were not there, and to bring rescue to those who are waiting for it.
14.tip: Verse 3 can lead to a heated debate about human nature. Say plainly that Christians read it differently, then bring the group back to what the whole psalm shows: God sees, God shelters the vulnerable, and God is the one people long for to set things right. Don't let the discussion turn into pointing at outsiders as the fools. Invite everyone to see themselves in the psalm.

15.open: Who is someone you would trust with your house key or your secrets, and what makes them that kind of person?
questions: The psalm opens with a question: "O LORD, who may abide in Your tent?" (v. 1). Why do you think people ask this before coming near God? What do you think they were hoping to hear?
Verse 2 says this person "walks with integrity" and "speaks the truth from his heart." What does it look like to be the same person inside as outside? Where is that hardest for you?
Verse 3 mentions "no slander on his tongue." Why might gossip be so easy to take part in, even for people who mean well?
In verse 4 the person "does not revise a costly oath." Can you think of a time when keeping your word cost you something, or when someone kept a promise to you at a cost to themselves?

The person in verse 5 "lends his money without interest" and "refuses a bribe against the innocent." What would these look like in everyday life today, at work, in business or in the way we treat people who are struggling?
Verse 5 ends, "He who does these things will never be shaken." What do you think it means to be unshaken, and how does honest living connect to that kind of steadiness?

Christians read this list in different ways. Some see it as the conditions for being accepted by God, and others see it as the life that grows in people God has already welcomed. How does this list land with you: as a challenge, a comfort, a weight, or something else? Say it as honestly as you can, including if you are not sure what you think.
Which quality in this list do you most want to grow in, and what is one small way that might show up this week?
15.life: Pick one line from verses 2 to 5 and watch for it this week. It might be a word you need to keep, a piece of gossip you can let drop, or a place where you can be more honest. Notice how it goes, and tell God about it at the end of the day.
15.prayer: Thank God that he invites people to live near him. Ask for honest hearts and kept promises, and for grace where we fall short.
15.tip: Some people will hear this list as a checklist they can never pass, and others may feel they pass easily. Say early that Christians read it differently, then keep the group on what each line looks like in daily life. Give quiet or discouraged people room to say it feels heavy without rushing to fix it.

16.open: What is something you have owned or inherited, big or small, that you would never want to give up?
questions: The psalm opens with "Preserve me, O God, for in You I take refuge" (v. 1). When have you felt the need to run to someone for shelter? What did that feel like?
In verse 2 David says, "apart from You I have no good thing." Translators find this line hard, but the idea of needing God is clear. Is that easy or hard for you to say about yourself? Why?
In verse 4 David refuses to join in worshipping other gods, not even speaking their names. What are the quiet rivals to God in our world today, and how do they promise us something?

Verse 5 says, "The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup." In Israel, land was handed out by family, and God himself was called the share of the priests. What does it mean to treat God as your share in life rather than an extra on top of it?
David says, "The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places" (v. 6). When you look at your life, where do you see good gifts? Where is it harder to say that?
Verse 7 says, "even at night my conscience instructs me." What helps you hear God's guidance, and what makes it hard to hear?
David says, "I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken" (v. 8). Think of a time you were shaken. What did you hold onto, and how well did it hold?

Verse 11 speaks of "the path of life" and being filled "with joy in Your presence." If you are unsure about God, or this kind of joy feels far away right now, what would you honestly like to say about that?
16.life: Each evening this week, take two minutes to name one good thing that came to you that day, and thank God for it. Then say out loud verse 8: "I have set the LORD always before me."
16.prayer: Thank God for being a safe place and a lasting gift. Ask him to show each person in the group what they lean on most, and to help them trust him more than anything else.
16.tip: Verses 9 to 11 raise questions about whether David was speaking of his own hope or of Jesus' resurrection. Say plainly that Christians differ, note that the New Testament reads these verses in connection with Jesus, and then bring the group back to the personal trust running through the whole psalm.

17.open: When you were a kid, who did you run to when you got in trouble or got scared?
questions: David opens like someone in a courtroom: "Hear, O LORD, my righteous plea" (v. 1). Have you ever felt that you needed someone to simply listen to your side? What was that like?

In verse 3 David says, "You have tested me and found no evil." Most readers take this as a claim of innocence against these particular charges, not a claim to be perfect. How do you feel reading a prayer like this? Does it sound confident, uncomfortable, or something else?
David says his feet have not slipped (v. 5). What helps you stay steady when people around you are pushing you toward something you don't want to do?

Verse 8 asks God, "Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings." Which picture speaks to you more, being something God protects as carefully as an eye, or being sheltered like a chick under a wing? Why?
In verses 10 to 12 the enemies are proud, hard-hearted, and waiting "like a lion greedy for prey" (v. 12). What does it do for a person to name their fear this honestly in prayer?
In verse 13 David asks God to "confront them" and bring them down. How do you think we should hold a prayer like this alongside Jesus' call to love our enemies? Where does it feel hard?

Verse 15 says, "I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence." What would it mean for you to be truly satisfied in God's presence, and what tends to compete for that place right now?
If you are in a season where God feels distant or you are unsure he is listening, what would you honestly want to say to him, using David's plain words as a pattern?
17.life: Pick one worry or one situation where you feel misjudged or pressured. Each night this week, say it to God in plain words, the way David does, and then pray verse 8 over it: keep me as the apple of your eye.
17.prayer: Ask God to hear the honest cries of everyone in the room, including the ones nobody has said aloud. Thank him that he is a shelter, and ask him to help each person rest in his care this week.
17.tip: Verses 3 to 5 can sound like boasting, and verses 13 and 14 can sound harsh. Do not rush to explain them away. Say that David is claiming innocence on these charges, not perfection, and that the psalm hands his anger to God instead of acting on it. Verse 14 is hard to translate, so note that scholars are unsure of its meaning and move on. Christians also differ on whether verse 15 points to life with God after death or to confidence in God's presence after a night of danger. Say so in one line and let people share what they think.

18.open: Think of a close call or a hard stretch that you can look back on now. What do you remember most about how it felt?
questions: David opens with "The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer" (v. 2). Which of the pictures he uses (rock, fortress, shield, stronghold) speaks most to you right now, and why?
In verses 4 and 5 David feels hunted and trapped, with death closing in like ropes and snares. What was the situation, and how would you describe the kind of trouble that feels like this today?
Verse 6 says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD." What do you do first when you are in trouble? If you have ever called out and felt like nothing happened, what was that like?
Verses 7 to 15 describe God coming down in earthquake, fire and thunder to help one man. What does that picture say about how seriously God takes the cries of his people?
Verse 19 says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me." How does it land to hear that God's help comes from delight and not only duty?

In verses 20 to 24 David talks about his "righteousness" and clean hands. Most readers take this to mean his loyalty to God while he was hunted, not a perfect life. How can we talk about faithfulness to God without pretending to be flawless?
David says, "my God lights up my darkness" (v. 28), and later, "Your gentleness exalts me" (v. 35). Where have you seen God's strength show up as gentleness, or light show up in a dark time?

Some of the victory language is harsh, such as "I ground them as dust in the face of the wind" (v. 42). How do you handle fierce words like these in a prayer or song? Christians also differ on how far the psalm speaks only of David and how far it points ahead to Jesus, so what do you make of verses 49 and 50?
18.life: When something good happens this week, stop and name out loud, or write down, who helped you and what God did in it. Do it at least three times, the way David looks back and says thank you.
18.prayer: Thank God for being a rock and a rescuer. Name one time he brought you through, and ask for trust for anyone in the group who feels trapped right now.
18.tip: Two spots may stall the group: David's claims of being blameless in verses 20 to 24, and the fierce enemy language in verses 37 to 42. Say plainly that David was not perfect and that this is a song of loyalty and thanks, then let people be honest if the harsh words bother them. Keep returning to the heart of the song, which is a rescued person saying thank you.

19.open: What is a place or a moment outdoors, like a sunrise, a night sky or a quiet walk, that made you stop and notice something bigger than yourself?
questions: Verse 1 says, "The heavens declare the glory of God." When you look at the sky, the stars or a sunrise, does it say anything to you? What?
Verse 3 says this speech comes "without speech or language, without a sound to be heard," yet verse 4 says it has gone "into all the earth." What do you think the poet means by a voice with no words?

Christians differ on how much creation alone can tell us about God. Some see it as a real path to knowing him, others as a pointer that needs God's spoken word to make sense. Where do you land, and why?
Many neighboring peoples worshiped the sun, but here it is simply something God made and gave a tent to live in (v. 4). What good things do people today admire or lean on almost like gods?

In verses 7 to 9 the poet gives God's teaching several names, and each one brings a good effect, such as "reviving the soul" and "bringing joy to the heart." Which of these effects do you most need right now?
Verse 10 says God's words are "more precious than gold" and "sweeter than honey." Be honest: does Scripture ever feel that way to you, or does it feel dull or confusing? What makes the difference?
Verse 12 asks, "Who can discern his own errors?" Why might it be hard to see our own blind spots, and who helps you see yours?
The psalm ends with "my Rock and my Redeemer" (v. 14). A redeemer was a close relative who bought back someone who was lost or sold. What does it mean to you that God is described this way?
19.life: Once this week, go outside at sunrise, sunset or after dark and spend five quiet minutes looking at the sky. Then pray verse 14 in your own words: ask God to be pleased with what you say and think.
19.prayer: Thank God for the sky that speaks without words and for his teaching that gives life and light. Ask him to show you the faults you cannot see and to keep you close to him.
19.tip: Questions 3 and 6 may bring out honest doubt or disagreement. Let people say where they are without fixing it. Remind the group that the psalm itself moves from awe to a humble prayer, so there is room for both wonder and questions.

20.open: When you have a big day coming, like a job interview or a trip, what do you do the night before to feel ready?
questions: The psalm opens with the people praying for their king: "May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble" (v. 1). Who in your life is facing a hard day, and how might you pray for them the way these people prayed for their king?

The people ask God to "send you help from the sanctuary" (v. 2). The sanctuary was the place where God was believed to be present among them. Where do you go, or what do you do, when you want to feel close to God?
Verse 5 says, "May we shout for joy at your victory." Why might it matter that the whole community stands behind the king and celebrates with him, instead of leaving him to face it alone?

In verse 4 they pray, "May He give you the desires of your heart and make all your plans succeed." How do you pray about your own plans, and how do you handle it when things don't turn out the way you hoped?

In verse 6 the voice shifts from "we" to "I": "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed." Scholars are not sure who is speaking. Have you ever gone from worry to a settled confidence while praying? What do you think changed?

Verse 7 says, "Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God." Chariots were the strongest weapons of the day. What are the modern chariots people lean on, such as money, status, a good plan, or being in control?
Be honest with the group: when something important is out of your control, what do you actually find yourself leaning on? How much weight can it really hold?
Verse 8 says, "They collapse and fall, but we rise up and stand firm." What would standing firm look like for someone who is tired, afraid, or unsure that God will answer?
20.life: Pick one thing this week that you cannot control, such as a health worry, a decision, or a relationship. Each day, pray Psalm 20:7 over it in your own words, and name the "chariot" you are tempted to lean on instead.
20.prayer: Ask God to answer you "on the day we call" (v. 9). Name one person or situation in the group that needs his help, and pray for it together.
20.tip: Verses 4 and 5 can sound like a promise that God will grant whatever we want, and that can sting for someone whose prayers went unanswered. Gently remind the group that this is a community's prayer for their king, a wish and a request, not a guarantee. Also note that Christians differ on whether the psalm is mainly about Israel's ancient kings or also points ahead to Jesus, the Anointed One, so you can leave room for both without settling it.

21.open: Think of a time something you had hoped and asked for finally came through. How did you celebrate, and who did you tell first?
questions: The psalm opens with the king rejoicing in God's "strength" and "salvation" (v. 1). Why do you think the song gives God the credit instead of the king's army or skill?

Verse 2 says God has given the king his heart's desire and "not withheld the request of his lips." What did this look like for a king of Israel, and what do you do with that verse when your own prayers feel unanswered?
In verse 3 God "placed on his head a crown of pure gold." What does it tell you about God that he is pictured giving gifts to the king, not just receiving honor?
Verse 7 says "the king trusts in the LORD" and "will not be shaken." Where do you feel shaken right now, and what would trusting look like there?

Verse 4 speaks of "length of days, forever and ever." Christians read this differently: some see it as about Israel's king, and others see it as pointing to Jesus. How does each reading shape the way you hear it?

Verses 8 to 12 are hard to read, with fire and the wiping out of enemies' families. Ancient wars were brutal, and these words come from that world. What stirs in you as you read them, and what questions would you want to ask God about them?

Verse 11 says "the schemes they devise will not prevail." What does it mean for you that God cares about justice when people do harm? How might that hope help you leave things in his hands instead of seeking revenge?
The psalm ends with the people promising to "sing and praise Your power" (v. 13). What is one way you could thank God for something he has done, even if you are not sure how you feel about him today?
21.life: Each day this week, name one thing you are thankful God has done, big or small, and say it out loud or write it down. If you are not sure he did it, say so honestly and thank him anyway for what you can.
21.prayer: Thank God for the ways he has answered prayer, and be honest about the prayers still waiting. Ask him to help you trust him so that you are not shaken.
21.tip: Verses 8 to 12 will likely trouble people, and some may want to skip them or defend them quickly. Don't rush. Say that the language is harsh, that it comes from ancient warfare, and that it is fine to feel uneasy. Then point back to verse 7 and verse 13, where the focus is trusting God and giving him the credit.

22.open: What is something you waited a long time for, and how did the waiting feel?
questions: The psalm opens, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (v. 1). He feels abandoned, yet he still says "my God." What do you make of praying that way?

In verses 3 to 5 he remembers that "our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them" (v. 4). Why do you think he turns to memory when God feels far away? What helps you hold on in a dry season?
The mockers say, "He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him" (v. 8). Where have you heard words like these, from other people or from your own head?

He says, "I am poured out like water" (v. 14) and describes bones, heart and mouth giving out. Why might the Bible include such raw prayers? What does that tell us about what we are allowed to bring to God?

Jesus cried the words of verse 1 from the cross, and the Gospels echo other parts of this psalm. Christians differ on whether the psalm directly predicts Jesus or is a real sufferer's lament that Jesus made his own. Either way, what does it mean to you that Jesus prayed these words?
Verse 24 says God "has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted." If you find that hard to believe right now, say so honestly. What would you need to see or hear for it to feel true?
The praise in verses 27 to 31 grows to include all nations and "a people yet unborn" (v. 31). Who passed their faith to you, and who might you pass something on to?
22.life: Write a short prayer this week with two parts: one honest complaint, as blunt as the psalm, and one thing you remember God doing in the past. Pray it out loud at least once.
22.prayer: Thank God that you can bring your real questions and pain to him without pretending. Pray for anyone in the group who feels far from God right now.
22.tip: Don't rush past verses 1 to 21 to get to the praise. Let the group sit with the pain first. If someone asks about verse 16, say plainly that the Hebrew is uncertain and translations differ, then bring the focus back to the whole psalm.

23.open: Who is someone who made you feel looked after when you were young, and what did they do?
questions: David begins, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (v. 1). What do you think a shepherd does for a sheep, and why might David choose that picture of God?
Verse 2 speaks of "green pastures" and "quiet waters." Sheep don't rest well when they are afraid or hungry. What helps you actually rest, and what gets in the way?
Verse 3 says, "He restores my soul." What does it feel like when you are worn out inside, and what has helped you recover?
The shepherd guides "for the sake of His name" (v. 3), which means because of who God is, not because the sheep has earned it. How does that sit with you? Is it easy or hard to believe?

Verse 4 says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." Notice that David doesn't say the valley disappears. When has the presence of someone, or of God, mattered more to you than having the problem solved?
Some days God can feel far away, even when we want to trust him. If you are in that place, or have been, what would you honestly say about it tonight?
In verse 5 God sets a table "in the presence of my enemies." What do you make of being cared for while the trouble is still around?
Verse 6 says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life." What would change if you pictured goodness and mercy chasing after you instead of trailing behind?
23.life: Each morning this week, read verse 1 aloud and name one thing you need. Then name one way you have already been provided for. Share with someone in the group how it went.
23.prayer: Thank God for being a shepherd who stays close in the dark valleys. Invite each person to name one place where they need to be led, restored or comforted this week.
23.tip: This psalm is often read at funerals, so someone may be carrying fresh grief. Let people speak or stay quiet without hurrying to comfort. On verse 6, say plainly that Christians differ on whether it first pointed to life after death or to closeness with God in this life, and many read it as both. Then move on.

24.open: If you were invited to meet someone very important, like a president or a hero of yours, how would you get ready?
questions: The psalm begins, "The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof" (v. 1). What changes in how you see your home, your work or your money if everything really belongs to God?

Verse 2 says God "has founded it upon the seas." Why might a writer in ancient Israel, where the sea stood for chaos and danger, find that picture comforting? What feels unsteady in your life that you could picture resting on something firm?

Verse 3 asks, "Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?" Have you ever felt that you did not belong in a church, a prayer or a conversation about God? What made you feel that way?

The answer is "clean hands and a pure heart" (v. 4). Hands stand for what we do and the heart for why we do it. Can someone look clean on the outside while their motives are not? Which matters more to you in someone you trust?
The psalm also mentions someone who "does not lift up his soul to an idol or swear deceitfully" (v. 4). What are some modern things that ask for our trust or our deepest loyalty?

Verse 5 says such a person will "receive blessing from the LORD" from "the God of his salvation." Notice that the blessing is received, not earned. How does that shape the way you read the demands of verse 4? And if you honestly feel you could never qualify, what do you do with that?
In verses 7 to 10 the gates are told to lift up so "the King of Glory may enter." What would it look like for you to open a door in your own life for God this week?
Verse 6 describes people who "seek Your face." What does seeking God look like on an ordinary day for you, and what makes it hard? It is fine to answer with doubts or with how little you feel you do.
24.life: Pick one room or space you use every day, like your kitchen, car or desk. Each time you walk into it this week, pause for a moment and quietly remember that it belongs to the Lord, along with everything in it. Then ask God to be welcome there.
24.prayer: Thank God that the earth and everyone in it belongs to him. Ask him for honest hands and a sincere heart, and for the courage to seek his face even when you feel unsure.
24.tip: Verses 3 and 4 can sound like a test nobody could pass, and some people will quietly feel shut out. Point to verse 5, where the blessing is something God gives, and let people say honestly where they feel the weight. Also, Christians differ on whether verses 7 to 10 are mainly about God entering ancient Jerusalem or point ahead to Christ. Name that in one line and keep moving.

25.open: Think of a time you were lost, on a road trip or in a new place. What helped you find your way?
questions: The psalm opens with "To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul" (v. 1). What does it look like for you to hand your whole self to God at the start of a hard day?
The writer asks, "Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths" (v. 4). Where in your life right now do you most need direction?
Verse 5 says, "all day long I wait for You." What is hard about waiting on God, and what helps you keep waiting?
In verse 7 the writer prays, "Remember not the sins of my youth." What do you think it means to ask God to remember us by his "loving devotion" instead of our record?
Verse 8 says God is "good and upright" and so "shows sinners the way." How does it change things to hear that God teaches people who have gone wrong, not only people who have it together?
Verse 11 says, "forgive my iniquity, for it is great." The writer does not shrink the wrong. Why might being honest about our failures be easier when we trust God's character?

In verse 16 the writer says, "I am lonely and afflicted." What do you make of a prayer this raw being in the Bible? If you have felt lonely or unsure God is listening, how would you say so honestly here?

Verse 14 says, "The LORD confides in those who fear Him." What do you think it means to be close enough to God that he shares his mind with you, and what does that closeness look like in everyday life?
25.life: Pray verse 4 each morning this week: "Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths." At the end of each day, note one moment where you sensed direction, even a small one.
25.prayer: Thank God that he is good and teaches people who have gone wrong. Ask him to guide each person in the group, to forgive what they carry from the past, and to be near anyone who feels lonely.
25.tip: Verses 3 and 19 to 21 talk about enemies and being kept from shame, and some may feel uneasy with that or wonder if it sounds self-righteous. Point out that the writer also confesses great sin in verse 11, and invite people to see the psalm as honest prayer from someone who needs both protection and mercy. Also be ready for someone who carries heavy regret from the past; let verse 7 do the work and do not rush to fix it.

26.open: Who is someone you trust enough to tell you the honest truth about yourself, even when it stings?
questions: The writer opens with "Vindicate me, O LORD!" (v. 1). What do you think might be going on in this person's life to make them pray this way?
In verse 2 the writer says, "Test me, O LORD, and try me; examine my heart and mind." What would make that prayer feel safe to you, and what would make it frightening?
The writer says, "I have walked with integrity" (v. 1). Most readers take this to mean wholehearted loyalty to God, not a perfect record. How would you describe integrity in your own words?
Verse 3 says, "Your loving devotion is before my eyes." How might keeping God's faithful love in view change the way a person lives day to day?

In verses 4 and 5 the writer says they do not sit with deceitful people or hypocrites. In that world, sitting with someone meant sharing in their plans. Who influences your choices most, and how do you decide whom to stay close to?
The writer says, "I love the house where You dwell" (v. 8). Where or when do you feel closest to God, and what helps you get there?
Even after claiming integrity, the writer prays, "redeem me and be merciful to me" (v. 11). Why might someone ask for both a clear name and mercy in the same breath?
If you are honest, does this psalm feel encouraging, distant or a bit uncomfortable to you right now? What is behind that?
26.life: This week, take five quiet minutes and pray verse 2 slowly: "examine my heart and mind." Then listen. Write down anything that comes to mind, and bring it back to God, trusting his mercy as much as his judgment.
26.prayer: Ask God to show you your own heart honestly and gently. Thank him that his "loving devotion" (v. 3) is the ground you stand on, and ask for mercy where you fall short.
26.tip: Some will hear the writer's claims of innocence as proud or unrealistic, and Christians do read them differently. Some see an honest person protesting a specific false charge, others hear the voice of Jesus, the one truly innocent person. Say so plainly, then steer toward the writer's openness before God. Be gentle with anyone who feels they could never pray this way.

27.open: When you were a kid, who or what did you run to when you were scared?
questions: David begins, "The LORD is my light and my salvation" (v. 1). What does it mean to you to call God your light, and when have you most needed light in your life?
He says, "Though an army encamps around me, my heart will not fear" (v. 3). What is the closest thing to an army in your life right now, and how does your heart actually feel about it?
In verse 4 David names "One thing" he wants most: to "gaze on the beauty of the LORD." If you had to name your one thing today, honestly, what would it be?
Verse 5 says that in the day of trouble God "will hide me in His shelter." What does being sheltered by God look like in real life? Where have you seen it, or where do you wish you could?

The mood changes at verse 7, and David cries, "Hear, O LORD, my voice when I call." Why might a person who sounded so confident suddenly sound so desperate? What does that say about how faith and fear can live side by side?
David prays, "Hide not Your face from me" (v. 9). Have you ever felt that God was distant or silent? You can answer honestly here, including if you are not sure what you believe.
Verse 10 says, "Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me." Who has let you down, and how might this verse speak to that hurt?
The psalm ends with "Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous" (v. 14). What are you waiting on right now, and what would courage look like while you wait?
27.life: Pick one fear or worry that keeps coming back this week. Each time it shows up, say verse 1 out loud or in your head, then tell God one honest sentence about how you feel.
27.prayer: Thank God that he is light and a safe place. Invite people to name one thing they are waiting on, and ask for strength and courage to wait.
27.tip: The shift from confidence in verses 1 to 6 to pleading in verses 7 to 14 may confuse people, and some may feel guilty that their own faith is not as steady. Note that scholars differ on whether this was one poem or two, then point out that either way the Bible lets trust and fear sit in the same prayer.

28.open: Think of a time you called or texted someone and waited a long time for a reply. What did the waiting feel like?
questions: David begins, "To You, O LORD, I call; be not deaf to me, O my Rock" (v. 1). What does it say about him that he calls God a Rock, and what would you call God when you are in need?
He fears that "if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit" (v. 1). Why would God's silence feel so frightening to him?
Verse 3 describes people who "speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts." What does that kind of two-faced behavior look like today, and why might it be so painful to be near?

In verses 4 and 5 David asks God to "repay them according to their deeds." Christians read this differently: some see a fair plea for justice, others an honest but limited human wish. How do you hear it, and what do you do with anger when you have been wronged?
In verse 6 the mood turns: "Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy." The psalm does not say what changed. What do you make of that sudden shift?
Verse 7 says, "The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped." Which fits your life right now, strength to keep going or protection from something, and why?
When you have asked for help and heard nothing back, what kept you hoping, or what made you stop? Be as honest as you like, there is room in this psalm for both.
David ends by praying beyond himself: "Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever" (v. 9). Who is someone you could carry in prayer this week?
28.life: Pick one prayer you have been waiting on. This week, pray it out loud in the plain way David does, asking God to hear you. Then, like verse 9, add a prayer for one other person or group.
28.prayer: Ask God to hear us when we call, and to be our strength and shield. Make room for anyone who is waiting on an answer, and thank God for the ways he has already helped.
28.tip: Verses 4 and 5 may stir up strong reactions, some uneasy about the payback, others glad for it. Say plainly that Christians read it differently, then steer back to the honesty of the prayer: David brings his anger to God instead of acting on it. Also leave space for those who feel silence from God, and do not rush them to the thankful ending.

29.open: What is the most impressive storm, or other force of nature, you have ever seen up close?
questions: The psalm opens by telling heavenly beings to "ascribe to the LORD glory and strength" (v. 1). What do you think it means to give someone glory, and how is that different from just admiring them?
Verse 2 says to "worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness." When has something beautiful or awe-inspiring made you want to worship, or at least go quiet?
The phrase "the voice of the LORD" comes back again and again, seven times in all. Why might the poet hear a thunderstorm as God speaking? What does that repetition do to you as you read it?

In verses 5 to 9 the storm splits cedars, shakes mountains and strips forests bare. Scholars think this poem borrowed the language people used for a storm god, Baal, and gave all that power to the LORD alone. What does it mean to say the power in nature belongs to God and not to nature itself?

Verse 9 says "in His temple all cry" out in praise while the storm rages outside. Why might praise come easier from inside a safe place? What is the safest place you have found to bring your awe, or your fear, to God?
Verse 10 says "the LORD sits enthroned over the flood." Where do you feel flooded right now, by work, family, news or worry? What changes, if anything, when you picture God as King above it?

The psalm ends quietly: "the LORD gives His people strength; the LORD blesses His people with peace" (v. 11). The same power that breaks cedars is offered as strength and peace. Is that hard to believe, or easy? Be honest about where you are.
29.life: This week, take five minutes during a storm, a windy evening, or just a walk outside. Read Psalm 29 slowly, out loud if you can, and tell God one thing you notice about him from what you see.
29.prayer: Praise God for his power and his glory. Ask him to give strength and peace to anyone in the group who is feeling flooded right now.
29.tip: Some people will feel uneasy that God's voice is pictured in such violent images, and others will wonder who the "heavenly beings" are. Most readers take them to be angels, though some older readers thought of earthly kings. Say that plainly, then steer back to the main point: the God of the storm is the same God who offers peace in verse 11.

30.open: Think of a time you were really relieved after a scare, like a medical result, a lost wallet or a close call. What did you do first?
questions: The psalm begins, "I will exalt You, O LORD, for You have lifted me up" (v. 1). Who or what has lifted you up at some point, and how did you thank them?
The singer says, "I cried to You for help, and You healed me" (v. 2). What do you think it meant for him to cry out like that, and what might it look like for us today?
Verse 5 says, "Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning." Have you lived through a long night? What did it feel like while you were in it?
Some nights feel like they never end. If the morning in verse 5 has not come for you yet, what would you want to say to God about that?
In verse 6 he says, "I will never be shaken." When life is going well, what makes it easy to forget how much we depend on God?
In verse 7, "When You hid Your face, I was dismayed." What does it feel like when God seems far away, and what do you do in those times?
In verses 8 to 10 he pleads and even argues with God. Does it surprise you that the Bible lets someone speak to God this way? Why or why not?
He ends with "my heart may sing Your praises and not be silent" (v. 12). What is one thing from your own story that you could tell someone else about God's help?
30.life: Write down one hard season God has brought you through, and one thing you are thankful for from it. This week, tell one person about it, or simply thank God for it out loud.
30.prayer: Thank God for the times he has lifted you up and carried you through. Ask him to keep you humble when life is easy and near when it is hard, and pray for anyone in the group who is in a long night right now.
30.tip: Verse 5 can sting for someone still in a hard season, so don't hurry past it. Let people say that the morning hasn't come yet, and point out that the psalmist also wept, begged and felt God's absence before he sang.

31.open: When you have a really bad day, what is the first place or person you run to?
questions: David opens with "In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge" (v. 1) and calls God "my rock and my fortress" (v. 3). Which of those pictures of safety speaks to you most, and why?
In verse 5 he says, "Into Your hands I commit my spirit." What do you think it means to hand your whole life over to God? What makes that hard?
Verse 6 says some people cling to "worthless idols." When life feels out of control, what do people today tend to cling to instead of God?

In verses 9 to 13 David says his eyes fail from sorrow, friends flee from him, and he is "like a broken vessel" (v. 12). What do you notice about how honest he is with God? How does that compare with how we pray?
Verse 10 can be read as weakness caused by his own wrongdoing or simply by his suffering, and translations differ. How might it change the way you read the psalm to take it each way?

In the middle of all this he says, "But I trust in You, O LORD" (v. 14), and then "My times are in Your hands" (v. 15). What do you think it means that your times, not just your problems, are in God's hands?

In verse 22 David admits that in his alarm he thought he was cut off from God's sight. Then he says God heard his plea for mercy. Has there been a time you felt unseen by God? You can answer honestly, even if you still feel that way.
The psalm ends by telling others, "Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD" (v. 24). Who around you needs that encouragement, and what could you say or do?
31.life: Pick one worry that is weighing on you this week. Each morning, say verse 15 out loud, "My times are in Your hands," and name that worry to God in your own words. Then send an encouraging message to someone who is struggling.
31.prayer: Thank God that he sees our distress and hears us when we call. Invite people to name, silently or out loud, one thing they want to place in his hands tonight.
31.tip: Verses 17 and 18 ask for enemies to be shamed and silenced, which can feel harsh. Let people say so. Point out that David brings his anger to God instead of acting on it, and that Christians read these prayers in different ways. Also note that the church has long linked verse 5 to Jesus, but Christians differ on whether it was written as prophecy or was David's own prayer that Jesus later borrowed. Name that in a sentence and keep the focus on trust.

32.open: Have you ever put off telling someone something you knew you needed to say? How did you feel once it was finally out?
questions: The psalm opens with "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered" (v. 1). Why do you think David begins with the happiness of forgiveness before he tells the story behind it?
Verse 2 describes someone "in whose spirit there is no deceit." What do you think it looks like to be that honest with God, and with ourselves?
David says, "When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long" (v. 3). What do you think hiding something does to a person, in body, mind or relationships?
He felt that God's "hand was heavy" on him (v. 4). What do you make of that? Is it hard to picture God that way, or does it ring true to you?
In verse 5 David says he "did not hide my iniquity," and "You forgave the guilt of my sin." What stands out to you about how quickly the forgiveness comes after the confession?
Maybe confessing feels risky, or you aren't sure God wants to hear it. What makes it hard for you to say things out loud to God? Be as honest as you like.
God is called "my hiding place" in verse 7, one who protects from trouble. When have you needed somewhere safe to run, and what did you run to?
Verse 9 warns against being like a horse or mule that has to be controlled "with bit and bridle." What do you think it means to come to God willingly instead of being dragged?
32.life: This week, set aside five quiet minutes and tell God honestly about one thing you have been avoiding or hiding. If it involves another person, think about whether there is a safe step toward making it right.
32.prayer: Thank God that he forgives and that we can come to him without pretending. Ask for the honesty to name what we have been carrying, and for the gladness that follows.
32.tip: Confession can feel heavy, and some people may hear verses 3 and 4 as proof that God is angry with them. Gently point the group to verses 1 and 5, where the weight is lifted as soon as David speaks. Don't ask anyone to share personal sins aloud. Let people answer at whatever depth they choose.

33.open: What is a song that always lifts your mood, and why?
questions: The psalm opens with a call to "Sing to Him a new song" (v. 3). What might a new song of thanks look like for you right now, based on something recent in your life?
Verse 4 says "the word of the LORD is upright, and all His work is trustworthy." Why do you think the psalmist starts with God's reliability as a reason to praise?
Verse 5 says "the earth is full of His loving devotion." Where have you seen signs of that kindness, even in an ordinary week?
Verse 9 says "He spoke, and it came to be." What does it do to you to think of the stars and seas as made by God's word? Does it feel comforting, distant, or something else?
Verse 10 says God "frustrates the plans of the nations." How do you tend to feel when you watch the news and see the plans of powerful people? How might this verse change that?
Verses 16 and 17 say armies, strength and horses cannot save. What do people today lean on in the same way, like money, status, health or being in control?

Verse 18 says God's eyes are "on those whose hope is in His loving devotion." If hope feels thin for you lately, what would you honestly say about it? What is it like to be seen by God when you are unsure?
The psalm ends with "Our soul waits for the LORD" (v. 20). Where are you waiting right now, and what makes waiting hard?
33.life: Pick one thing you usually lean on to feel safe. This week, each time you reach for it, pause and say verse 22 as a short prayer: "May Your loving devotion rest on us, O LORD, as we put our hope in You."
33.prayer: Praise God for making the world by his word and for watching over every person. Ask him to help you rest your hope in his steady love, and pray for anyone in the group who is waiting on something hard.
33.tip: Verses 18 and 19 speak of rescue from death and famine, and someone may be thinking of a loved one who was not rescued. Do not rush to explain it. Let the group say that this is hard, and point to the psalm's closing note of waiting together (v. 20), which admits that hope and waiting go hand in hand.

34.open: Think of a time you were really relieved after something scary or stressful. What was it, and who did you tell first?
questions: The singer says, "I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears" (v. 4). Notice he says fears, not only dangers. What fears do people your age or stage of life carry around quietly?
The heading ties this psalm to a time David pretended to be insane to escape a king. What does it tell you that a song of praise came out of such a messy, undignified moment?
In verse 3 he says, "Magnify the LORD with me." Why do you think he invites others in, instead of just thanking God on his own?
Verse 8 says, "Taste and see that the LORD is good." What would it look like to try that out for yourself, and what makes that easy or hard right now?

Verse 10 says "those who seek the LORD lack no good thing," yet verse 19 admits "many are the afflictions of the righteous." Christians read these promises in different ways, some as what to expect now and some as pointing mainly to a final rescue. How do you hold the two verses together?
Verses 13 and 14 say to keep your tongue from evil, turn from evil, and "seek peace and pursue it." Which of these is hardest for you in an ordinary week, and why?
Verse 18 says, "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted." Have you ever felt close to God in a low time, or far from him? Say it honestly, either answer is welcome here.
Think back to a hard time you came through. What do you think actually carried you, and how does that sit alongside what this psalm says about God?
34.life: Each day this week, write down one sentence of thanks for something God has done or helped with, however small. At the end of the week, share one with a friend, as David invites others to join him.
34.prayer: Thank God that he is "near to the brokenhearted." Ask him to be close to anyone in the group who is carrying fear or sadness tonight, and to help each person taste and see his goodness.
34.tip: Verses 10 and 19 can sting for someone who has prayed and still lost a job, a loved one or their health. Do not rush to explain it away. Name that Christians read these promises differently, let people be honest about their struggles, and point back to verse 18, where God is close in the pain.

35.open: Have you ever been blamed for something you didn't do? What did you want to say in that moment?
questions: David asks God to "Take up Your shield and buckler" and come to his aid (v. 2). What does it say about how he sees God that he pictures him as a fighter on his side?
In verse 3 David asks God to tell his soul that God is his salvation. Why might hearing that matter as much as being rescued? When do you most need to hear it?
David says his enemies "laid their net for me" and "dug a pit for my soul" "without cause" (v. 7). What does this tell us about what he is facing, and why does it hurt?
In verses 13 and 14, David says he fasted and grieved for these people when they were ill. Then he says, "They repay me evil for good" (v. 12). Why does betrayal by someone you cared for cut so deep?
David says that when he stumbled, "they assembled in glee" (v. 15). Why can it be so painful when people enjoy someone else's trouble? Have you seen that, or felt it?

David asks, "How long, O Lord, will You look on?" (v. 17), and later, "be not silent" (v. 22). Have you ever felt that God was watching and not acting? How did you handle it, or how are you handling it now?

Some of David's prayers ask for his enemies to be shamed and ruined (vv. 4 to 8). Christians read these differently: as prophecy of God's justice, as honest anger handed to God, or as something Jesus' call to love enemies goes beyond. How do you read them, and what do you do with your own anger?
David ends by promising to speak of God's righteousness "all day long" (v. 28). What would it look like to praise God while a hard situation is still unresolved?
35.life: Think of one person who has hurt or wronged you. This week, tell God plainly how you feel, using your own words, the way David does. Then ask God to be the one who judges, and ask for help with your next step toward them.
