35.prayer: Thank God that we can bring him our hurt and anger honestly. Pray for anyone in the group who feels betrayed or falsely accused, and ask God to be their defender and to assure them that he is their salvation.
35.tip: Verses 4 to 8 may make some people uncomfortable, and others may feel relieved to see anger in the Bible. Don't rush to fix it. Say plainly that Christians read these prayers differently, let people share how they respond, and keep returning to the main point: David takes his anger to God instead of taking revenge himself.

36.open: What is a place where you have felt completely welcome, like you could just sit down and be yourself?
questions: David says the wicked man has "no fear of God before his eyes" (v. 1). What do you think it means to take God seriously, and how can you tell when someone has stopped?
Verse 2 says his eyes are "too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." How does a person get to the point where they cannot see their own wrongs? Where might that start small?
Verse 4 says "even on his bed he plots wickedness." Why might the quiet hours of the night be when our thoughts go to their best or their worst?
In verses 5 and 6 David reaches for the sky, the clouds, the mountains and the deep sea to describe God. Which of those pictures speaks to you most right now, and why?
Verse 7 says people "take refuge in the shadow of Your wings." When have you needed a place of shelter, and what did you run to? Is it fair to say that God has felt close or far lately?
Verses 8 and 9 talk about feasting, a river of delights and a fountain of life. What do they suggest about how God wants us to live, compared with a life of rules and duty?
Verse 9 says "in Your light we see light." Can you think of a time when something finally made sense to you, and what helped you see it?
Verse 11 is a real prayer to be kept safe from the proud and the wicked. What would it look like to pray that honestly, without pretending you are not afraid?
36.life: Psalm 36 puts the worst of people beside the best of God. This week, each time you read or hear bad news, stop for a moment and say verse 5 aloud or in your head: "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens."
36.prayer: Thank God that his love and faithfulness are bigger than anything we can measure. Ask him to keep you under his wings, and to show you any place where you have stopped seeing your own sin.
36.tip: The first four verses can drag the group into talking about how bad other people are. Gently bring it back by asking where we might see a small version of this in ourselves, then move on to verses 5 to 9 so the group ends on God's love rather than on the wicked.

37.open: When you were a kid, what did you think was most unfair, and do you still feel the same about it?
questions: The psalm opens with "Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong" (v. 1). When did you last feel that pull, watching someone get ahead by doing wrong?
Verse 2 says the wicked "wither quickly like grass." Why do you think the writer uses a picture like this instead of just giving a rule?

Verse 4 says, "Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart." Some hear that as a promise that God hands over whatever we want. What do you think it means, and what changes when delight comes first?

Verse 5 says, "Commit your way to the LORD." The word behind this can be read as rolling your way onto him, like setting down a heavy load. What is one thing you keep carrying that you could try setting down?
Verse 7 says, "Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him." What makes waiting hard for you, and what has helped you wait, even a little?
Verse 8 says anger "can only bring harm." How have you seen anger toward someone else end up hurting the person who carries it?

In verse 25 the writer says, "never have I seen the righteous abandoned." Many of us have seen good people suffer. Christians read the psalm's promises differently: some see how life usually goes, others see a final setting right of things beyond this life. How do you hold this verse alongside what you have seen? Honest doubt is welcome here.
Verse 24 says, "Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand." When have you stumbled and found something or someone holding you up?
37.life: Think of one person whose success or behavior has been eating at you. This week, each time they come to mind, pray verse 7 in your own words: be still, and hand the matter to God. If there is one good thing you can do for someone else that day, do it.
37.prayer: Be honest with God about who or what you envy or are angry about. Ask him to take that weight and to help you trust him and do good while you wait.
37.tip: Verses 4 and 25 can sound like a guarantee of an easy life, and someone in the room may have lived the opposite. Don't defend the verses too quickly. Name that Job and Psalm 73 wrestle with the same question, let people say what they have seen, and keep the focus on the psalm's call to trust God and not be consumed by anger.

38.open: When you were a kid and knew you had done something wrong, what did you do: hide, confess right away, or hope nobody noticed?
questions: David begins, "O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath" (v. 1). What does it tell you that he prays this to God rather than running from him?
In verse 4 he says, "my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear." What does guilt feel like when it piles up? Where have you felt that weight?

Verses 5 to 8 describe a body and spirit breaking down. Scholars are not sure if this is a real illness, a picture of inner pain, or both. Why might it matter less than the fact that he says it all out loud to God?
Verse 9 says, "my groaning is not hidden from You." When you are in a hard place, does it comfort you or unsettle you to know God already sees it? Be honest, whichever it is.
Verse 11 says friends and family "stand at a distance." Have you ever felt avoided in a hard season, or been the one who kept your distance? What would have helped?

In verses 13 and 14 David stays silent before those who attack him, and then says, "I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer" (v. 15). When is staying quiet wise, and what makes it hard to trust God to speak for you?

In verse 18 he says, "I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin," yet in verse 19 he says his enemies hate him "without reason." How can someone be honest about their own failures without accepting every accusation?
The psalm ends with no relief yet, only "Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior" (v. 22). What do you make of a prayer that ends still waiting? Where are you waiting right now?
38.life: This week, take five quiet minutes and tell God plainly what is weighing on you, the way David does, without cleaning it up. If it helps, write it down first. Then pray verse 22 as your last line.
38.prayer: Thank God that he sees every groan and that nothing is hidden from him. Ask for honesty about what weighs on us, and for his nearness while we wait for help.
38.tip: Christians differ on whether this psalm shows illness can be God's direct punishment for sin, or is one person's honest experience that should not become a rule. Say so in a line, then keep the group on what David does: he brings everything to God. Be careful that no one in the room hears that their own suffering must be their fault.

39.open: When you have had a rough day, do you tend to talk it out, keep it to yourself, or something in between?
questions: David says, "I will guard my mouth with a muzzle as long as the wicked are present" (v. 1). Why might he have decided to stay quiet? When have you kept something in for a reason like that?
Verse 3 says, "My heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned." What happens inside you when you hold in pain or frustration for a long time?

Look at what happens next: "Then I spoke with my tongue" (v. 3). Instead of spilling it to the people around him, he speaks to God. Some readers see this as breaking his vow and others see it as a healthy turn to honest prayer. How do you see it?
David calls a lifetime "as nothing before You" and says each person is "but a breath" (v. 5). How does it feel to read that: heavy, freeing, uncomfortable, or something else?

In verse 6 David says people hurry about in vain and pile up riches without knowing who will end up with them. What do people around us work hardest for, and how might remembering life is short change that?

In verse 7 David says, "My hope is in You." He says it right in the middle of his complaint. What does it look like to hope in God when things are still hard? If you are not sure you can say that, what honest words could you use instead?
David calls himself "a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers" (v. 12). What do you think it means to be a guest in this world? Does that thought comfort you or unsettle you?
The psalm ends with a blunt plea and no neat answer (v. 13). Why do you think the Bible includes prayers that end without resolution? What do they give us permission to do?
39.life: Pick one thing you have been holding in this week, a worry, a hurt, or a frustration, and say it to God in plain words, the way David does. Do it once a day for a few minutes, and let it be unpolished.
39.prayer: Ask God to make room in your group for honest words. Pray for anyone who is carrying something quietly, and ask God to teach each of you to number your days with hope in him.
39.tip: Verses 10 and 13 can sound harsh, and David links his suffering to God's hand and to his own wrongdoing. Be careful not to suggest that every hardship is a punishment. Name that David felt this way as he prayed, keep the focus on his honesty before God, and let people say how the psalm sits with them even if it does not sit well.

40.open: Tell us about a time you had to wait a long time for something, and how you handled it.
questions: David says, "I waited patiently for the LORD" (v. 1). What does waiting on God look like for you right now, and is it patient or restless?
He describes being lifted "from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay" (v. 2). What picture would you use for a hard time you have been through, and what helped you get out?
Verse 3 says God "put a new song in my mouth." Why might God's rescue of one person lead others to trust him too?
In verse 6 David says God did not desire sacrifice and offering, but "my ears You have opened." What do you think it means that God wants a listening heart more than religious activity?
Verse 8 says, "Your law is within my heart." What is the difference between knowing what God asks and having it written on your heart?
In verses 9 and 10 David says he has not "concealed" God's faithfulness from the gathered community. What helps you speak honestly about what God has done, and what holds you back?

After all the praise, verse 12 says "evils without number surround me" and his "heart has failed within me." Have you ever come through something hard only to face trouble again? Did remembering the first time make the second easier or harder?

The psalm ends with "But I am poor and needy" and "do not delay" (v. 17). What do you make of a prayer that ends still waiting? What would you want to say to God if you were honest tonight, even if you are not sure he is listening?
40.life: Think of one time God helped you or someone you know. This week, tell one person that story in a few sentences. If you are in a hard stretch now, write your own short prayer like verse 17 and say it each day.
40.prayer: Thank God for the times he has lifted you up and set your feet on solid ground. Ask him to help anyone in the group who is still waiting or feels worn down, and to hold them until help comes.
40.tip: The psalm swings from joyful praise to desperate pleading, and some people feel uneasy that David can do both. Say plainly that faith and need can sit side by side. Also, Christians differ on whether verses 6 to 8 are mainly David's own words that later pointed to Jesus, or a prophecy in Jesus' voice as Hebrews applies them. Name it in a line and move on, and keep the group on the central question of trusting God while still waiting.

41.open: Think of a time you were sick or laid up. Who showed up for you, and what did they do that helped?
questions: The psalm begins, "Blessed is the one who cares for the poor" (v. 1). Who has cared for you when you were weak, and what did that care look like?
Verse 3 says the LORD "will sustain him on his bed of illness." What do you think it means to be sustained by God when you are not healed yet?

In verse 4 David prays, "heal me, for I have sinned against You." People then often linked sickness with wrongdoing. How would you separate the two today, and when does it help to ask God honestly about both?
His enemies ask, "When will he die and be forgotten?" (v. 5), and a visitor "spreads it abroad" (v. 6). Why can gossip hurt so much when a person is already down?
Verse 9 says, "Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me." Why does a betrayal by a friend cut deeper than an attack by an enemy?
In verse 10 David asks to be raised up "that I may repay them." Some read that as personal revenge and others as a king seeking justice. What do you make of such a blunt prayer being in the Bible?
In verse 11 David says, "By this I know that You delight in me." What do you lean on when you want to know God is on your side, especially when life is hard or God feels quiet?
If you are in a season of pain, doubt or loneliness, what would you honestly like to say to God right now, even if it is only that you don't know what to say?
41.life: Choose one person who is sick, worn down or lonely and care for them in a practical way this week: a meal, a visit, a call or a ride. Do it quietly, and keep their private struggles private.
41.prayer: Thank God that he upholds us in our weakness. Pray for anyone who is ill or has been let down by a friend, and ask for the grace to be faithful to people when they are at their lowest.
41.tip: Verse 9 may lead people to share painful stories of betrayal, and verse 10 may stir up talk of revenge. Let people speak without rushing to fix anything. Note in one line that Christians differ on whether this psalm is mainly David's own prayer that Jesus later applied to himself, or a prediction of Judas, and then bring the group back to the whole psalm.

42.open: When was the last time you were really thirsty, and what did that first drink feel like?
questions: The writer says, "As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God" (v. 1). What picture would you use to describe your own longing for God, or the lack of it, right now?
He says, "My tears have been my food both day and night" (v. 3). What does it tell you that a psalm in the Bible begins with this much open grief?
People keep asking him, "Where is your God?" (v. 3). When have you heard that question from others, or from inside your own head?
In verse 4 he remembers leading "the festive procession to the house of God." Why might remembering better days make pain sharper? Can memories also help? How?

In verse 5 he asks, "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" and then tells it, "Put your hope in God." What do you think it looks like to talk to your own heart this way, and what would you say back to your discouragement?
He writes, "all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me" (v. 7). He also says that at night God's song is with him (v. 8). How can both feel true at once?
In verse 9 he says to God, "Why have You forgotten me?" Why do you think the psalm lets him ask that so bluntly? What questions would you like to ask God if you felt free to?
The psalm ends by repeating its call to hope (v. 11), but the trouble is not described as over. What do you make of hope that comes before things get better?
42.life: This week, take one honest question or complaint you have been holding back and say it to God in your own words, the way the writer does in verse 9. Then say verse 5 or verse 11 to yourself out loud, even if you only half believe it.
42.prayer: Thank God that we are allowed to come with tears and hard questions. Ask him to be near anyone in the group who feels thirsty, tired or far from home.
42.tip: Some in the room may be in real grief or doubt, and may feel pressure to jump to the hopeful ending. Let the first half of the psalm stand without fixing it. Point out that the writer does not hide his pain, and that verse 11 hopes without saying the trouble is gone. Make it fine for someone to say they are not there yet.

43.open: When you are feeling down, what is one small thing that usually helps you feel a bit better?
questions: The writer asks God to "plead my case" against people who treat him unfairly (v. 1). Why might it help to bring a sense of being wronged to God instead of keeping it inside?
He says, "You are the God of my refuge," and then asks, "Why have You rejected me?" (v. 2). What do you make of someone saying both things in the same breath?
He asks why he must "walk in sorrow" (v. 2). When have you felt like you were walking through a hard season with no end in sight? What was that like?
In verse 3 he asks God to "send out Your light and Your truth" to lead him. What would it look like for light and truth to lead you right now?
He longs to go to God's "holy mountain" and the altar, where he can praise with the harp (vv. 3-4). Where do you feel closest to God, and what do you do when you can't get there?
He calls God "my greatest joy" (v. 4) while his soul is still downcast. Can joy and sadness exist together? Tell about a time that was true for you.
In verse 5 he asks his own soul, "Why are you downcast?" and then says, "Put your hope in God." What do you say to yourself on a heavy day, and is it kind, honest, or both?
He says "I will yet praise Him" (v. 5). He doesn't say he feels like praising now. If you feel stuck or unsure about God tonight, what is the honest answer you could give?
43.life: This week, when discouragement shows up, answer it out loud the way the writer does. Say what you are feeling honestly to God, then say verse 5 slowly. Notice what changes, even if it is small.
43.prayer: Tell God honestly where you feel wronged, worn down or far away. Ask him to send his light and truth to lead you, and pray for anyone in the group who is struggling to hope.
43.tip: Verses 2 and 5 sit side by side: the writer trusts God and also feels rejected by him. Some people may feel uneasy that doubt appears in a prayer. Gently point out that the psalm puts it right in the Bible, and that the writer takes it to God rather than away from him. Don't rush anyone toward a tidy answer. Verse 5 is a hope he speaks to himself, not a feeling he has already reached.

44.open: What is a story your family tells again and again, and why do you think it keeps getting told?
questions: The psalm opens with stories handed down: "our fathers have told us the work You did in their days" (v. 1). Who passed on their faith to you, and what did they tell you or show you about God?
The singer says, "I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me" (v. 6). What are the modern versions of a bow and sword, the things we lean on to feel secure?
In verse 12 the people say, "You sell Your people for nothing." What do you notice about speaking to God this bluntly? Does it feel disrespectful, honest, or something else?

The people say, "we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant" (v. 17). They are saying this suffering is not a punishment for sin. How does that differ from how we often explain hard things that happen to us?
Verse 22 says, "for Your sake we face death all day long." Why do you think later Christians, including Paul in Romans 8, found their own struggles in these words?

The singer cries, "Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?" (v. 23) and asks, "Why do You hide Your face" (v. 24). Have you ever felt that way, or felt that you were not allowed to? Say as much or as little as you like, including if God has felt silent or far away.
The psalm ends with no answer, only a plea: "Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion" (v. 26). What does it mean to keep praying when nothing has been resolved? What would help someone do that?
44.life: Write your own short, honest prayer this week, saying to God exactly what feels unfair or unanswered, the way this psalm does. End it by naming one thing you still know about God's love, even if you can only whisper it.
44.prayer: Thank God that we are allowed to bring our hardest questions to him. Pray for anyone in the group, or anyone they know, who is hurting through no fault of their own.
44.tip: Someone may try to explain the suffering away or suggest the people must have done something wrong. Gently point out that the psalm itself refuses that answer, and that it ends with a plea rather than a solution. Resist tying it up neatly. Let the group sit with the honesty of it.

45.open: What is the best wedding or big celebration you have ever been to, and what made it stick in your memory?
questions: The poet says, "My heart is stirred by a noble theme" (v. 1). When have you felt so moved by something that you wanted to put it into words, a song or a letter or a toast?

The king is praised because he rides out "on behalf of truth and humility and justice" (v. 4). Why might a good ruler need humility as much as strength? Where do you see that mix, or its absence, today?
The poem openly wishes that the king's enemies will fall (v. 5). How do you feel about a worship song that includes that kind of line, and how might it have sounded to people living under threat?

Verse 6 says, "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever." Christians read this as pointing to Jesus as truly God, while others see a lofty title for God's chosen king. How does each reading shape the way you hear the psalm?
Verse 7 says, "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness." What does it look like in daily life to love what is right and not just avoid what is wrong?

The bride is told, "Forget your people and your father's house" (v. 10). What do you imagine it would cost someone to leave family behind and start over in an unfamiliar place? When have you faced a smaller version of that?
Parts of this psalm, such as the bride bowing to the king, can sound strange or uncomfortable to modern ears. What stands out to you, and what questions does it raise? Honest doubts are welcome here.
The poet ends by promising to make the king's name remembered "through all generations" (v. 17). What do you hope people in your family or community will remember and pass down?
45.life: Pick one person who has shown truth, humility or justice in a quiet way. This week, write or tell them what you have noticed, and thank God for them.
45.prayer: Thank God for the gift of joy and celebration. Ask him to make you someone who loves what is right, and to bring justice and peace where they are missing.
45.tip: Verse 6 and the bride's instructions in verses 10 and 11 are the likely hard spots. Say plainly that Christians read verse 6 differently, and that verses 10 and 11 reflect an ancient royal wedding. Let people voice discomfort without hurrying to fix it, and keep returning to the king's love of justice and the poet's joy.

46.open: When a big storm or a power cut hits, what is the first thing you reach for or do?
questions: The psalm opens with "God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble" (v. 1). Which of those words, refuge, strength or help, do you most need right now, and why?

Verses 2 and 3 picture mountains toppled into the sea and waters that "roar and foam." In the ancient world the raging sea stood for chaos. What does it feel like in your life when things that seemed solid start to shake?
The singer says, "Therefore we will not fear" (v. 2). Is that a feeling, a decision, or something else? If you honestly feel afraid, how might you read that line?

Verse 4 speaks of "a river whose streams delight the city of God." Jerusalem had no great river, so many readers see this as a picture of God's gentle, life-giving presence set against the roaring sea. Where have you found quiet gladness in the middle of a loud season?
Verse 6 says "Nations rage, kingdoms crumble," yet the earth melts "when He lifts His voice." When the news feels overwhelming, what helps you remember who is really in charge?

Verses 8 and 9 say "Come, see the works of the LORD," and describe both devastation and an end to war. How do you hold together a God who is powerful and severe with a God who stops the fighting and brings peace?

Verse 10 says, "Be still and know that I am God." Christians differ on whether this is mainly God telling warring nations to stop, or mainly an invitation for believers to rest in him. Which part speaks to you tonight, and why?
The refrain in verses 7 and 11 says, "The LORD of Hosts is with us." What would change for you this week if you took that line as simply true, even on days when it does not feel true?
46.life: Pick one thing that is worrying you this week. Each day, take two quiet minutes, put your phone away, and say verse 1 out loud before naming that worry to God.
46.prayer: Thank God that he is a refuge and an ever-present help. Name one shaking thing in your life or in the world, and ask him for steadiness and peace.
46.tip: The group may split on whether verse 10 is a comfort for anxious believers or a warning to hostile nations. Say plainly that Christians read it both ways, let people share what the verse means to them, and keep returning to the refrain that God is with us.

47.open: What is a moment when you couldn't help cheering or clapping out loud, maybe at a game, a concert or a family event?
questions: The psalm opens with "Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout unto God with a voice of triumph" (v. 1). What does it say that worship here is loud and joyful, and how does that compare with the worship you are used to?
Verse 2 calls the LORD "the great King over all the earth." What did it mean for people in ancient Israel to call God their king, and what might it mean for us today?
The psalm says God "chooses our inheritance for us" (v. 4). What parts of your life feel chosen for you rather than picked by you, and how do you feel about that?

Verse 3 talks about God subduing nations, and older Christian readers took this to mean nations being gathered under his rule rather than crushed. How do you hear that verse, and what questions does it raise for you?
Verse 5 says "God has ascended amid shouts of joy." Some read this as a festival procession to Jerusalem, and some read it in light of Jesus going up to heaven. What do you notice in either picture?
The word "sing praises" appears four times in verse 6. Why might the psalmist repeat it, and when has repeating something helped you get past a flat or dry moment in prayer or worship?

The psalm ends with the leaders of other nations gathering "as the people of the God of Abraham" (v. 9). What do you make of a song that celebrates one people's story while inviting everyone else to join in?
If you came tonight feeling more tired or doubtful than joyful, what in this psalm is hard to say out loud, and what, if anything, still rings true for you?
47.life: Pick one song of praise this week and sing it or play it out loud, even if you don't feel like it. Afterward, take a minute to tell God honestly how it felt.
47.prayer: Thank God that he is "King of all the earth" (v. 7), not just of our own corner of it. Ask him to help each person in the group praise him honestly, whether they feel joyful or not.
47.tip: Verses 3 and 4 can sound like cheering for conquest, and people may feel uneasy. Name the unease as fair, note that Christians read these lines differently, and gently steer back to the psalm's main point: God is king and the invitation reaches every nation.

48.open: What is a place you love to show visitors when they come to your town, and why?
questions: The psalm opens, "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised" (v. 1). Notice that God is praised first and the city second. Why might it matter which comes first?
Verse 2 calls Zion "the joy of all the earth." What do you think made a city feel like joy to the people who lived there? What makes a place feel that way to you?
Verse 3 says, "God is in her citadels; He has shown Himself to be a fortress." What does it mean for a place or a people to feel safe because of who is with them, not because of the walls?
In verses 4 to 6 the kings "saw and were astounded; they fled in terror." Scholars are not sure which event this describes. What does the picture tell us about how the psalm writers saw God's power?
Verse 8 says, "As we have heard, so we have seen." Think of something about God you first heard from others. Has it ever become more real to you, or does it still feel secondhand? Be honest.
In verse 9 the people "contemplate Your loving devotion" within the temple. What helps you slow down and think about God's faithful love? What gets in the way?

Verses 12 and 13 tell worshipers to walk around the city and count its towers "that you may tell the next generation." What would you want to pass on to younger people about what you have found trustworthy?
The psalm ends, "He will be our guide even till death" (v. 14). How does it feel to read that line right now, whether comforting, hard to believe, or somewhere in between?
48.life: Choose one person younger than you, a child, a niece, a neighbor or a friend. This week, tell them one true story of a time you found God faithful, and let them ask questions.
48.prayer: Praise God for being present with his people. Ask him to help each person in the group see his faithfulness for themselves, and to give you words to pass it on.
48.tip: Verse 8 says the city will stand "forever," yet Jerusalem was later destroyed. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether this points to the earthly city, to God's people the church, or to a future heavenly city. Do not settle it. Bring the group back to the main point: God's presence is the people's real security.

49.open: What is something you once saved up for and were really excited to buy?
questions: The singer calls on everyone, "both low and high, rich and poor alike" (v. 2). Why might it matter that this lesson is meant for all kinds of people?
He asks, "Why should I fear in times of trouble" (v. 5). Who or what makes you feel small or anxious when it comes to money or power?
Verse 6 says some people "trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches." What does it look like today to trust in money, even quietly?
Verse 7 says, "No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God." What is the writer saying money cannot do, and why do you think that is hard for us to believe?
Verse 14 pictures a flock of sheep with "Death" as their shepherd. How does that image strike you, compared with a shepherd who cares for his sheep?

In verse 15 the writer says, "But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself." Christians read this differently: some hear hope of life with God after death, others hear trust that God will rescue him from an early death in this life. However you read it, how sure do you feel of a hope like this? Be as honest as you can, including if you are unsure.
Verse 16 says, "Do not be afraid when a man grows rich." When do you find yourself envying or being impressed by people who have more than you?

The psalm ends with, "A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish" (v. 20). What do you think the understanding is that the writer has in mind, and where might you see it in someone's life?
49.life: This week, pay attention to one moment when you feel envy or feel small next to someone who has more. Pause and remind yourself of verse 17, "he will carry nothing away." Then do one small, quiet thing with your time or money that helps someone else.
49.prayer: Thank God that he is the one who can truly rescue a life. Ask him to loosen the grip that money, status or comparison has on you, and to give you understanding about what really lasts.
49.tip: Some people will hear this psalm as saying that being wealthy is wrong, and others will feel guilty or defensive. Gently point out that the psalm is about where we put our trust, not about condemning anyone's bank account. Also, say plainly that Christians read verse 15 differently, and let the group share their hopes without needing everyone to agree.

50.open: What is a family tradition or routine you keep doing, even if you can't quite remember why it started?
questions: God "speaks and summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets" (v. 1). What does it say about God that he calls the whole world to witness this moment with his own people?

In verse 3 "Consuming fire precedes Him, and a tempest rages around Him." Many readers hear echoes of Mount Sinai. How does this picture of God sit with you: comforting, unsettling, or something else?
God says, "I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices" (v. 8), yet he also says he has no need of them. What do you think he is correcting in the way these people think about worship?
In verse 12 God says, "If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine." When have you caught yourself acting as if God needed something from you, or owed you something in return?
God asks for a thank offering and for trust: "Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you" (vv. 14, 15). Why might thanks and asking for help belong together in the same relationship?

In verses 16 to 20 God confronts people who recite his statutes but befriend thieves, deceive, and slander their own family. How can we say the right words about God and still live in a way that doesn't match? Where is the gap easiest to miss?
God says, "you thought I was just like you" (v. 21). Where might we shrink God down to our own size, especially when he seems quiet?
Be honest here. Is there a part of your faith, like prayer, church, or giving, that feels more like going through the motions right now? What do you think is behind that?
50.life: Pick one habit of faith that has become routine, such as a mealtime prayer or Sunday worship. This week, do it slowly and start by naming three specific things you are thankful for. Then say one honest word to God about what is hard.
50.prayer: Thank God that everything already belongs to him and that he still invites us to call on him in trouble. Ask him to make our thanks real and to close the gap between what we say and how we live.
50.tip: Verses 22 and 23 contain a stark warning about God tearing people to pieces, and some may feel afraid or wonder if they are the "wicked." Read the warning plainly, then point to verses 14, 15 and 23, where God keeps offering rescue to those who turn to him. Also note that Christians read the psalm's view of sacrifice differently, some seeing only a critique of insincere offerings and others a hint that animal sacrifice would one day be set aside, and don't try to settle that tonight.

51.open: What is the hardest stain you have ever tried to get out of something, and did it work?
questions: The heading ties this psalm to King David after he took Bathsheba and arranged her husband Uriah's death. He begins, "Have mercy on me, O God" (v. 1), and points to God's love, not to any excuse. Why might that be the only place to begin after a serious wrong?
David says, "my sin is always before me" (v. 3). What is the difference between guilt that keeps a person stuck and honest ownership that leads somewhere new?
David prays, "Against You, You only, have I sinned" (v. 4), even though he clearly harmed Bathsheba and Uriah. How do you understand that line, and what do we do with the people we have hurt?
Verse 6 says God desires "truth in the inmost being." Where is it hardest for you to be honest: with God, with other people, or with yourself?

David asks, "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (v. 10). He does not ask God to help him clean it up. Why might he ask for something only God can make? What part of change is ours, and what part do we ask for?
David worries, "Cast me not away from Your presence" (v. 11). Have you ever wondered whether God might be finished with you? Say as honestly as you like what makes forgiveness hard to believe.
Verse 17 says, "a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise." How does that compare with the way people often respond to someone who has failed badly?
When someone has done real and lasting harm, what do you think it takes for them to be able to start again? What might David's prayer for "the joy of Your salvation" (v. 12) add to your answer?
51.life: This week, take a few quiet minutes and name one thing you need to own, plainly and without excuses. Tell God about it using David's words, such as verse 10. If it involves someone you have wronged, ask God what one next step might be.
51.prayer: Thank God that he meets honest confession with mercy. Ask for a clean heart and a willing spirit, and pray for anyone in the group carrying guilt tonight.
51.tip: Verse 5 may pull the group into a debate about whether we are all born sinful, since Christians read it differently. Say that plainly, then steer back to the heart of the psalm: an honest confession and a God who does not despise it.

52.open: Think of a time when something you said, or something said about you, spread farther than you expected. How did it feel?
questions: The heading ties this psalm to Doeg, who told Saul where David had gone. Why might David have written a psalm about this, and what does it show about taking hurt to God?
The psalm says, "Your tongue devises destruction like a sharpened razor" (v. 2). Why is a razor a fitting picture for harmful words? How can words cut without anyone noticing at first?
Verse 3 says, "You love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking truth." Where do you see the pull toward half-truths or flattering stories today, at work, at school, in families or online?
Verse 5 says God will "uproot you from the land of the living." How do you feel reading a promise like that? What does it say about how God treats people who ruin others?
The onlookers say this man "did not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth" (v. 7). What do people lean on today to feel secure, and what happens when it gives way?
The writer says, "I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God" (v. 8). What do you think it takes to grow like that? What helps you stay rooted, and what makes it hard?
He says, "I trust in the loving devotion of God forever and ever" (v. 8). If trusting feels hard for you right now, what is the honest thing you would say to God about it?
In verse 9 he promises to praise God "in the presence of Your saints." Why might it matter to give thanks with other people and not only alone?
52.life: This week, pay attention to your own words. Before you pass along a story about someone, ask whether it is true, whether it is fair, and whether it helps. Then pick one thing you tend to lean on for security and tell God about it.
52.prayer: Thank God that his "loving devotion" endures when other things fail. Ask for honest words, for help if someone has hurt you with theirs, and for roots that go deep in his love.
52.tip: Verses 5 to 7 can sound harsh, and some people will be uneasy with talk of God tearing someone down or people laughing at it. Don't rush past that. Let people say so, then point out that the psalm is a cry from someone who was wronged, and that it ends on trust in God's love, not on revenge.

54.open: Who is someone you would call without thinking twice if you were in trouble?
questions: The heading says this was written when the Ziphites told Saul where David was hiding (v. 1). What do you think it felt like to be betrayed by people from his own region?
David begins, "Save me, O God, by Your name" (v. 1). What does it mean to ask for help based on who God is, and what do you know about God's character that you could lean on in a hard moment?
Verse 3 describes people "with no regard for God." How does it change a struggle when you see it as something bigger than a personal conflict, or does it?
In verse 4 the psalm turns: "Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul." What do you think moved David from pleading to trust, and what tends to move you?

David prays, "He will reward my enemies with evil" (v. 5). Many readers are uneasy with prayers like this. Why might the Bible include such honest words, and what do you notice about David leaving the payback to God?
Honestly, how do you pray about people who have hurt you? What is easy to say to God and what is hard?

David promises, "Freely I will sacrifice to You" and says he will praise God's name "for it is good" (v. 6). Why might thanking God before the trouble is fully over be meaningful, and what makes thanks hard when you are still hurting?
If you are in a place where trust in God feels thin, or you are not sure anyone is listening, what would you want to say in your own words, even if it is only that you are not sure?
54.life: Think of one person who has hurt or betrayed you. This week, tell God plainly how you feel about it, as David does, and ask him to be your helper. Then name one thing you are grateful for.
54.prayer: Thank God that he is "my helper" and the sustainer of our souls (v. 4). Pray for anyone in the group who feels betrayed, hunted or alone right now.
54.tip: Verse 5 may stir up discomfort, and someone may ask whether Christians should pray this way. Don't rush to fix it. Point out that David hands the matter to God instead of acting on it himself, and that the psalm lets hurting people be honest in prayer. Also leave room for a person who has been betrayed to simply talk.

55.open: When you need a break from a stressful week, where do you most want to escape to?
questions: The writer says, "My heart pounds within me, and the terrors of death assail me" (v. 4). What does fear feel like in your body, and what do you usually do with it?
In verse 6 he says, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest." What is he really asking for, and why might that wish feel so familiar?
Verse 12 says, "it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure." Why does harm from a close friend hurt so differently from harm done by a stranger?
Verse 14 remembers "sweet fellowship" and walking together "into the house of God." How does betrayal change the way someone feels about the good memories they shared?

In verse 15 he prays, "Let death seize them by surprise." Christians read this differently: some hear honest anger handed over to God, others a kind of prayer Jesus calls us beyond. What do you make of it, and why do you think it is in the Bible at all?
Verse 21 says the friend's "speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart." Why can gentle words that hide something else be so painful? How do we guard against doing that to others?

Verse 22 says, "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you." What is one burden that feels hard to hand over, and what makes it hard? It is fine to say if this verse feels far away right now.
The psalm ends with "But I will trust in You" (v. 23), though little around him has changed. What do you think trust looks like when the pain is still there?
55.life: Think of one burden you keep carrying alone. Each day this week, say it out loud to God in a sentence or two, using verse 22 as your guide. If a hurt involves a friend, consider also telling one trusted person.
55.prayer: Invite people to name, silently or aloud, a hurt or fear they are carrying. Ask God to hear and to sustain them, and pray for anyone in the group who has been let down by someone close.
55.tip: Verses 15 and 23 will make some people uneasy, and others may be reminded of a painful betrayal of their own. Say plainly that Christians read the harsh prayer differently, and that the psalm lets us be honest with God. Don't rush anyone to forgive, and let people share only as much as they choose.

56.open: What is something small that scares you more than it probably should?
questions: The heading says David wrote this when the Philistines seized him in Gath. Knowing that, how does it change the way you hear the opening cry, "Be merciful to me, O God" (v. 1)?
Verse 3 says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You." The writer admits the fear and trusts anyway. Why might it help that he does not pretend to be fearless?

In verse 4 he asks, "What can man do to me?" The note on this verse says the original word is literally "flesh," a reminder that even dangerous people are frail. Is that comforting to you, or does it feel too simple? Why?
Verse 5 says, "all day long they twist my words." Have you ever been misunderstood or had your words used against you? What did that feel like?
In verse 7 the writer asks God, "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations." It is a raw prayer. What do you make of bringing anger and a longing for justice to God instead of hiding it?
Verse 8 pictures God saying, "Put my tears in Your bottle." What does it mean to you that God notices and keeps count of your sorrow? If that is hard to believe right now, say so honestly.

The chorus in verses 4 and 11 comes back a second time, and the writer looks ahead to "walk before God in the light of life" (v. 13). What truth do you need to repeat to yourself while a hard situation is still going on?
56.life: Pick one short line from this psalm, such as "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You" (v. 3). Say it out loud each time fear or worry shows up this week, and notice what happens.
56.prayer: Tell God plainly what you are afraid of right now. Ask for help to trust him in the middle of it, and pray for anyone in the group who feels hunted, misunderstood or worn down.
56.tip: Verse 7 may make some people uncomfortable, and others may want to skip it. Don't rush past it or explain it away. Point out that the writer brings his anger to God instead of acting on it himself, and let people say honestly how that sits with them.

57.open: When you were a kid, where did you go to hide or feel protected when things got scary?
questions: The heading ties this psalm to David hiding in a cave from Saul. What do you imagine it was like to write or pray these words in that place?
David prays, "in You my soul takes refuge" (v. 1). What does it look like to run to God for shelter, as opposed to running somewhere else?
He says he will shelter "in the shadow of Your wings" "until the danger has passed" (v. 1). What does that tell you about what he expects from God in the middle of the trouble?
David describes enemies with "tongues are sharp swords" (v. 4). Have you ever been hurt by words, or seen someone else hurt by them? What helped, if anything?
Twice David breaks off to say, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens" (vv. 5, 11). Why might someone in danger turn their attention to God's glory instead of only their own rescue?

In verse 6 the traps set for David have caught the people who set them. In the story in 1 Samuel 24, David spares Saul. What do you make of that contrast between how David was treated and how he treated Saul?

David says, "My heart is steadfast, O God" (v. 7), and then promises to sing, though the danger is not yet over. What has helped you feel steady before a hard situation was resolved? If nothing has, what is that like for you right now?

David says he will praise God "among the nations" (v. 9) because God's "loving devotion reaches to the heavens" (v. 10). What would it take for you to talk about God's faithfulness with someone outside your usual circle?
57.life: Pick one hard thing you are facing this week. Each morning, say a short prayer about it that starts with "Have mercy on me, O God" and ends with one sentence of praise, even if it feels small.
57.prayer: Thank God that he is a shelter when we are afraid. Ask him to help each person in the group feel steady in whatever they are facing, and to be honored in it.
57.tip: Some people will wonder how David could sing while still in danger, and a person in a hard season may feel they cannot. Make clear that the psalm begins with a cry for mercy, so honest fear belongs here. Invite people to share where they are, without pressure to sound confident.

58.open: When have you seen something unfair happen and felt your blood boil? What did you do with that feeling?
questions: The psalm opens by asking rulers, "Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers?" (v. 1). What would it look like for a person with power to judge fairly, and why does that matter so much to ordinary people?
Verse 2 says "in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth." How does harm usually begin in the heart before it shows up in actions?
Verses 4 and 5 picture a cobra that "shuts its ears" and will not listen. What does it feel like to deal with someone who will not listen, whether a boss, an official or someone close to you?
Verse 6 says, "O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths." The language is harsh. What is your honest reaction to prayers this raw in the Bible?
Notice that the speaker asks God to act rather than taking revenge personally. Why might it matter that anger is brought to God and not acted out on others?

Christians read prayers like this differently alongside Jesus' call to love enemies. Some see honest anger handed to God, some see a stage Jesus moves beyond, and some see a pointer to God's final judgment. Which way of reading helps you most, and what questions does it leave you with?
Verse 11 ends with, "There is surely a God who judges the earth!" If you have ever wondered whether God sees injustice, or whether doing right makes any difference, what has made you wonder that?
When people with power use it to harm others, what do you think a fitting response looks like, and where does anger belong in it?
58.life: Think of one unfair situation you care about, close to home or far away. This week, tell God plainly how it makes you feel, then take one small step: pray for the people harmed, give, speak up, or offer help.
58.prayer: Bring one injustice to God by name and tell him honestly how it feels. Ask him to protect those being hurt, and to keep your own heart from turning hard or cruel.
58.tip: Verses 6 to 10 may make some people uneasy, especially verse 10 with its image of feet in blood. Don't rush to explain it away or defend it. Say that the psalm is a raw prayer, that Christians read it in different ways, and that it asks God to act rather than telling us to take revenge. Then let people say what they feel, including discomfort.

59.open: When you were a kid, what was the safest place you knew, and what made it feel safe?
questions: The heading says David wrote this when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. What do you notice about how David talks to God when he is in real danger?

In verses 3 and 4 David says these things happen "for no transgression or sin of my own" (v. 3). Why might it matter to him to say that out loud to God? Have you ever needed to tell God that something isn't fair?
Verse 7 describes enemies who spew "sharp words from their lips." What did Words as weapons look like in David's day, and where do you see them today, in person or online?
In verse 8 God laughs at those who think no one hears them. What picture of God does that give you, and how does it sit with you?
David calls God "my fortress" in verses 9, 16 and 17. What is a time when you needed a place to run to? What would it look like to run to God there?

Verses 11 to 13 are a raw prayer for the enemies to be brought down. Christians read these prayers differently: some see honest anger handed over to God, others see a stage that Jesus' call to love our enemies goes beyond. What do you make of praying this way?

The psalm moves from "They return in the evening" (v. 14) to "I will sing of Your strength" in the morning (v. 16). What would it take for you to sing, or even hope, after a hard night? If you honestly can't get there right now, what would you say to God instead?
59.life: Think of one situation where you feel wronged or afraid. Tell God about it in plain words this week, including the anger, then end by saying out loud that God is your fortress, as David does in verse 17.
59.prayer: Thank God that we can bring our fear and anger to him honestly. Ask him to be a safe place for anyone in the group who feels hunted, hurt or slandered right now.
59.tip: Verses 11 to 13 may shock people, and some will want to skip them or defend them. Don't rush to settle it. Name that Christians read these prayers differently, and keep coming back to what the whole psalm does: David takes his anger to God and does not take revenge himself.

60.open: When did you last feel the ground shift under you, even in a small way, like a job change, a move or an unexpected bill?
questions: The psalm opens with "You have rejected us, O God" (v. 1). The writer blames God out loud instead of hiding it. What do you make of a prayer that starts this way?
Verse 2 pictures the land as "quaking" and torn open, and verse 3 says "we are staggered from the wine You made us drink." What do these pictures tell us about how the people felt?
Even while shaken, the people ask, "restore us!" (v. 1) and "Heal its fractures" (v. 2). Why might it matter that they take their complaint to God instead of away from him?
In verses 6 to 8 God speaks and says the land and the nations are His: "Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine." What do you think it did for the people to remember who owns it all?
The psalm says "Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter" (v. 7). What does it say about God that He names His own people as His helmet and scepter?
In verse 10 the writer asks, "Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies?" Have you ever felt that God was not going out with you? How did you handle it, or how are you handling it now?
Verse 11 says "the help of man is worthless." Where are you most tempted to rely on your own strength, money, plans or other people instead of God?
The psalm ends with "With God we will perform with valor" (v. 12). What would it look like for someone who is still hurting or unsure to say that line honestly?
60.life: Pick one thing that feels shaky in your life right now. Each day this week, tell God plainly how it feels, even if it is anger or confusion, and then say one thing you remember He has promised.
60.prayer: Bring God the places that feel broken or shaken, and ask Him to restore and heal. Thank Him that the people He calls His own are not forgotten.
60.tip: The psalm's war language and the lines about Edom and Moab can feel distant or harsh. Don't get stuck there. Say briefly that this was a nation fighting for its land in its own time, then steer the group back to the heart of the psalm: honest complaint and leaning on God when things fall apart.

61.open: When you were a kid and got scared or hurt, where did you go to feel safe?
questions: The writer says, "From the ends of the earth I call out to You whenever my heart is faint" (v. 2). What do you think "the ends of the earth" might mean here, and when have you felt like you were at the edge of your own limits?
The prayer begins with "Hear my cry, O God; attend to my prayer" (v. 1). How does it feel to know a prayer can be that plain and that desperate? What makes it hard to pray like this?
The writer asks, "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I" (v. 2). Why might someone need to be led to a safe place instead of getting there on their own?
In verse 3 the writer remembers, "You have been my refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy." How does remembering past help change the way we pray in a hard season?

The writer longs to "dwell in Your tent forever" and "take refuge in the shelter of Your wings" (v. 4). Which of those pictures speaks to you more, and which feels harder to believe right now? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 5 says, "You have heard my vows, O God." What do you think it means that God hears us, and what do you do when it doesn't feel like anyone is listening?

Verses 6 and 7 pray for the king. Christians read this differently: David speaking of himself, a later king, or ultimately the Messiah. How might praying for leaders, or for someone you love, be part of a prayer that starts with our own need?
The psalm ends with "I will ever sing praise to Your name and fulfill my vows day by day" (v. 8). What small daily habit helps you remember what God has done?
61.life: This week, when you feel worn down, pray the words of verse 2 out loud: "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I." Keep it short and honest, and note afterward what you noticed.
61.prayer: Thank God for being a refuge and a strong tower. Ask for help for anyone in the group who feels faint or far from home tonight.
61.tip: Verses 6 and 7 can seem like a sudden change of subject. Say briefly that Christians read the king differently, then bring the group back to the whole prayer: a tired person cries out, asks for shelter, and promises to keep giving thanks.

62.open: When you are stressed or worried, what is the first thing you usually reach for, like a phone, a snack, a call to a friend, or a long walk?
questions: The psalm opens with "In God alone my soul finds rest" (v. 1). What does rest for your soul look like to you, and how is it different from just getting a day off?
The writer calls God "my rock" and "my fortress" (v. 2). Which of those pictures speaks to you more right now, and why?
Verse 4 says his enemies "with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse." What was it like for the writer to be surrounded by people like that, and have you ever felt something similar?
In verse 5 he talks to himself: "Rest in God alone, O my soul." Why might he need to say it again? What do you tell yourself when you feel shaky, and does it help?
Verse 8 says, "pour out your hearts before Him." What does it look like to be that honest with God? What makes it easy or hard for you?
Verse 9 says people, high and low, "are but a vapor." What do you make of that? Where have you leaned on people or on money and found it could not hold your weight?
Verse 10 warns, "If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them." Why is it so easy to do that, even when we have only a little?

The psalm ends by saying power belongs to God, and "loving devotion" does too (vv. 11-12). Why does it matter that he has both? If you are unsure about trusting God, what would help you most: his strength, his love, or something else?
62.life: Each day this week, when you notice yourself worrying or reaching for your usual comfort, stop for one minute. Say the first line of the psalm slowly, then tell God honestly what is on your heart.
62.prayer: Thank God that he is a rock and a refuge who does not give way. Ask him to help each person in the group pour out what they are carrying, and to rest in him alone.
62.tip: Verse 12 says God "will repay each man according to his deeds," and some people will hear that as a threat or as pressure to earn God's favor. Read it alongside the rest of the verse, where God's "loving devotion" sits right beside his power. Let the group say what troubles them, and keep returning to the psalm's main point: God is safe to trust.

63.open: When was the last time you were really, truly thirsty or hungry, and what was the first thing you reached for?
questions: The heading says David wrote this in the Wilderness of Judah. He says, "my soul thirsts for You" and speaks of "a dry and weary land without water" (v. 1). Why might a real desert make a good picture of longing for God?

David says, "I have seen You in the sanctuary" (v. 2). He remembers meeting God in a place he is now cut off from. What places, people or habits have helped you sense God, and what happens when you lose them?
Verse 3 says, "Your loving devotion is better than life." What do you think David means, and what would it take for you to say that and mean it?
In verse 5 David says, "My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods." Where do you usually go when you want to feel satisfied, and how does that compare with what David describes?
David remembers God "through the watches of the night" (v. 6). What tends to fill your mind when you lie awake, and what might it look like to turn some of that toward God?

Verse 8 says, "My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me." Which part feels more true to you right now, your clinging or God's holding? How would you describe it honestly, even if the answer is neither?

Verses 9 and 10 speak bluntly about what will happen to David's enemies. How do you react to that? How might we be honest with God about anger and danger while still following Jesus' call to love our enemies?
In the last verse David says "the mouths of liars will be shut" (v. 11). Why might it matter that the psalm ends with hope that truth wins, and where do you most want to see that hope come true?
63.life: Pick one moment this week when you are waiting or cannot sleep, like a commute, a queue or a restless night. Use it to talk to God in your own words about what you are longing for, even if all you can say is that you feel dry.
63.prayer: Thank God that his loving devotion is better than life. Ask him to meet anyone in the group who feels dry or far from him, and to help each person bring real longing and real fear to him honestly.
63.tip: Verses 9 and 10 may feel harsh, and some people will want to skip them. Don't rush past them or explain them away. Say that David is being honest with God about real danger and leaving the outcome with him, then ask what it means to bring anger to God instead of acting on it.

64.open: Can you remember a time when something someone said about you, or to you, stuck with you far longer than they probably knew?
questions: The psalm opens with "Hear, O God, my voice of complaint" (v. 1). What do you notice about David bringing a complaint to God instead of hiding it? When is it hardest for you to do that?

David pictures cruel talk as people who "sharpen their tongues like swords" and "aim their bitter words like arrows" (v. 3). Why do you think words can hurt so deeply? Where have you seen this at home, at work, at school or online?
The plotters say, "Who will see them?" (v. 5). What does that tell us about how people can feel when they think no one is watching? When have you been tempted to think that way yourself?

Verses 3 and 4 say the attackers act "without fear." Some readers take this to mean they feel sure they will get away with it, and others that they have no respect for God. Which reading makes more sense to you, and why?

In verses 7 and 8 God answers suddenly, and the plotters' "own tongues" are "turned against them." What do these verses say about how God deals with injustice? How do they sit with you, whether comforting, uneasy or both?
Maybe you have prayed about being hurt and still feel nothing has changed. What would you honestly say to God, or to this group, about waiting for justice?
The psalm ends with the righteous who "rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him" (v. 10). What does taking refuge in God look like on an ordinary day, when someone has wronged you?
Most of us have been on the receiving end of hurtful words, and most of us have also spoken them. What does this psalm make you think about your own tongue?
64.life: Pay attention to your words this week. When you feel the urge to run someone down or pass on gossip, stop and say a short prayer instead. If you are the one being hurt by someone's words, tell God plainly what happened, the way David does in verse 1.
64.prayer: Thank God that he hears a "voice of complaint" and is a safe place to run. Pray for anyone in the group or in your life who is being hurt by words, and ask for help to use your own words well.
64.tip: Verses 7 and 8 can sound harsh, and some people will wonder whether it is right to want enemies hurt. Don't rush past that. Point out that David hands the matter to God instead of taking revenge himself, and let people say honestly how they feel about it. Also be aware that someone in the room may be hurting right now from words said about them, so leave space for quiet and don't push anyone to share.

65.open: What is a meal or a season of the year that makes you feel especially thankful?
questions: The psalm begins with praise that "awaits" God in Zion, and with vows to be fulfilled (v. 1). What does it mean to you that praise can be waiting and ready, even before we feel like singing?
God is called the One "who listen to prayer" (v. 2). When you think about God listening, what picture comes to mind, and how easy or hard is it to believe?
In verse 3 the singer says "iniquities prevail against me," and then, "You atone for our transgressions." Why do you think forgiveness comes before the praise for rain and harvest?
Verse 4 says, "Blessed is the one You choose and bring near." What does being brought near to God look like in ordinary life, and what makes us feel far away?
Verses 6 and 7 say God formed the mountains and "stilled the roaring of the seas" and "the tumult of the nations." What feels loud or out of control in the world or in your life right now?
Verse 9 says "You attend to the earth and water it." Where do you see everyday gifts like food, weather or work that are easy to take for granted?

Verse 11 says, "You crown the year with Your bounty." Looking back over this past year, what would you put in that crown, and what felt missing? Be as honest as you like, including if thankfulness feels hard right now.
The hills and valleys "shout in triumph" and "sing" (v. 13). How might you let thankfulness show up in your week, in words, in actions, or just in noticing?
65.life: Each day this week, name one thing you did nothing to earn, like a meal, a kind word or good weather, and thank God for it out loud or in writing. At the end of the week, share one with someone else.
65.prayer: Thank God for forgiving what was too heavy to carry and for the ordinary gifts that arrive each day. Ask for calm where life feels loud and for a thankful heart.
65.tip: The psalm jumps from forgiveness to oceans to farming, and some will wonder how it fits together. Point out that the singer sees one God who forgives, steadies the world and feeds people. Also remember that not everyone in the room has had a good harvest this year, so let thanks and struggle both be welcome.

66.open: Think of a time someone insisted you had to come and see something they had found. What was it, and why did they want you to see it?
questions: The psalm opens by calling "all the earth" to praise God (v. 1). Why do you think the singer invites everyone, not just God's own people?
Verse 5 says, "Come and see the works of God." What is one thing God has done, in the Bible or in your own life, that you would point someone toward?
Verse 6 remembers the sea turned into "dry land," and the singer says "there we rejoiced in Him." Why might it matter to count ourselves as sharers in what God did for people long ago?

Verse 10 says, "You have refined us like silver," and verse 11 says, "You led us into the net." What do you make of a song that sees God's hand even in the hard times? Does that comfort you, trouble you, or both?
Verse 12 says, "we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance." Think of a hard stretch you came through. What did you notice about how you got through it, and who or what helped?
In verses 13 and 14 the singer keeps vows "promised" "in my distress." Have you ever made a promise to God when things were hard? What happened to it afterward?

Verse 18 says, "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened." The singer is claiming an honest heart, not a perfect record. What does it look like to come to God honestly?
In verse 19 the singer says, "God has surely heard." If you are in a season where prayer feels unanswered or quiet, what would you honestly say to God, or to this group, about that?
66.life: Think of one time God helped you through something hard. This week, tell one person that story in a few plain sentences, the way verse 16 does: "I will declare what He has done for me."
66.prayer: Thank God for the ways he has brought you through hard times. Ask for honest hearts, and pray for anyone in the group who is still waiting for an answer.
66.tip: Verses 10 to 12 say God tested the people and led them into the net, and that can sting for someone in pain right now. Don't explain it away or hurry anyone toward the happy ending in verse 12. Let the group sit with the honest tension, and note that the psalm itself says they went through fire and water before they came out.

67.open: What is a meal, a gift or a piece of good news that you enjoyed most because you got to share it with other people?
questions: The psalm opens, "May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us" (v. 1). What do you picture when you hear that God's face shines on someone?
Verse 2 says why the blessing is asked for: "that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." Why do you think the writer ties God's blessing to other people knowing him?
The chorus asks, "Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You" (vv. 3, 5). What does it tell you about God that the psalm keeps including everyone, not only Israel?
Verse 4 says the nations can be glad "for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." When you hear that God judges, does it feel like good news or a worry? Be honest about why.
Verse 6 says, "The earth has yielded its harvest." What are the ordinary good things in your life right now that you rarely think of as coming from God?
Many scholars think this psalm was sung at a harvest festival, and Christians later read its hope as pointing to the message of Jesus reaching every nation. How do you hear verse 7 in light of that?
If you are not sure you feel blessed right now, or not sure God is looking on you kindly, what would you want to say about that? What would it mean to ask for verse 1 anyway?
The psalm treats blessing as something meant to spill over to others. Where could the good things you have been given reach someone beyond your own circle?
67.life: Pick one good thing God has given you, such as food, a skill, a friendship or some free time. This week, share it with someone outside your usual circle, and pray for that person by name.
67.prayer: Ask God to be gracious to your group and to let his kindness through you reach others. Pray for one nation or people group you rarely think about.
67.tip: Verse 4 on God judging may make some people uneasy. Read the whole sentence together: the psalm says the nations sing for joy because God judges "justly." Let people say honestly what they feel, and don't rush to smooth it over.

68.open: Who is someone that always made you feel welcome, even when you were the new person in the room?
questions: The psalm opens with "God arises" (v. 1). Why might people who were tired or under threat want to sing a song like this?
Verse 5 calls God "A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows." Why do you think the psalm praises God first for caring for people with no power?
Verse 6 says God "settles the lonely in families." Where have you seen loneliness eased by a family, a church or a group of friends? What could our group do for someone who is on their own?

Verses 7 to 10 remember God leading his people through the wasteland and giving rain to "Your weary inheritance" (v. 9). Where have you felt worn out, and what would it look like for God to refresh you?
Verse 19 says God "daily bears our burden." What burden are you carrying right now? If you would rather not name it, what is it like to hear that God carries it daily?
Verses 21 to 23 describe enemies crushed and feet dipped in blood. This is harsh war language. How do you feel reading it, and how does it sit beside the God who defends widows and orphans?
Verses 29 to 31 picture kings and envoys from Egypt and Cush coming to worship God. Why might it matter that the song ends with the nations joining in, and not only Israel?
The psalm ends with "the God of Israel Himself gives strength and power to His people" (v. 35). Is this easy or hard for you to believe right now? Tell us honestly.
68.life: Verse 5 says God defends the fatherless and widows. This week, look for one person who is alone or overlooked, such as a neighbor, a coworker or someone at church, and do one small thing to include them: a call, a meal or an invitation.
68.prayer: Praise God as the one who defends the helpless and carries our burdens daily. Name before him one person you know who feels alone, and ask what part you might play in their care.
68.tip: Verses 21 to 23 may unsettle people. Don't rush to explain them away or defend them. Say that this is the rough language of ancient war songs, let people say honestly what bothers them, and then bring the group back to the fuller picture of the psalm, a God who is both mighty and tender to the weak.

69.open: When was the last time you felt completely in over your head, even over something small?
questions: The writer says "the waters are up to my neck" (v. 1) and "I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing" (v. 2). What picture would you use to describe a time you felt overwhelmed?
In verse 3 the writer says, "My eyes fail, looking for my God." Have you ever felt like you were looking for God and not finding him? You can answer honestly, including if that is where you are now.

Verse 5 says, "You know my folly, O God," yet verse 7 says, "I have endured scorn for Your sake." Why might the writer say both? How can we tell the difference between pain we bring on ourselves and pain that comes from other things?
Verse 8 says the writer became "a stranger to my brothers." Has your faith ever cost you something with family or friends, or made you feel out of place?
In verse 20 the writer says, "I looked for sympathy, but there was none." What do you most need from people when you are hurting, and how could we offer that to each other?

Verses 22 to 28 are harsh. The writer asks God to "Pour out Your wrath upon them" (v. 24). Christians read these verses differently: some hear honest anger given to God, some hear a picture of judgment, and some think followers of Jesus should no longer pray this way. What do you make of it?
The New Testament connects this psalm to Jesus, including the sour wine in verse 21: "gave me vinegar to quench my thirst." What does it mean to you that Jesus knew this kind of rejection and thirst?

Verse 29 says, "But I am in pain and distress," and then the writer still chooses praise, trusting that "the LORD listens to the needy" (v. 33). Does praise come easily or slowly for you when things are hard? What helps?
69.life: This week, take ten minutes and tell God exactly how you feel, with no cleaning it up, on paper or out loud. Then end with one line of trust, like the writer's "my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor" (v. 13).
69.prayer: Thank God that he "listens to the needy" (v. 33). Ask for the freedom to be honest with him, and pray for anyone in the group who feels like they are sinking.
69.tip: The curses in verses 22 to 28 will probably come up, and some people may feel uneasy or even upset. Don't try to settle the question or explain it away. Say plainly that Christians disagree, then ask what the group notices about the writer taking anger to God instead of acting on it. Make room for anyone who has been badly hurt, and don't rush to fix their pain.

70.open: When you are in a hurry or in trouble, who is the first person you call, and why them?
questions: The psalm opens with "Make haste, O God, to deliver me!" (v. 1). What does it tell you that a prayer in the Bible can be this short and this urgent?
The speaker asks God to "Hurry" (v. 1) and later says "do not delay" (v. 5). Why do you think people feel free to talk to God this bluntly, and do you ever feel free to?
In verses 2 and 3 the speaker faces people who "seek my life" and who say, "Aha, aha!" What does it feel like when someone seems to enjoy your trouble?
Verses 2 and 3 ask for enemies to be ashamed and turned back. Many readers see this as honest anger handed over to God instead of acted on. How do you think about bringing angry feelings into prayer?
In verse 4 the focus widens to "all who seek You," who are asked to "rejoice and be glad in You." Why might someone in trouble think about other people who look to God?
The speaker says, "I am poor and needy" (v. 5). Where do you feel helpless or out of options right now? Share only what you are comfortable sharing.

The psalm ends with no answer yet, only "O LORD, do not delay" (v. 5). If you have waited for help that was slow to come, what did the waiting do to you, and what do you honestly think about God in that waiting?
70.life: Pick one short prayer from this psalm, such as "You are my help and my deliverer" (v. 5). Say it out loud whenever you feel anxious or stuck this week, and notice how it changes the moment.
70.prayer: Thank God that we can come to him in a hurry, without polished words. Ask him to meet anyone in the group who is waiting for help, and to give them strength while they wait.
70.tip: Verses 2 and 3 may make some people uneasy because they sound harsh. Don't rush to explain them away. Name the discomfort, and point out that the speaker is asking God to act instead of taking revenge. Also leave room for the person who is still waiting and doubting, since the psalm itself ends without an answer.

71.open: Who is someone older than you who taught you something you still use today?
questions: The writer asks God to be "my rock of refuge, where I can always go" (v. 3). What place or person do you run to when life feels unsafe, and how does that compare to running to God?
The writer says, "You are my hope, O Lord GOD, my confidence from my youth" (v. 5). What has helped your trust in God grow, or what has made it hard to grow?

In verse 9 the writer prays, "Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails." Why might this fear be especially strong when someone is getting older? Who in your life might feel it?
The enemies say, "God has forsaken him" (v. 11). Have you ever been tempted to read hard times as a sign that God has walked away? What did you do with that thought?

Verse 13 asks that the accusers be ashamed and disgraced. It is a blunt, honest plea for justice. What do you make of a prayer that raw being in the Bible, and what does it suggest about how we can pray?

The writer says, "I will always hope and will praise You more and more" (v. 14), yet also admits that God has allowed "many troubles and misfortunes" (v. 20). How can hope and honest pain sit side by side? If hope feels thin for you right now, you can say that here too.
The writer wants to live long enough to proclaim God's power "to the next generation" (v. 18). What would you most want a younger person to know about God from your own life?
Verse 20 pictures being brought back up "from the depths of the earth." Where have you seen or hoped for new life after a very low time?
71.life: Get in touch with someone from a different generation, older or younger, and share one way God has been faithful to you. Then ask them for one of their own stories.
