71.prayer: Ask God to stay close to everyone in the group who feels worn down or forgotten, whatever their age. Thank God for the people who passed the faith on to you, and ask for the words to pass it on.
71.tip: Verse 13 may feel uncomfortable to people who think a prayer should always be gentle. Point out that the writer hands the anger to God instead of acting on it, and that the psalms often pray this way. Also keep the older and younger members on equal footing, since everyone has something to give to this psalm.

72.open: Think of a leader, teacher, coach or boss you admired. What did they do that made you trust them?
questions: The psalm opens by asking God to "endow the king with Your justice" (v. 1). Why might a leader need to receive fairness from God rather than simply have it on their own?
Verse 4 asks that the king "vindicate the afflicted" and "crush the oppressor." What does this tell us about what a good ruler is for, and what does it say about how God sees the poor?
Verse 6 compares the king to "rain that falls on freshly cut grass." What do you think that picture says about the kind of leader the psalm hopes for?
Verses 8 to 11 describe a king honored by distant lands. How does that picture strike you today: hopeful, uncomfortable, distant, or something else? Be honest about why.

Verse 12 gives the reason for the praise: "he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper." Who in your town or workplace feels like they have no helper, and what could our group do about it?
Verse 14 says the lives of the oppressed are "precious in his sight." Have you ever felt overlooked or unimportant? How does this verse land with you, even if you find it hard to believe right now?

The psalm hopes that "in him may all nations be blessed" (v. 17). Jews and Christians have read this as pointing to a future ideal king, and Christians see Jesus here. How does the psalm shape what you expect from Jesus?
The psalm ends with "Blessed be the LORD God" (v. 18). Why might a prayer about politics and poverty end in praise?
72.life: This week, pray each day for one person who holds power over others, such as a local official, a boss or a school leader. Then take one small, concrete step to help someone who has little power, like a donation, a visit or a favor.
72.prayer: Ask God to give leaders his fairness and a heart for the poor. Thank him that he hears people who cry out with no one to help, and ask him to show you where you can help.
72.tip: Some people will want to turn this into an argument about current politics. Gently bring it back to the psalm's own test in verses 12 to 14: how does power treat the weak? Also say plainly that Christians differ on whether the psalm was first about Solomon or a direct prophecy of the Messiah, and that you do not need to settle it tonight.

73.open: When did you last feel that something was unfair, even over something small like a line, a game or a grade?
questions: The writer starts with the ending he finally reached: "Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart" (v. 1). Then he says, "my feet had almost stumbled" (v. 2). Why might he begin with the answer before telling us how he struggled?
He says, "I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (v. 3). Have you ever envied someone you did not even admire? What was that like?
In verses 4 to 12 he describes people who are healthy, rich and carefree, and who say, "How can God know?" (v. 11). Which parts of that picture look familiar in our world today?
In verse 13 he says, "Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure." Have you ever wondered if doing the right thing is worth it? If you have a doubt like that, this is a safe place to say it honestly.
He held back his complaint because it "would have betrayed Your children" (v. 15). When is it wise to keep a struggle to yourself, and when does that leave you alone with it?
Things changed for him when he "entered God's sanctuary" (v. 17). What helps you step back and see your life from a bigger view: worship, quiet, friends, Scripture, or something else?

In verse 22 he admits, "I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You." Yet right after he says, "Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand" (v. 23). What stands out to you about how God treats him in his bitterness?

Verse 26 says, "My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever." What would it look like for God to be enough for you, even when other things feel unfair or unsteady?
73.life: Think of one person whose life makes you envious or resentful. This week, tell God honestly how you feel about it, and then pray one good thing for that person. Notice if anything shifts in you.
73.prayer: Thank God that we can bring our envy and doubts to him without hiding them. Ask him to hold your hand this week and to be enough for you, even when life seems unfair.
73.tip: Verse 24 says God will "later receive me in glory," and Christians read it differently: some see hope of life with God after death, others see God restoring the writer's honor in this life. Say so in one line, don't try to settle it, and keep the group on the writer's honesty and on God holding his hand.

74.open: Think of a place that meant a lot to you, like a childhood home, a church building or a favorite spot. What made it special?
questions: The psalm opens with "Why have You rejected us forever, O God?" (v. 1). What do you notice about someone asking God this question so bluntly? How does it compare with the way we usually pray?
The people call themselves "the sheep of Your pasture" and remind God he "purchased" them "long ago" (vv. 1-2). Why might they start by recalling who they are to God before describing the damage?
Verses 4 to 8 describe enemies smashing and burning the place where God was worshiped. What was lost for these people besides a building? What places or things carry that kind of weight for us?
Verse 9 says, "There are no signs for us to see. There is no longer any prophet." What do you think it is like to wait for God and hear nothing? Have you ever been in a season like that?
In verse 12 the mood turns: "Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth." Why do you think the poet starts remembering what God has done before asking for anything more?

Verses 13 to 17 praise God as the one who split the sea and set the sun, moon and seasons in place. How might remembering God's power help someone who feels forgotten? How might it feel hollow to someone in deep pain?
The psalm ends with the enemies' noise still rising and no answer given (v. 23). If you were honest, where does that ending leave you? What would you want to say to God about it?
Verse 19 pleads, "do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever." Who around us is hurting and feeling forgotten, and what could our group do about it?
74.life: This week, take one question you have been holding back from God, a real "why" or "how long," and say it to him plainly in the words of your own heart. Then write down one thing God has done in your life that you can remember, as the psalmist does in verse 12.
74.prayer: Thank God that we are allowed to bring our hardest questions to him honestly. Ask him to be near anyone in the group who feels abandoned or is grieving a loss.
74.tip: Verse 11 and parts of verses 22 and 23 ask God to strike enemies, which can feel uncomfortable. Name that gently: this is an honest cry from people in great pain, not a template to copy. Don't rush to tidy up the ending either. The psalm leaves the question open, and it's fine for the group to sit with that.

75.open: Think of a time you saw someone get a promotion, an award or a win you thought they didn't deserve, or one you thought they did. How did it feel to watch?
questions: The psalm opens with thanks: "We give thanks to You, O God" because "Your Name is near" (v. 1). When have you felt God was close, and when has he felt far away?
Verse 1 says "The people declare Your wondrous works." Whose stories of what God has done have strengthened your faith?
In verse 2 God says, "When I choose a time, I will judge fairly." Why might it be hard to wait for God's timing when things look unfair? What does it mean that the judge is fair?

Verse 3 says "When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars." What in your life or in the world feels like it is shaking right now, and what would it look like to trust that something is holding it up?
The proud are told, "Do not boast" (v. 4). In the psalm's day, lifting your horn meant flaunting your strength. What does that look like today, at work, online or at home?
Verse 7 says "it is God who judges; He brings down one and exalts another." When you watch someone rise or fall, what do you think is really behind it? How does this verse challenge or comfort you?

Verse 8 pictures God's judgment as a cup of foaming wine that the wicked drink to the dregs. Some readers find this image hard to hear. If it troubles you, or if you wonder whether God really sets things right, what would you like to say honestly?
In verse 9 the singer says, "I will proclaim Him forever." Even without answers, what is one reason you might keep praising God, or one thing that keeps you coming back?
75.life: This week, notice one moment when you are tempted to boast, to envy someone who is rising, or to despair over someone who seems to be getting away with wrong. Stop and tell God in your own words that he is the judge and that you are handing this to him.
75.prayer: Thank God that his name is near and that he judges fairly. Ask him to hold steady what feels shaky, to keep you humble, and to give patience for his timing.
75.tip: Verses 8 and 10 may stir up uncomfortable feelings about judgment, or tempt people to name enemies they hope will fall. Keep the focus on God as the fair judge and on our own humility. Note that Christians differ on who speaks in verses 2 to 5, God or a king, and that this does not change the main message. Leave room for honest doubt about justice.

76.open: When you were a kid, who or what did you count on to protect you?
questions: The psalm begins by saying "God is known in Judah" and "His name is great in Israel" (v. 1). What would you say it means for God to be truly known, and not just known about?
Verse 3 says God "shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war." What do you picture when you read that? What did a rescue like this mean for the people of Jerusalem?
The poet says the enemy soldiers "sleep their last sleep" and that "no men of might could lift a hand" (v. 5). The language is blunt and hard. How do you feel reading it, and why?
Verse 7 says, "You alone are to be feared." What do you think fear of God means here? Is it terror, deep respect, or something else?
Verse 9 says God rose up "to judge, to save all the lowly of the earth." Why might it matter that God's power is used for people with no power of their own?

Verse 10 is hard to translate, and scholars are not sure of its exact sense. It seems to say that even human anger ends up bringing God praise. Where have you seen something painful or angry turn out in a way you did not expect?
Verse 11 says, "Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God." What promises, big or small, have you made to God or to others, and what makes them hard to keep?
The psalm shows a God with enough power to break armies and the pride of rulers. If you are honest, does that make you feel safe, uneasy, or something in between? Why?
76.life: Pick one promise you have made, to God or to another person, and take one step this week to keep it. If you are carrying a worry about someone with power over you, bring it to God by name each day.
76.prayer: Praise God as the one who stands with the lowly and the afraid. Ask him to help you trust his power and to keep your promises.
76.tip: Verses 3 to 6 are about enemy soldiers dying, and some people will be uncomfortable with that. Let them say so. Point out that the psalm is a song of relief from people who had been threatened, and that verse 9 names its purpose as saving the lowly. You do not need to resolve every discomfort tonight.

77.open: When you can't sleep, what does your mind tend to do: replay the day, worry about tomorrow, or something else?
questions: The writer says, "I cried out to God; I cried aloud to God to hear me" (v. 1). What stands out to you about a prayer that is this raw and this honest?
Verse 2 says, "my soul refused to be comforted." Have you ever been in a place where comfort felt out of reach? What was that like?
In verse 3 the writer remembers God and "groaned." Why might thinking about God make a hurting person feel worse before it makes them feel better?

In verses 7 to 9 the writer asks, "Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?" What does each question reveal about what the writer fears most? Which one sounds closest to something you have wondered?
In verse 11 the writer decides, "I will remember the works of the LORD." What do you think it means to choose to remember in the middle of pain? What might that look like in daily life?

Verses 16 to 19 describe the sea, thunder and lightning, and then say, "Your footprints were not to be found" (v. 19). How could God be at work in a way that is hard to see? When have you only seen that looking back?

The psalm ends at verse 20 with God leading "like a flock" and says nothing about the writer's trouble being solved. How do you feel about an ending like that, and why might the psalm have been left this way?
If you were writing your own few lines like verses 7 to 9, honest and unfiltered, what would you put down tonight? Share only what you are comfortable with.
77.life: Pick one time God has come through for you or someone you know, and write it down in a few lines. When a hard night comes this week, read it out loud and tell God honestly how you feel.
77.prayer: Thank God that we are allowed to bring our hardest questions to him. Pray for anyone in the group who feels far from God tonight, and ask him to lead them like a flock.
77.tip: Verses 7 to 9 may sound shocking to people who think faith means never doubting. Let the questions stand without rushing to fix them. Point out that the psalm is in the Bible, that the writer keeps praying through the doubt, and that the ending is quiet rather than neat. Don't press anyone to say they feel better by the end.

78.open: What is a story from your family that gets told again and again at gatherings?
questions: The psalm opens with a teacher saying, "We will not hide them from their children" (v. 4). Who passed the faith or any important story on to you, and what did they do that stuck?
Verse 7 says the goal is that they "put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works." Why do you think remembering matters so much for trusting God?
The poet recalls the sea split and water from the rock (vv. 13 to 16), yet the people still doubted. Why can it be so easy to forget what God has done, even when we have seen real help?

In verse 19 the people ask, "Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?" When have you wondered whether God could provide in a dry or hard season? You can answer honestly, even if you are still wondering.
Verse 38 says "He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them." How does this sit alongside the harsher parts of the psalm, like verses 21 and 31?
Verse 39 says God "remembered that they were but flesh." What does it mean to you that God knows how frail and forgetful we are?
The psalm is honest about the failures of the ancestors, even the shameful ones. Why might telling the hard parts of a story help the next generation more than telling only the good parts?
The story ends with God choosing David, who was taken "from the sheepfolds" (v. 70). What does it say about God that the story ends with a shepherd, not a perfect people?
78.life: Choose one story of God's help, from your own life or from someone you know, and tell it this week to a child, a younger friend or a family member. Include a part that was hard or that you got wrong.
78.prayer: Ask God to help the group remember what he has done and to trust him in places where it is hard. Pray for the people who handed on the faith to you, and for the ones you might hand it to.
78.tip: The psalm describes God's anger and judgment plainly, including deaths in verses 31 and 50 to 51. Don't rush past them or explain them away. Let the group say it is hard to read, then point back to verses 38 and 39, where the same psalm describes God's compassion.

79.open: When you have had a really bad day, who do you call or tell first, and why that person?
questions: The psalm opens with an invasion: the nations "have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble" (v. 1). What do you notice about the way the writers describe their pain? Is it calm, angry, numb, or something else?

Verse 3 says "there is no one to bury the dead." In that world, an unburied body was a deep disgrace as well as a grief. Why might that detail have hurt so much, and what do we do today to honor the people we lose?
In verse 5 they ask, "How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever?" Have you ever wondered how long God would let something go on? What did you do with that question?

Verse 6 asks God to "pour out Your wrath on the nations." It is a raw prayer for revenge, and the psalm does not soften it. Why do you think the Bible includes prayers like this? How do you feel when you read it?
In verse 8 they pray, "Do not hold past sins against us." They own their own failures even in the middle of being wronged. Why is that hard to do, and what does it show about who they think God is?
Verse 9 asks for help "for the glory of Your name" and not because they deserve it. What difference does it make to pray that way instead of listing all the reasons God should act?
Verse 10 pictures neighbors mocking, "Where is their God?" Have you ever felt that your faith looked foolish when life fell apart? What was that like?
The psalm ends with a promise to "thank You forever" (v. 13), though nothing has changed yet. If you are in a place where you cannot honestly say that, what would you want to tell God instead?
79.life: This week, take one hurt or unfair thing that is weighing on you and tell God about it in plain words, even the angry parts, the way this psalm does. Then hand the outcome to him and note how it feels.
79.prayer: Bring to God someone you know who is grieving or has been treated cruelly. Ask him to comfort them, to bring justice, and to help the group be honest with him about pain and anger.
79.tip: Verses 6 and 12 will stir strong reactions. Christians differ here: some see honest grief that hands justice over to God instead of taking it into their own hands, and others see prayers that fall short of Jesus' call to love enemies. Name that fairly, then keep the group on what the psalm shows about bringing real feelings to God. Let quiet people pass on any question.

80.open: Think of something you once fixed or brought back to life, like a garden, a car, a friendship or a recipe. What was it, and what did it take?
questions: The psalm opens by calling God "O Shepherd of Israel" (v. 1). What does a shepherd do for a flock, and what does it say about the people that they start their prayer here?
Verses 3, 7 and 19 repeat nearly the same plea: "Restore us, O God." Why might someone in deep trouble keep praying the same words? When have you done that?

In verse 4 the people ask, "how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people?" This is a bold thing to say to God. What do you make of a prayer that sounds this honest and this frustrated?
Verse 5 says, "You fed them with the bread of tears." What would it mean for sorrow to become your daily bread? Where do you see that in people around you?
In verses 8 to 11 Israel is a vine God planted, cleared ground for and watched spread across the land. Why might the psalmist remember the good days before describing the ruin?
In verse 12 the psalmist asks, "Why have You broken down its walls?" Have you ever wanted to ask God why? If you are unsure whether God is listening, how would you say so honestly here?

In verse 18 the people say, "Then we will not turn away from You; revive us." Do they sound like people who can fix themselves or people who need help? What does that teach us about how we come to God?
Verse 17 mentions "the man at Your right hand," and Christians read it differently. Some see Israel's king or people, and others also see Jesus. How does either reading shape the hope in this psalm?
80.life: Pick one thing in your life or family that feels broken or worn down. Each day this week, pray verse 3 over it in your own words: "Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us." Notice what happens in you as you keep asking.
80.prayer: Bring God one place where you feel like a ruined vine, and ask him to look on you with favor and revive you. Pray for anyone in the group who is tired of waiting.
80.tip: Verses 4 to 6 sound like the people are accusing God, and some in the group may feel uneasy or may relate a little too well. Point out that the psalm is in the Bible, so honest complaint is welcome in prayer, and notice that the psalmist still keeps talking to God instead of walking away.

81.open: Think of a song that always makes you want to sing along, even badly. What is it, and why?
questions: The psalm opens with singing, tambourines, harps and the ram's horn (vv. 1-3). Why might God's people be told to celebrate out loud, with noise and music, instead of only thinking quietly about him?
Verse 5 is hard to translate, and Bible versions differ on who is speaking and what is heard. What do you do when a verse is unclear to you, and how does it affect the way you read the rest?
God says, "I relieved his shoulder of the burden" (v. 6). What burden has God lifted from you, or what burden do you still wish he would lift?
God recalls, "You called out in distress, and I rescued you" (v. 7). When have you cried out for help? If you are not sure God heard you, you can say so honestly.
God says, "Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it" (v. 10). What does that picture say about how God wants to treat us? What makes it hard to take him up on it?
Verses 11 and 12 say, "My people would not listen to Me," and so God "gave them up to their stubborn hearts." What do you make of the idea that God sometimes lets people go their own way?
God says, "If only My people would listen to Me" (v. 13). Does it surprise you to hear God sound so longing and sad instead of angry? What does that tell you about him?
The psalm ends with "the finest wheat" and "honey from the rock" (v. 16). What would it look like for you to be satisfied by God this week instead of by the other things you reach for?
81.life: Pick one ordinary time each day this week, like your morning coffee or your commute, and spend two minutes simply listening for God. Read one verse from this psalm, then sit quietly and notice what comes to mind. Jot down one thing you want to remember.
81.prayer: Thank God for the times he has rescued and carried you. Ask him for ears that are quick to listen and for a heart that trusts him to provide.
81.tip: Verse 12 can sound harsh, as if God simply gives up on people. Read it alongside verse 13, where God longs for them to return, and let the group see the sadness in his voice. Verse 15 is also unclear in Hebrew, so if it comes up, say plainly that translators differ and move on to the main point.

82.open: Think of a referee, teacher or boss you thought was fair. What did they do that made you trust them?
questions: The psalm opens in a courtroom where "God presides in the divine assembly" (v. 1). How does it feel to picture God as a judge who holds the powerful to account?
God asks, "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?" (v. 2). Where do you see unfairness in the world today that makes you ask "how long?"
Verses 3 and 4 name the weak, the fatherless, the afflicted and the needy. Who are the people in our town or church who have no one speaking up for them?
Christians differ on who the "gods" are in verse 1: human judges and rulers, or heavenly beings thought to oversee the nations. Does it change how you hear the psalm either way? Why or why not?
Verse 5 says "all the foundations of the earth are shaken" when justice fails. What do you think happens to a family, a workplace or a country when those in charge stop protecting the vulnerable?

God says, "You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High," and then, "But like mortals you will die" (vv. 6-7). What do you make of being given great honor and great responsibility, and still being mortal?
The psalm ends with a cry: "Arise, O God, judge the earth" (v. 8). Is that a prayer you find easy to pray, hard to pray, or something in between? Be as honest as you like.
Most of us hold some small power: over a child, an employee, a vote, a budget or a decision. Where might God be asking you to use yours for someone who has less?
82.life: Verse 3 says to "defend the cause of the weak and fatherless." This week, choose one person or group who is overlooked, and do one concrete thing for them: give, visit, speak up or learn their story.
82.prayer: Ask God to help the weak and the afflicted, and to correct leaders who fail them. Ask him to show each person one way to stand with someone who has no voice.
82.tip: Verses 1 and 6 can pull the group into a debate about who the "gods" are. Say once that Christians read it differently, and then steer back to verses 3 and 4, where the message is clear: God cares about the poor and the powerless.

83.open: When was the last time you felt like nobody was listening, and what did you do about it?
questions: The poet opens with "O God, be not silent" (v. 1). Have you ever felt that God was quiet while something painful was happening? What did that feel like?
The enemies say, "Come, let us erase them as a nation" (v. 4). What does it tell us that the poet takes this threat straight to God instead of keeping it inside?
Verses 6 to 8 name a whole ring of nations on every side. When have you felt surrounded by problems, with no safe direction to turn?
In verses 9 to 12 the poet remembers old victories like Midian and Sisera and asks God to do it again. What past moments of help do you look back on when things feel uncertain?
The enemies say, "Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God" (v. 12). Why might the poet see this as an attack on God and not only on Israel?

Verse 16 asks that enemies be covered with shame "that they may seek Your name, O LORD," while verse 17 asks that they "perish in disgrace." What do you notice about how those two hopes sit side by side?

Christians read prayers like this in different ways: as a fair cry for justice against real violence, as honest anger later shaped by Jesus' call to love enemies, or as being about spiritual evil. Which of these helps you most, and why?
Verse 18 ends with the hope that all would know God "alone" is "Most High over all the earth." If you are not sure that is true right now, what would you honestly say to God about it?
83.life: Think of one person or situation that has made you angry or afraid. This week, tell God exactly how you feel, as bluntly as the poet does, and then ask him what he would have you do next.
83.prayer: Bring God the things that feel threatening, using your own plain words. Ask him to act with justice, and to help you want what is good even for those who have hurt you.
83.tip: Verses 13 to 17 can sound harsh, and some people will feel uneasy or even defensive about them. Let the group say so. Name that Christians read these prayers differently, then point to the honesty of bringing raw anger to God instead of acting on it, and keep the focus on verse 18.

84.open: Where is the one place that feels most like home to you, and what makes it feel that way?
questions: The writer says, "My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD" (v. 2). What do you think it is like to want God's presence that much? Does it sound familiar or foreign to you right now?
In verse 3 even the sparrow "has found a home" near God's altars. Why do you think the writer notices the small birds? What might that say about how he sees himself?

Verse 4 says, "How blessed are those who dwell in Your house!" For the writer, that meant the temple in Jerusalem. Where do people meet with God today, and what does being at home with God look like for you?
Verse 5 speaks of those "whose hearts are set on pilgrimage." What does it mean to be on a journey toward God rather than already arrived? Where do you feel you are on that road?

In verse 6 pilgrims pass through the Valley of Baca and "make it a place of springs." Think of a hard stretch in your life, past or present. Where, if anywhere, have you seen something refreshing show up along the way?

Verse 7 says they "go from strength to strength." That sounds good, but many days feel more like running on empty. How would you describe where your strength comes from lately, and what happens when it runs low?

The writer says, "better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere," and would rather be "a doorkeeper" than live comfortably among the wicked (v. 10). What would you be tempted to trade away for comfort, and what makes that choice hard?

Verse 11 says God is "a sun and a shield" and "withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity." How do you read that promise alongside times when a good thing you hoped for did not come? You can answer honestly, including with doubt.
84.life: Choose one regular moment this week, like a commute, a walk or the first minutes of the morning, and make it your own small pilgrimage. Spend it simply being with God, and say out loud one line from this psalm, such as "My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD" (v. 2).
84.prayer: Thank God that he is a place to belong and not only a place to visit. Ask him to stir up a real longing for his presence, and to give strength to anyone in the group who is walking through a dry valley right now.
84.tip: Verse 11 can sting for someone whose prayers seem unanswered. Don't rush to explain it away. Let people say that gap out loud, and point back to the psalm itself, where the writer is aching and longing, not already satisfied, and still turns toward God.

85.open: Think of a time something got fixed or rescued, and then a little later it needed help again. What was it?
questions: The psalm begins by remembering: "You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin" (v. 2). Why might it help to start a prayer by recalling what God has already done?

In verse 4 the people ask, "Restore us, O God of our salvation." Most readers think life had turned hard again after an earlier rescue. Why might God's people ask for help a second time, and what does that tell you about how God is pictured here?
Verse 5 asks, "Will You be angry with us forever?" Is there a question you have been afraid to ask God out loud? Take as much or as little space as you like to answer honestly.
Verse 6 says, "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" What would feeling revived look like for you, your family or this group?
In verse 8 the speaker says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say." What makes it hard for you to stop talking and listen, and what helps?
The promise is peace, and also that He "will not let them return to folly" (v. 8). How do you hear that line: as a comfort, a warning, or both?

Verse 10 says, "Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed." We often feel these pull against each other. Where have you seen kindness and truth, or justice and peace, come together in real life?
Verses 12 and 13 picture goodness showing up in the land and righteousness going before God to prepare the way. What is one small place where you would like to see that kind of goodness grow?
85.life: Pick one hard thing in your life right now. Each day this week, spend two minutes telling God about it, then two minutes in quiet, simply listening, as the psalmist does in verse 8. Jot down anything that comes to mind.
85.prayer: Thank God for one way he has helped you or your family in the past. Then ask him honestly to do it again where help is needed now, and to give each person peace.
85.tip: Christians differ on whether verses 10 to 13 mainly describe Israel's hoped-for restoration after exile or look ahead to Christ. Say so in a sentence, let people share what they see, and bring the conversation back to the psalm's honest mix of remembering, asking and waiting. Leave a little silence after question 3 so quieter or doubting people have room to answer.

86.open: When you have a problem you can't fix yourself, who is the first person you call, and why them?
questions: David opens with "I am poor and needy" (v. 1). Why do you think he starts there instead of with praise? What is it like to come to God with nothing to offer?

In verse 2 he says, "You are my God; save Your servant who trusts in You." He calls himself God's servant more than once. What does it mean to belong to God in that way, and how does it differ from earning God's favor?
Verse 5 says God is "kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You." Which of those words is easiest for you to believe about God, and which is hardest?

In verse 7 he says, "In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me." What has your own experience of prayer been like when things were hard? Answer honestly, including if God has felt quiet.
Verse 11 asks, "Give me an undivided heart." What tends to pull your heart in different directions, and what would it look like to be more whole?

In verse 14, "the arrogant rise against me" and seek his life. Yet in verse 15 he turns with the word "But" and speaks of God as "compassionate and gracious." Why might remembering who God is matter most when we feel under threat?
Verses 8 to 10 say that "You alone are God," and that all nations will come and worship. What do you make of the idea that God's care reaches beyond one group of people to every nation?
In verse 17 he asks God to "show me a sign of Your goodness." What would a sign of God's goodness look like in your life right now, and what small signs have you already noticed?
86.life: Pick one line from this psalm, such as verse 15, and pray it each morning this week, using your own words to add what you are facing that day.
86.prayer: Thank God that he is "compassionate and gracious," slow to anger and full of faithfulness. Ask him to give each person in the group a whole heart, and to meet them in whatever need they carry tonight.
86.tip: People may hear verse 2, "for I am godly," as David bragging or as a claim that he deserves help. Gently point out that the word suggests someone tied to God by loyal love, and that the rest of the psalm leans on God's mercy, not David's record. This also helps anyone who feels too messy to pray.

87.open: Where did you grow up, and what is one thing that still makes you feel like you belong to that place?
questions: Verse 2 says "The LORD loves the gates of Zion." Why do you think the psalmist begins by speaking about God's love for a place and not only for people?
Verse 3 says "Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God." What would you say are some of the glorious things people say about God's people today? Are they always true of us?

In verse 4 God names Rahab (a poetic name for Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush. These were rivals and sometimes enemies of Israel. What do you think the first singers felt when they heard those names?
God says of each one, "This one was born in Zion" (v. 4). What does it mean to you that God speaks of outsiders as if they were native born?

Verse 6 pictures God recording names in "the register of the peoples." What is it like to think of your name being written down by God? Be honest about whether that feels comforting, strange or hard to believe.

Scholars are not sure whether the psalm means foreigners who came to worship Israel's God or Jewish people living abroad. Christians also read it as people of every nation joining God's family through Jesus. How does each reading shape the way you hear the psalm?
Who is someone you once saw as an outsider, or even an opponent, and how did your view of them change? What would it take for you to see them as fully one of your own?
The psalm ends with "All my springs of joy are in You" (v. 7). Where do you tend to look for joy, and how well do those places hold up?
87.life: Think of one person or group you tend to keep at a distance, at church, work or in your neighborhood. This week, take one small step toward them, like a greeting, an invitation or a real conversation, and ask God to help you see them as he does.
87.prayer: Thank God that he welcomes people from every background and counts them as his own. Ask him to help you make room for others and to be a source of joy for you.
87.tip: Some of the names in verse 4 will be unfamiliar, and Rahab here is not the woman from Joshua. Spend a minute at the start explaining that these were rival nations, then note that Christians differ on whether the psalm is fulfilled now in the worldwide church or also points to a future gathering of nations around Jerusalem. Leave it there and keep the focus on God welcoming outsiders.

88.open: When you have had a really bad day, who do you want to talk to, and what do you hope they will do?
questions: The psalm opens with "O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You" (v. 1). What do you notice about how the speaker begins, given how the rest of the psalm goes?
In verses 3 to 5 the speaker feels "like a man without strength" and already counted among the dead (v. 4). What words would you use to describe what this kind of weariness feels like?

The speaker says to God, "Your wrath weighs heavily upon me" (v. 7), and "You have removed my friends from me" (v. 8). Why do you think the writer is willing to say this straight to God instead of softening it?

In verses 10 to 12 the speaker asks if God's wonders and faithfulness can be known among the dead. Many readers hear this as: help me now, while I am still alive. What do you make of that kind of bargaining prayer?

Verse 14 asks, "Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?" Have you ever felt that God was silent or far away? You can answer honestly, including if you feel that way now or have doubts.
The psalm ends with no turn toward hope, and the last line is hard: "darkness is my closest companion" (v. 18). Why might God have let a prayer like this stay in the Bible?
Christians disagree about whether there is a quiet thread of hope here, since the speaker keeps praying, or whether this is meant to be an unanswered cry. Which reading feels truer to you, and why?
How can we sit with someone in a dark season without rushing to fix it or hand them a quick verse?
88.life: This week, think of one person who is going through a long hard stretch. Reach out with a call or a visit, and instead of offering answers, simply listen and stay with them.
88.prayer: Ask God for the honesty to bring him the real state of things, even when words are few. Pray for anyone in the group or beyond it who is in a dark place tonight.
88.tip: The psalm has no happy ending, and people may feel pressure to add one. Resist the urge to wrap it up with a hopeful verse. Let the silence of the ending stand for a moment, and make clear that it is fine to be honest about doubt or darkness in this group.

89.open: Think of a promise someone made to you, big or small, that you were counting on. How did you feel while you waited to see if they would keep it?
questions: The psalm opens, "I will sing of the loving devotion of the LORD forever" (v. 1). Why do you think the poet starts with praise when he is about to complain?
God is pictured as ruling the sea and crushing Rahab, the sea monster of chaos (vv. 9, 10). What kinds of chaos in life or in the world make it hard to believe God is in charge?
In verses 3 and 4 God swears a covenant with David, and in verses 33 and 34 he says, "I will not violate My covenant." Why does the poet keep coming back to God's own words?
Verses 30 to 33 say that if David's sons stray, God will discipline them, but he will not "withdraw My loving devotion." What does this show about how God deals with people who fail?

Then the mood turns: "Now, however, You have spurned and rejected him" (v. 38). What did the poet's world look like, and how would it have felt to hold on to a promise like this while living through it?
The poet asks, "How long, O LORD? Will You hide Yourself forever?" (v. 46). Have you ever asked God a question like that, or wanted to? You can answer honestly, including if you mostly feel silence.
Verse 49 asks, "Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old?" Why might God keep a prayer like this in the Bible instead of leaving it out?

The psalm ends with "Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen" (v. 52), but nothing has been fixed. What do you make of that ending? Some read it as trust holding firm, others as a protest left open on purpose.
89.life: This week, take one thing you have been quietly disappointed about with God and say it to him plainly, the way the poet does. Write a few lines if that helps. If you can, end with one true thing about God that you still hold on to.
89.prayer: Thank God for being faithful to his word across generations. Ask for honesty to bring him your disappointments, and for patience to keep trusting while you wait. Pray for anyone in the group who feels let down.
89.tip: Verses 38 to 51 are blunt, and some people will feel uneasy hearing a prayer that accuses God. Don't rush to soften it or tie it up neatly. Point out that this complaint is in Scripture, and that the poet is still talking to God. Also expect some to say the praise and the complaint belong together, and others to say the pain is left standing. Both can be shared without settling it.

90.open: What is something you have owned or used for a long time, and why have you held on to it?
questions: The psalm begins, "You have been our dwelling place through all generations" (v. 1). What does it mean to you to think of God as a home? When have you felt at home, or not, with God?
Verse 2 says, "from everlasting to everlasting You are God." How does it feel to set your own life next to a God who has no beginning and no end?

Verse 4 says "a thousand years are but a day that passes," and the following verses compare people to grass that is fresh in the morning and withered by evening. What is your honest reaction to how short this psalm says life is?

In verse 8 our "secret sins" are "in the light of Your presence." Christians read the anger in verses 7 to 11 differently: some see it as explaining why all people die, others as the hardship of one generation, such as Israel in the wilderness. How do you hear these verses, and what questions do they raise for you?

Verse 9 says "we finish our years with a sigh," and verse 10 speaks of "labor and sorrow." Where does life feel heavy for you right now? If you are not sure God is listening, you can say that here too.
Verse 12 asks God to "teach us to number our days." What would change in your week if you took that seriously? What might you stop doing, and what might you start?
In verse 14 the writer asks, "Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion." What would it look like for God's steady love to be the first thing that fills you each day?
The psalm ends by asking God to "establish the work of our hands" (v. 17). What work, paid or unpaid, do you hope will outlast you, and what do you want God to do with it?
90.life: Take ten quiet minutes this week to number your days. Write down three things you most want your remaining years to be about. Then bring that list to God and ask him to teach you to live by it.
90.prayer: Thank God that he has been a home for his people in every generation. Ask for wisdom to use your days well, for his steady love each morning, and for him to give lasting meaning to the work of your hands.
90.tip: This psalm is honest about death and God's anger, and some people will find that heavy or even upsetting. Do not rush to smooth it over. Let people say what troubles them, note that Christians read verses 7 to 11 in different ways, and then guide the group toward the plea for mercy and gladness in verses 13 to 17.

91.open: When you were a kid, where did you go when you were scared or sick, and who did you want nearby?
questions: The psalm begins with someone who "dwells in the shelter of the Most High" (v. 1). What does it look like to treat God as a home you live in and not just a place you visit?
In verse 2 the writer says, "You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust." Is it easy or hard for you to say those words in the first person right now? What makes it so?
Verse 4 says, "He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge." What does a mother bird's wing tell you about God that a fortress does not?
Verses 5 and 6 list fears by night, by day, in darkness and at noon. Which of these fears feels closest to the ones you carry today?

Verse 7 says, "Though a thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, no harm will come near you." Many of us have seen faithful people suffer. How do you hold that promise and that experience together?
In verses 11 and 12 God promises angels who "will lift you up in their hands." What did that kind of promise mean to the first singers of this psalm, and what might it mean for us?

In verse 15 God says, "I will be with him in trouble." How is being with someone in trouble different from keeping trouble away? Have you ever known God's nearness in a hard season, or wondered where it was?

God ends the psalm by speaking directly: "Because he loves Me, I will deliver him" (v. 14). If you imagined God saying those words to you, what would you feel, and what might get in the way of believing it?
91.life: Each morning this week, say verse 2 aloud in your own words, starting with "You are my refuge." When a fear comes up during the day, name it to God and repeat the line.
91.prayer: Thank God that he is a shelter and a faithful shield. Ask him to be close to anyone in the group who is afraid or struggling right now, and to help each person trust him honestly, even with doubts.
91.tip: Verses 7 and 10 can sting for anyone who has lost someone or been through illness. Christians differ on whether these promises mean physical safety or a deeper security in God's presence, so say that plainly. Make room for people to be honest about pain without hurrying to fix it, and keep returning to verse 15, where God promises to be with us in trouble.

92.open: What is one thing you do every week that you would hate to lose, a habit, a meal or a place?
questions: This psalm is a song for the Sabbath day, and verse 1 says, "It is good to praise the LORD." What does rest, or setting time aside for God, look like in your week right now, and what gets in the way?
The singer says God has "made me glad by Your deeds" (v. 4). What has God done, in the world or in your own life, that makes you glad?
Verse 7 says "the wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish." When people who cause harm seem to thrive, what, if anything, helps you make sense of it? It is fine to say nothing helps yet.
Verse 8 sits at the center of the poem: "But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!" Why might the writer put that line in the middle of a song about the wicked and the righteous?

Verses 7, 9 and 12 speak of the wicked being destroyed and the righteous flourishing. Christians differ on whether this is mainly about this life or mainly about a final judgment. How does each reading change the way you hear the psalm?
In verse 11 the singer says, "My eyes see the downfall of my enemies." How do you feel reading that, and how do you hold it alongside the rest of what you know about God?
Verse 12 says "The righteous will flourish like a palm tree," and verse 13 says they are "Planted in the house of the LORD." What helps you stay rooted, and what tends to pull you loose?
Verse 14 says "In old age they will still bear fruit." Who do you know, older than you, who is still fruitful, and what do you see in their life?
92.life: Each morning this week, say one sentence about God's loving devotion toward you. Each night, name one way you saw his faithfulness that day. If you can, thank an older person who has shown you what a lasting life with God looks like.
92.prayer: Thank God that he is "exalted forever" and that his love and faithfulness are there morning and night. Ask him to root each person in the group deeply, and to give honest peace to anyone struggling with unfairness.
92.tip: Verses 7 and 11 can sting for someone who has been hurt by a person who seems to have gotten away with it. Let people speak honestly without rushing to fix anything. Say plainly that Christians read the promises of this psalm differently, and keep the group looking at verse 8, where the poem rests.

93.open: Have you ever been caught in a big storm, or watched one from somewhere safe? What was it like?
questions: The psalm opens with "The LORD reigns!" (v. 1). Why might someone sing that out loud as good news? What does it say about who is in charge?
God is described as "robed in majesty" and "clothed and armed" with strength (v. 1). What do those pictures tell you about what kind of king he is?
Verse 2 says, "Your throne was established long ago; You are from all eternity." How does it feel to think of God as older than everything else? Comforting, distant, or something else?
In verse 3 the floods and seas "lift up their pounding waves." To an ancient reader the sea meant chaos and danger. What feels like rising water in your life or in the world right now?

Verse 4 says that "above the roar of many waters" the LORD "is majestic." The psalm does not say the waves disappear. What difference does it make to be told God is above them, not that they are gone?
Some readers see the floods as hostile nations, and others as life's upheavals. Which picture speaks to you, and why?
Verse 5 says, "Your testimonies are fully confirmed." What has ever felt steady enough to hold on to when life was rough? If nothing has, what would you want to be true of God?
The psalm ends with "holiness adorns Your house, O LORD, for all the days to come" (v. 5). What do you think it means for God's presence to be holy and lasting, and why might that matter to us?
93.life: Pick one thing that feels like rising water this week. Each morning, say verse 1 or verse 4 out loud as a reminder of who is above it, and tell God honestly how you feel about the situation.
93.prayer: Thank God that he reigns and is steady when everything else is not. Invite people to name a worry, then ask him to be their firm place to stand.
93.tip: Christians differ on whether "the LORD reigns" describes God's rule right now or looks ahead to a fuller kingdom still to come, and many hold both. Say so briefly. If someone is going through real hardship, do not rush to explain why the waves exist. Let the psalm say what it says: the waves are loud, and God is louder.

94.open: When did you last feel something was unfair, even in a small way, and what did you do about it?
questions: The writer begins with "O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth" (v. 1). What do you feel when you hear the word vengeance used of God? What do you think the writer is asking for?
The writer asks, "How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?" (v. 3). Why do you think the Bible lets people complain to God this honestly?
Verse 6 says, "They kill the widow and the foreigner; they murder the fatherless." Why does the psalm single out these people, and who are the people today with no one to speak for them?
The oppressors say, "The LORD does not see" (v. 7). When have you wondered whether God sees what is going on, in the world or in your own life?

Verse 9 asks, "He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?" How does this argument land for you? Does it settle the question, or does something still feel unanswered?
Verse 12 calls the person God disciplines and teaches blessed. How can hard seasons teach us something without God being the one who causes the harm? What have you learned in a difficult time?
The writer says that when his foot is slipping, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me" (v. 18). Where do you feel your footing is slipping right now, and what would being held up look like?

The psalm ends by asking God to destroy the wicked (v. 23). Christians differ on how to pray words like these. What do you think a person can honestly pray when they have been hurt or have seen others hurt?
94.life: This week, pick one person or group who is being treated unfairly, in your town or in the news. Pray for them by name each day, and ask God if there is one small thing you could do to help.
94.prayer: Bring God one injustice that weighs on you and say it plainly, as the psalm does. Thank him that "the LORD will not forsake His people" (v. 14), and ask him to hold up anyone in the group who feels their foot slipping.
94.tip: Verses 1 to 3 and 23 can make some people uneasy, and others may jump to say they are the whole point. Say once, fairly, that Christians pray these lines differently, then steer back to the heart of the psalm: God sees, and he holds up the weary. Let quiet people know it is fine to say they are not sure God is paying attention.

95.open: What is a song that gets you singing, even if you sing badly?
questions: The psalm opens with "Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD" (v. 1). When has worship, singing or otherwise, felt like real joy to you? When has it felt more like a duty?
God is called "the Rock of our salvation" (v. 1). What does a rock picture for you, and when have you needed something solid to stand on?
Verses 4 and 5 say the depths, the mountain peaks and the sea all belong to God. How does it change the way you see your worries to hear that he holds all of it?
In verse 6 the mood moves from shouting to bowing: "let us kneel before the LORD our Maker." What helps you slow down and be quiet before God, and what gets in the way?
Verse 7 says "we are the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care." What do you like about being called a sheep? What do you find hard about it?

God warns, "do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah" (v. 8). That generation had "seen My work" and still tested him (v. 9). Why can it be so hard to trust God in a dry season, even after good ones? Feel free to answer honestly if trust is hard for you right now.
Verse 7 says "Today, if you hear His voice." What might it look like to listen for God today, and not put it off?
The psalm ends with a sad line: "They shall never enter My rest" (v. 11). Christians read "rest" in different ways, as peace now, a home after death, or both. What does rest with God mean to you?
95.life: Each day this week, pause for two minutes and read verse 7 slowly. Ask God what he might be saying to you today, and write down one thing you notice, even if it is only a worry you need to hand over.
95.prayer: Thank God for being your Maker and your Shepherd. Ask him to soften any place where your heart has gone hard, and to help you listen today.
95.tip: Verses 10 and 11 can sound harsh, and someone may feel afraid that God is angry with them. Point out that the warning is aimed at stubborn distrust, not at honest struggle, and that the psalm begins with joyful welcome. Let people name their doubts without hurrying to fix them.

96.open: What is a song that instantly puts you in a good mood, and why?
questions: The psalm opens with "Sing to the LORD a new song" (v. 1). Readers take "new song" in different ways. What would a fresh song of thanks from your own life sound like right now?
Verse 2 says to "proclaim His salvation day after day." Why do you think praise is meant to be daily and not only for special occasions? What does a daily habit of thanks look like for you?
Verse 3 says to "declare His glory among the nations." The invitation goes to everyone, not only one people. How does it change the way you see people who are different from you?

Verse 5 says "all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens." What do people around you look to for security or meaning in place of God, and why do those things so often fall short?
Verse 8 says "bring an offering and enter His courts." What do you have to bring to God right now? What makes it hard to come at all, whether through doubt, tiredness or distance?
Verse 10 announces, "The LORD reigns!" and says "the world is firmly established." When the world feels unsteady, what does it mean to you, or what would you want it to mean, that God is king?

Verse 13 says creation rejoices because "He is coming to judge the earth." Most of us find judgment frightening. Why might this psalm treat it as good news, and what in the world would you most want to see set right?
Christians read the coming in verse 13 in different ways. Some see it pointing to Jesus returning, others see it describing God's rule at any time. How does each reading give you hope?
96.life: Each day this week, name one specific thing God has done or made that you are thankful for, and say it out loud or write it down. Share one with someone outside the group.
96.prayer: Praise God as the maker of the heavens and the true king. Ask him to set right what is broken in the world, and for the courage to bring your honest self into his presence.
96.tip: Verse 13 about judgment may make some people uneasy, and others may think of people who have hurt them. Name that gently, point to the psalm's emphasis on "righteousness" and "faithfulness," and note that Christians read the timing differently. Leave room for honest unease.

97.open: What is the most impressive storm you have ever seen, and how did it make you feel?
questions: The psalm begins, "The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice" (v. 1). What does it mean to you, in everyday terms, that God is king?
Verse 2 says, "Clouds and darkness surround Him; righteousness and justice are His throne's foundation." Why might a psalm put mystery and fairness side by side?

In verses 3 to 5 God comes with fire, lightning and mountains that "melt like wax." The original readers likely thought of Sinai. How do these pictures make you feel about God: afraid, comforted, something else?
Verse 6 says, "The heavens proclaim His righteousness." Where have you seen something in the world that pointed you toward what is right and good?
Verse 7 speaks of those who "boast in idols." What are some modern things people lean on that cannot actually save or help them?

Verse 8 says Zion rejoices "because of Your judgments." Many of us find God's judgment hard to celebrate. When might the hope that wrongs will be set right be good news? You can answer honestly if it still feels difficult.
Verse 10 says, "Hate evil, O you who love the LORD!" and promises that He "preserves the souls of His saints." What does it look like to turn from evil while trusting God to keep us?

Verse 11 says, "Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart." Has there been a time when light or gladness came after a dark stretch? If you are in the dark now, what would help you hold on to hope?
97.life: Each day this week, pause once and name one thing you are tempted to trust more than God. Then say verse 1 aloud: "The LORD reigns." Notice what changes.
97.prayer: Praise God as the one who is "Most High over all the earth" (v. 9). Ask him to bring light to anyone in the group who is walking through darkness right now.
97.tip: The fire and judgment language can unsettle people. Don't rush to explain it away. Let the group say honestly what it stirs up, and point back to verses 8 and 12, where the psalm treats God's just rule as a reason for gladness. Christians also differ on whether the psalm describes God's rule now or a future kingdom, so you can name that in one line and keep moving.

98.open: What is a song that instantly lifts your mood, and why does it work for you?
questions: The psalm opens, "Sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done wonders" (v. 1). What is one thing God has done, in the Bible or in your own life, that you could sing about?
Verse 1 says His "right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory." Why might the psalm stress that God wins this rescue himself? What does that say about how we receive it?

Verse 3 says God "has remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel." Many think this looks back to the return from exile. What does it tell us about God that he keeps his promises to people who have wandered?
Verse 3 also says "all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God." Why does it matter that this song is for every nation and not only for Israel?
Verses 4 to 6 pile up loud sounds: harps, trumpets and the ram's horn, all "before the LORD, the King" (v. 6). Where do you find it easiest to praise God, and where does it feel awkward or empty?
Some days you may not feel like singing at all. What would you say honestly about where you are with God right now, and what might it mean that this psalm invites everyone to join in anyway?
In verses 7 to 9 even the sea, rivers and mountains rejoice because God "comes to judge the earth" (v. 9). Most of us hear judgment as a threat. How does the psalm make it sound like good news?

The psalm says God will judge "with righteousness" and "with equity" (v. 9). Think of a time you longed for someone truly fair to set things right. What would make that feel like hope rather than dread?
98.life: Sing or play one song of praise each day this week, even if it is only in the car or the kitchen. Let it be a way to tell God thanks for one specific thing.
98.prayer: Thank God for the "wonders" he has done, and for being a King who is fair and faithful. Ask him to help you praise him honestly, whether you feel like singing or not.
98.tip: Verse 9 may bring up questions about judgment. Christians differ on whether the coming King points to Israel's own day, to Jesus' first coming, or to his return. Say so in a line, then steer back to the psalm's tone: joy that God will finally make things right.

99.open: Who is someone you would trust to listen to you and take your side, and what makes them that kind of person?
questions: The psalm opens with "The LORD reigns; let the nations tremble!" (v. 1). Does picturing God as a king comfort you, unsettle you, or both? Why?
Verse 3 calls God's name "great and awesome" and says "He is holy!" What does the word holy mean to you in plain words, and where did you pick up that idea?
"The mighty King loves justice" (v. 4). Where in the world, or in your own life, do you long to see things made right?
Verse 6 says of Moses, Aaron and Samuel, "They called to the LORD and He answered." Has there been a time when you prayed and it felt like silence? What was that like for you?
God spoke to these leaders "from the pillar of cloud" (v. 7), which recalled Israel's journey after Egypt. Why might the writer remind worshipers of old stories like this?

Verse 8 says God was "a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds." Scholars are not sure whose wrongdoing is meant, but the pairing is clear. Have you ever been forgiven and still faced consequences? How did that feel?
Verses 5 and 9 both say "Exalt the LORD our God," and the refrain "He is holy" returns three times. Why repeat it, and what would it look like to honor God this week in ordinary life?
99.life: Pick one thing you have been hesitant to bring to God in prayer, and say it to him plainly each day this week. Notice how it feels to speak to a God who is both holy and willing to listen.
99.prayer: Praise God as the holy King who hears those who call on him. Ask for honesty to bring him what you are really carrying, and thank him for being forgiving.
99.tip: Verse 8 puzzles readers, and it is not certain whose wrongdoing is meant. Say that briefly, then turn to the question of forgiveness and consequences from real life. Also leave room for anyone who feels their prayers have gone unanswered, and let them speak without rushing to fix it.

100.open: When was the last time someone said thank you to you in a way you still remember?
questions: The psalm opens with "Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth" (v. 1). Who is being invited here, and what does that tell us about who God is for?
Verse 2 says to "Serve the LORD with gladness." When have worship or service felt more like a duty than a joy? What was going on?
Verse 3 says, "Know that the LORD is God." Why might the writer ask us to know this before asking us to sing or give thanks?

The psalm says "It is He who made us, and we are His" (v. 3). Some ancient copies read this a little differently, saying God made us and not we ourselves. Either way, how does it feel to hear that you belong to God?
We are called "the sheep of His pasture" (v. 3). What does a good shepherd do for sheep, and where have you seen God do something like that for you?
Verse 4 says to "Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise." What helps you slow down and arrive in a thankful frame of mind, whether at church, at home or on your commute?

The psalm gives its reason in verse 5: "the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever." If gratitude feels hard right now, what is getting in the way, and what is one small thing you can still honestly thank God for?
Verse 5 also says "His faithfulness continues to all generations." Who handed faith down to you, and who might you pass it to?
100.life: Each day this week, write down one thing you are thankful for and one way you have seen God's goodness. Say thank you to God out loud, and tell one person about something on your list.
100.prayer: Thank God that he made you, that you belong to him, and that he cares for you like a shepherd. Ask him to grow a thankful heart in each person, including anyone who finds gratitude hard right now.
100.tip: Some people will hear "joyful noise" and "gladness" as pressure to feel happy when they don't. Say plainly that the psalm gives reasons for thanks (God is good and faithful) and does not demand a mood. Let honest answers to the gratitude question stand without trying to fix them.

101.open: What is one small habit you keep at home that nobody outside your household would guess about you?
questions: The psalm begins, "I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice" (v. 1). Why might the king start with praise before he makes any promises?
The king says, "I will walk in my house with integrity of heart" (v. 2). Why might he begin with his own home rather than the whole land? What changes when no one is watching?
In the middle of verse 2 he asks, "when will You come to me?" Scholars are not sure what lies behind that question. What do you hear in it, and have you ever felt that kind of waiting for God?
Verse 3 says, "I will set no worthless thing before my eyes." What are the things competing for our eyes and attention today, and how do you decide what to let in?
The king vows to silence "whoever slanders his neighbor in secret" (v. 5). Why do you think gossip and slander are taken so seriously here? When have you seen words in secret do real damage?
In verse 6 he looks for "the faithful of the land" to be near him. Who are the people you trust to tell you the truth, and what makes them that kind of person?
Verse 8 speaks of removing the wicked every morning, which is hard language. How do you react to it? Think about a king's real power in that day, and how it differs from what we have now.
Here the king makes promises he must keep by his own strength. Where do you find it hard to live up to your own good intentions, and what do you do with that honestly before God?
101.life: Pick one private area of your life, such as what you watch, what you say about people when they are not there, or how you speak at home. Choose one small change this week, and ask God to help you keep it.
101.prayer: Thank God for his loving devotion and justice. Ask him to help you be the same person at home as in public, and to bring honest, faithful people into your life.
101.tip: Verse 8 can sound harsh, and some will wonder how it fits with grace. Name it plainly as a king's vow about his court and city, and note that Christians differ on whether the psalm is mainly a model for any leader or chiefly a picture of the ideal king, which many see fulfilled in Jesus. Then steer back to the personal questions about home and integrity.

102.open: What is something in your life that has lasted much longer than you expected, like a car, a friendship or a pair of shoes?
questions: The heading calls this the prayer of one who "pours out his lament before the LORD" (v. 1). What does it say about God that a prayer like this ended up in the Bible?
In verses 3 to 7 the writer describes smoke, burning bones, no appetite and a "lone bird on a housetop" (v. 7). Which picture comes closest to what exhaustion or loneliness feels like for you?

The writer asks, "Do not hide Your face from me in my day of distress" (v. 2), and later says God has "picked me up and cast me aside" (v. 10). Many people feel this way but are afraid to say it to God. What do you make of a prayer this blunt?

In verse 12 the mood shifts: "But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever." The pain has not gone away, so what do you think changed? Have you ever had a moment when you were still hurting but looked up anyway?
Verse 17 says God "will turn toward the prayer of the destitute." What would it mean for you to believe that your prayer, even a weak or doubtful one, is not despised?
The writer wants this recorded so that "a people not yet created may praise the LORD" (v. 18). Who has written down or passed on their faith in a way that helped you? Who might you do that for?

In verses 24 to 27 the writer feels his life is cut short, yet he says of God, "You remain the same, and Your years will never end" (v. 27). When life feels fragile or short, does that thought bring comfort, frustration or something else? Be honest.
Christians read verses 25 to 27 in different ways, and some connect them to Jesus because of Hebrews. However you read them, how does a God who outlasts everything change the way you face this week?
102.life: This week, write your own short lament: two or three honest sentences telling God exactly how things are, without tidying them up. Then add one line about who God is, the way verse 12 does, and read both aloud.
102.prayer: Ask God to hear the honest cry of anyone in the group who is tired, sick or alone. Thank him that he stays the same when everything else wears out.
102.tip: The psalm moves from deep despair to confidence without explaining how. Don't hurry anyone toward the happy part. Let people sit in verses 1 to 11 first, and remind the group that the writer's circumstances never visibly change, only where he is looking.

103.open: What is a small kindness someone did for you that you still remember?
questions: The poet talks to himself: "Bless the LORD, O my soul" (v. 1). Why might someone need to give themselves that kind of pep talk? When have you had to do something like it?
Verse 2 says, "do not forget all His kind deeds." What are one or two things from your own life that you would put on that list?
Verse 8 says, "The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion." Is that how you usually picture God? If not, what picture tends to come to mind?
Verse 10 says, "He has not dealt with us according to our sins." Does being treated better than you deserve feel more like relief or more like something that is hard to accept? Why?

Verse 12 says, "As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us." What does it mean to you that wrongdoing can be taken that far away? Is there something you find hard to believe has been removed?

Verse 14 says, "He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust." How does it feel to know that God understands how fragile and limited we are? How might that change how you treat your own failures, or other people's?

Verses 15 and 16 say our days are "like grass" and quickly gone, yet God's love lasts from one generation to the next (v. 17). Some days it is hard to feel that any of this is true. What makes it hard for you, and what would you most want to be true?
103.life: Write down three or four specific things God has done for you, the kind of "kind deeds" verse 2 means. Read your list aloud once each day this week and thank God for each item.
103.prayer: Thank God that he is compassionate and gracious and does not treat us as our sins deserve. Ask him to help each person remember his kindness on the days when it is hard to feel.
103.tip: Verse 3 says God "heals all your diseases," and that can sting for someone who is sick or grieving. Don't rush past it. Say that the psalm is praising God for his care and forgiveness, and let people say honestly where healing has not come. Keep the focus on God's compassion for those who are fragile (vv. 13 and 14).

104.open: What is a place outdoors, big or small, where you feel most at ease?
questions: The psalm begins with the poet talking to himself: "Bless the LORD, O my soul!" (v. 1). Why might someone need to tell their own soul to praise God? When do you need that reminder?
God is pictured as a king who "wraps Himself in light as with a garment" (v. 2). What does this picture tell us about who God is?

Verse 9 says God "set a boundary" for the waters so they would never again cover the earth. The poet sees a world that is kept safe by God and not left to chaos. Where do you see order and steadiness in the world, and where does life feel out of control?

Verse 15 mentions "wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine, and bread that sustains his heart." What everyday gifts do you tend to take for granted? Which one could you thank God for today?
In verse 21 even the young lions "seek their food from God." What does it mean that every creature, strong or small, depends on him? How does that change the way you think about your own needs?

Verse 24 says, "How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all." What in nature has ever stopped you in your tracks, and what did you make of that feeling? If nothing has, what do you make of that?

Verses 27 to 30 describe creatures fed when God opens his hand, and dying when he takes away their breath. How do you feel about a God who holds both life and death? Say honestly what comes up for you.
The poet ends with "I will sing to the LORD all my life" (v. 33). What would it look like for your ordinary days, your work and rest, to be a kind of song to God?
104.life: Once a day this week, go outside for five minutes with no phone. Notice one thing God made, and thank him for it by name, whether that is a bird, a tree, the sky or the weather.
104.prayer: Ask God to open your eyes to his gifts in daily life. Thank him for one thing he has provided this week, and pray for anyone in the group who is finding it hard to feel thankful.
104.tip: Verse 35 asks for "sinners" to "vanish from the earth," and it can jar a group. Don't skip it or explain it away. Say plainly that it is a harsh line, that many readers take it as a wish to be rid of whatever spoils this good world, and then bring the group back to the praise that frames it.

105.open: If someone asked you to tell your family's story in two minutes, what is one event you would be sure to include?
questions: The psalm begins with a string of commands: give thanks, sing, tell, seek (vv. 1-4). Which of these comes most naturally to you, and which is hardest right now?
Verse 4 says, "seek His face always." What does seeking God look like in an ordinary week for you, and what gets in the way?
Verse 8 says God "remembers His covenant forever." What do you think it meant for Israel to hear that, and what might it mean for us?
Abraham's family were "few in number" and "strangers in the land" (v. 12), yet God protected them. When have you felt small or like an outsider? What was that like?
Joseph was chained and forgotten, and the psalm says God "sent a man before them" (vv. 17-18). How does seeing Joseph's story this way sit with you, especially if you are in a hard stretch yourself?

The psalm says God turned Egypt's hearts to hate His people (v. 25), and it tells of the plagues and the firstborn (v. 36). Some readers find this hard to hear. What troubles you or puzzles you here, and what do you still want to ask God about it?

Verse 44 says Israel received "the fruit of others' labor." The psalm is honest that the land had belonged to other peoples. How do we keep praising God for his faithfulness while staying honest about what his people's story cost others?
The psalm ends by saying the purpose was "that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws" (v. 45). Why might the psalmist tie God's rescue to a way of living? How does that fit with grace?
105.life: Take ten minutes this week to write out a short list of times God has come through for you or your family, even in small ways. Share one of them with someone who needs encouragement.
105.prayer: Thank God that he "remembers His covenant forever" (v. 8). Ask him to help you remember what he has done, and to trust him in the part of your story that still feels unfinished.
105.tip: The psalm says God turned Egypt's hearts to hate Israel and tells of the plagues without explanation, and the land promise is also a sensitive subject. Let people say these parts are hard. Note plainly that Christians differ on whether the land promise still applies to the Jewish people today or is fulfilled in a spiritual way through Jesus, then bring the group back to the psalm's main point: God keeps his word.

106.open: What is something you keep forgetting, like keys, a name or a password, no matter how many reminders you set?
questions: The singers say, "We have sinned like our fathers" (v. 6). They own the failures of the past as their own. Why might it help to be honest about the patterns in our family, church or country instead of blaming or ignoring them?

At the Red Sea God saved the people "for the sake of His name, to make His power known" (v. 8), even though they had not grasped his wonders. How does it feel to hear that rescue did not depend on them getting it right?
Verse 13 says, "they soon forgot His works." What helps you remember what God has done, and what tends to make you forget?
In verse 15, "He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them." Have you ever gotten something you wanted that turned out not to be good for you? What did you learn?
Verse 23 says "Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach," like a soldier in a gap in a broken wall. Who has stood in the gap for you, and who might need you to do that for them?
The people "despised the pleasant land" (v. 24), walking away from something good God had promised. Why do people turn from good things? Where do you see that tendency in yourself?
