In verses 34 to 36 the people did not fully break with the nations around them, and their idols "became a snare" to them. What small compromises can slowly pull people away from God today?

This psalm is full of hard stories and God's anger, and some of it may be difficult to read. What questions or doubts does it raise for you? Then look at verses 44 and 45. What do you notice about how God responds to his people?
106.life: Take ten minutes this week to write down three times God helped you or your family, even if you did not see it then. Thank him for each one. Then name one pattern you keep repeating and ask for his help with it.
106.prayer: Thank God that "His loving devotion endures forever" (v. 1). Confess honestly the patterns you keep falling into, and ask him to rescue and gather his people again.
106.tip: Verses 17 and 18, 30 and 37 and 38 are hard to read, and the group may get stuck on them. You do not need to explain every judgment. Say that the psalm itself calls these acts wrong, and bring people back to the whole shape of the chapter: the people fail again and again, and God's mercy has the last word (v. 45).

107.open: Think of a time you were lost, whether on a road, in a city or in a store. What did you do, and who or what finally got you back on track?
questions: The psalm opens with "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever" (v. 1). Why do you think the writer starts with thanks before telling any of the stories?
Verse 2 says, "Let the redeemed of the LORD say so." Why might saying it out loud to other people matter, and not only feeling grateful on our own?
Four groups are in trouble: wanderers, prisoners, the sick and sailors. Which picture is closest to where you have been, or where you are right now?
Four times we hear the same line, "Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble" (v. 6). What does it tell you that the cry comes first, before they have fixed anything?

The prisoners and the sick are in trouble partly because of their own choices (vv. 11, 17). Yet God still rescues them. How does that sit with you, and what does it say about how God treats people who have made a mess?
The sailors say "all their skill was useless" (v. 27). When have you reached the end of your own ability, and what was that like?
Some of us find it hard to cry out, or wonder if anyone is listening. What makes it hard for you to ask God for help, and what would an honest first sentence sound like?
Verse 43 closes by urging us to "consider the loving devotion of the LORD." What is one moment from your own life you could look back on and think about in that way?
107.life: Pick one rescue or answered prayer from your life, big or small, and tell it to someone this week, either face to face or in a message. Use the psalm's pattern: where I was, what I did, how I got through, and a thank you.
107.prayer: Thank God for his "loving devotion" that does not run out. Invite people to name quietly or aloud one place where they need rescue now, and one place where they have already been helped.
107.tip: The psalm links the trouble of the prisoners and the sick to their own wrongdoing, and that can sting anyone who is suffering through no fault of their own. Say plainly that the psalm does not claim all hardship is a punishment, and keep the group focused on the repeated cry and rescue.

108.open: What is a song that gets you moving or lifts your mood when you are having a rough morning?
questions: The psalm opens with "My heart is steadfast, O God" (v. 1). What does a steady heart look like to you, and when has yours felt the opposite?

The singer says, "I will awaken the dawn" (v. 2). What does it say about this person that praise comes first thing, before the day's troubles? What is the first thing you usually turn to in the morning?
Verse 3 says, "I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations." Why might it matter that this praise is public and not private? Where do you find it easy or hard to speak openly about God?
Verse 4 says God's "loving devotion extends beyond the heavens." Think of a time you felt loved or stuck with. How does that picture of God's love compare?

In verses 7 to 9 God speaks and claims places and peoples as his own, even calling Moab his "washbasin." What do you think those images were meant to say to Israel then? How might they sound to us today?

In verse 11 the singer asks, "Have You not rejected us, O God?" Why do you think this honest complaint sits right beside the praise? Have you ever felt that God was far away while still wanting to hold on?
Verse 12 says, "the help of man is worthless." Where are you tempted to lean on people, money, plans or your own strength instead of God? What would it look like to lean on God there, too?
The psalm ends with "With God we will perform with valor" (v. 13). What is one hard thing in your life right now where you need courage, and what would help you take the next step?
108.life: Pick one hard thing you are facing this week. Before you deal with it each morning, spend a minute giving thanks to God for his love and faithfulness, then say honestly where you need his help.
108.prayer: Praise God for a love that reaches "beyond the heavens" (v. 4). Then tell him honestly where you feel stuck or let down, and ask for his help in the place where you need it most.
108.tip: Verses 7 to 13 talk about war and enemies, which can make some people uneasy. Briefly note that Christians read this differently: some see it mainly as about ancient Israel, others as also pointing to God's wider rule in Jesus. Then steer the group back to the psalm's honest mix of praise, doubt and trust, which anyone can relate to.

109.open: When someone has treated you unfairly, what is the first thing you usually want to do: fix it, vent to a friend, or go quiet?
questions: The writer says his enemies "repay me evil for good, and hatred for my love" (v. 5). What does it feel like when kindness is answered with an attack? Have you been there?
Verse 4 says his accusers attack him but he is a man of prayer. What does it say about him that prayer is where he takes his hurt?
In verses 6 to 15 he asks for terrible things, including for the man's wife and children (v. 9). What is your honest reaction as you read them?
Verses 16 to 18 give a reason: the man "pursued the poor and needy and brokenhearted, even to their death" (v. 16). Does knowing the reason change how you hear the curses, or not?

Christians read verses 6 to 19 differently. Some see prophecy about Judas, some see honest anger given to God, some think they are unfit for Christian prayer, and some think the writer is quoting his enemies. Which of these makes the most sense to you, and what question does it leave you with?
In verses 22 to 25 he says, "I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me." Underneath anger there is often pain. Where do you see that in your own life?
Verse 28 says, "Though they curse, You will bless." What would it look like to leave justice with God instead of taking it into your own hands?
The psalm ends with "He stands at the right hand of the needy one" (v. 31). If you are in a season where God feels far or silent, how do you hear that line? Be as honest as you like.
109.life: Take ten minutes this week and tell God, out loud or on paper, exactly how you feel about someone who has hurt you, with no cleaning it up. Then ask him to deal with it and to keep you from acting on it.
109.prayer: Thank God that we can bring him our anger and pain as they really are. Ask him to stand beside anyone in the group who feels accused, lied about or alone.
109.tip: Verses 9 to 15 may shock people, and some will want to skip or explain them away. Let the group say that they are hard, name plainly that Christians read them differently, and then point back to the ending, where the writer puts the matter in God's hands.

110.open: Who is someone you would trust to be in charge if things got hard, and what makes you trust them?
questions: The psalm begins, "The LORD said to my Lord," and then invites the king to "Sit at My right hand" (v. 1). Why do you think a place beside God is pictured as the highest honor?
God promises to make the king's enemies "a footstool for Your feet" (v. 1). What does that picture tell you about who is really winning this story, the king or God?

Verse 3 is very hard to translate, but it seems to picture people who are "willing" to follow this king. What is the difference between following someone because you have to and following because you want to?
Verse 4 says, "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." Why might it matter that one person is both king and priest, someone who rules and also stands between people and God?
Verses 5 and 6 describe a violent end for the king's enemies, with the dead heaped up. How do you honestly react to that kind of language in the Bible?
Christians read this psalm as pointing to Jesus, and the New Testament does too. What does it add to your picture of Jesus to think of him seated beside God and also serving as priest?
When people say a leader has been chosen or backed by God, what would make that claim seem trustworthy to you, and what would make it seem dangerous?
Verse 7 says the king "will lift up His head." If you are tired or discouraged right now, what would it look like to be refreshed and lifted up?
110.life: Pick one place of worry or conflict in your life this week. Each day, say verse 1 out loud as a reminder that God has the final word, and ask him to help you wait and trust him there.
110.prayer: Thank God for a King who rules with his help and who also stands as priest for his people. Ask him to teach you to follow willingly, and to hold on to hope where things feel unfinished.
110.tip: Verses 5 and 6 may unsettle people. Don't rush to explain them away. Name that the language is violent and reflects how ancient people pictured God defending his king, let people say how it lands, and also mention that Christians differ on whether the psalm was first about a human king or pointed only to the Messiah.

111.open: What is a family story or tradition that gets told again and again at your table, and why do you think it sticks?
questions: The psalm begins, "I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart" (v. 1). What does thanks with your whole heart look like for you, compared with thanks that is only polite?
Verse 2 says God's works "are pondered by all who delight in them." What is something about God or his work that you find yourself thinking over?

Verse 4 says, "He has caused His wonders to be remembered." The psalm likely points to festivals like Passover that retold Israel's rescue each year. What practices help you or your church remember what God has done?
The psalm calls the LORD "gracious and compassionate" (v. 4). When have you seen that kindness in your own life, or in someone else's?
Verse 5 says, "He remembers His covenant forever." What does it mean to you that God keeps his promises, especially on days when you forget them or doubt them?

Verse 6 celebrates the land given to Israel, though those stories involve war and conquest that many readers find troubling. How can we hold thanks for this psalm and honest questions about the story behind it?
Verse 9 says, "He has sent redemption to His people." Redemption means being bought back out of slavery. Where in your life have you needed to be set free, or still do?
Verse 10 says, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." What do you think that kind of respect looks like in everyday choices, and what makes it hard?
111.life: Each night this week, write down one thing God has done, in your own life or in the Bible, and say thank you for it. At the end of the week, read the list aloud to someone you trust.
111.prayer: Thank God for being gracious and compassionate, and for remembering his promises. Ask him to help each person in the group remember what he has done and to grow in wisdom.
111.tip: The questions about verse 6 and about the fear of the LORD may stir up honest unease, since the land story involves conquest and the word fear can sound harsh. Don't rush to smooth either one over. Say that thoughtful Christians wrestle with these, explain that fear here means reverent awe, and let a doubting person say what they really think.

112.open: Think of the most generous person you know. What is one small thing they do that you remember?
questions: The psalm opens with "Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments" (v. 1). What do you think it looks like to enjoy God's instructions instead of just putting up with them?
Verse 4 says "Light dawns in the darkness for the upright." Notice it says darkness comes first. What does that tell us about what the writer expects life to be like for good people?

Verse 5 says, "It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely, whose affairs are guided by justice." What would generosity and fairness look like in your work, your home or your money this week?

Verses 2 and 3 promise strong descendants and "wealth and riches." Christians read these promises differently. Some expect them to come true in this life, and others see general wisdom or a lasting reward beyond this life. How do you hear these verses, especially when you think of good people who have lost a great deal?

Verse 7 says, "He does not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD." Think of the last piece of bad news you received. What did you reach for first, and what does that tell you about where your trust sits?
Be honest here: verse 8 says this person "does not fear." If fear or doubt still shows up in you, what would it mean to keep trusting God while you are still afraid?
Verse 9 says, "He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor." Why do you think the psalm links giving with a steady heart? Where have you seen that connection, or not seen it?
The psalm ends with the wicked grieved and wasting away (v. 10). Some find this hard to read. How do you sit with the psalm's hope that wrong will not win in the end?
112.life: Pick one practical act of generosity or fairness this week, such as giving to someone in need, paying a bill you have been putting off, or making a dealing right. When worry comes up, say verse 7 quietly as a prayer.
112.prayer: Thank God for the people whose kindness has steadied you. Ask him for a heart that trusts him when news is bad and hands that give freely.
112.tip: Verses 2 and 3 can sting for anyone who has been faithful and still suffered loss or has struggled with money or family. Say plainly that Christians read these promises in different ways, let people share their own experience without trying to fix it, and keep returning to the steady, trusting heart in verse 7.

113.open: Who is someone who made time for you when they didn't have to, and what did it mean to you?
questions: The psalm begins by calling God's servants to "praise the name of the LORD" (v. 1). What do you think it means to praise God's name, and not just to say nice things about him?
Verse 3 says "From where the sun rises to where it sets, the name of the LORD is praised." What does it do for you to picture people all over the world praising God at the same time?
Verse 5 asks, "Who is like the LORD our God, the One enthroned on high?" What makes God different from the powerful people and things you know?
Verse 6 says God "humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth." Why do you think the psalm shows God as stooping down rather than staying far above?

In verse 7 God "raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump." Who in your town or your world sits in that kind of place today? What might it look like for us to be part of lifting them?

Verse 9 speaks of the barren woman, who in that world often faced shame and an uncertain future, being settled "in her home as a joyful mother." Where do people you know feel overlooked, left out, or waiting for something that hasn't come?
Some days it can feel as if God is far away and not looking at us. If you are honest, how does verse 6 sit with you right now: comforting, hard to believe, or something else?
Christians hear this psalm echoed in Mary's song in Luke 1 and see God's stooping down pointing toward Jesus. How does knowing that change the way you read these verses?
113.life: This week, pay attention to one person who is usually overlooked, such as a coworker, a neighbor, or someone at church. Do one small thing to notice them: learn their name, ask a real question, or offer help.
113.prayer: Praise God as the One who is above everything and still bends down to see us. Name one person or situation that feels low or forgotten, and ask God to lift them.
113.tip: Verses 7 to 9 can sound like a promise that every poor or childless person will be lifted up, which can hurt someone still waiting. Keep the focus on who God is and how he looks at people, and make room for anyone whose life does not yet look like these verses. Question 7 is there for that.

114.open: What is a family story that gets retold every holiday, and who tells it best?
questions: The poem opens by remembering when Israel "departed from Egypt" (v. 1). Why do you think the poet starts with a story the people already knew?
Verse 2 says "Judah became God's sanctuary, Israel His dominion." What does it say about God that he made a freed people his own dwelling place?
Verses 3 and 4 say the sea "fled," the Jordan "turned back," and the mountains "skipped like rams." What picture comes to mind, and why might the poet have made it playful instead of solemn?
The sea and the Jordan were the two big obstacles in Israel's story, one on the way out and one on the way in. What obstacle in your own life has felt that big?
In verses 5 and 6 the poet asks the sea, the river and the hills why they ran. Why might a writer ask a question like that when everyone already knows the answer?

The answer in verse 7 is "the presence of the Lord." When have you sensed something like that presence, or when have you wondered where it was? Answer honestly, including if the honest answer is that you haven't.
Verse 8 says God "turned the rock into a pool, the flint into a fountain of water." Where have you seen something hard and dry become a source of life, in your story or someone else's?
This poem was probably sung as a way of remembering. What turning point in your past do you keep returning to, and what does retelling it do for you?
114.life: Pick one time God helped you, or someone you know, through a hard place. Write it in a few lines and share it with one person this week, the way the poet retells Israel's story.
114.prayer: Thank God for the times he has made a way where there seemed to be none. Ask him to help you remember them, and to meet anyone in the group who is feeling stuck at their own sea or desert.
114.tip: The poem is short, so the hard part may be the strange images, like skipping mountains and fleeing seas. Let people smile at them. Explain that it is poetry that exaggerates on purpose, and keep the focus on the answer in verse 7. Also keep an eye on the quiet question about God's presence, and let people say they feel distant without rushing to fix it.

115.open: What is something you own or use every day that you would hate to lose?
questions: The psalm opens, "Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory" (v. 1). Why might it be hard to pray that, and what changes when we do?
Other nations ask, "Where is their God?" (v. 2). Has anyone ever asked you something like that, or have you quietly asked it yourself? What was going on at the time?
Verse 3 says, "Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases." Does that feel comforting, unsettling, or a bit of both to you? Why?
Verses 4 to 7 make fun of idols: "They have mouths, but cannot speak" (v. 5). What do people today lean on for security that looks impressive but cannot actually help when things go wrong?
Verse 8 says, "Those who make them become like them." How have you seen the things people give their lives to shape the kind of people they become?
Three times the psalm says, "He is their help and shield" (vv. 9, 10, 11). When has God felt like a help or shield to you, and when has trusting him felt hard or far away?
Verse 12 says, "The LORD is mindful of us." What does it mean to you to be remembered or thought of by God, especially on an ordinary or discouraging day?
The psalm ends, "it is we who will bless the LORD, both now and forevermore" (v. 18). What is one simple way you could bless the LORD in your everyday life this week?
115.life: Pick one thing you tend to rely on for security, such as money, a routine, your reputation or your phone. This week, each time you reach for it, pause and remind yourself in your own words that the LORD is your help and shield.
115.prayer: Ask God to be the one who gets the glory in your life and in your group. Name one thing you are tempted to trust instead of him, and ask him to help you trust him with it.
115.tip: The mocking of idols can sound harsh or turn into a joke about other religions. Steer the group toward our own modern idols instead. Also, verse 17 is about the dead being silent, which is how the psalm speaks of death. Don't let it turn into a debate about the afterlife; keep the focus on praising God while we are alive.

116.open: Think of a time someone helped you when you really needed it. How did you say thank you?
questions: The writer begins, "I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice" (v. 1). What does it mean to you that love for God starts here, with being heard, and not with a list of things to do?
Verse 3 says, "The ropes of death entangled me." The psalm never says what the danger was. Why might it help that the writer leaves it open? What would you put in that space from your own life?
In verse 4 the prayer is short: "O LORD, deliver my soul!" What does it tell you that this was enough for God to hear?
Verse 6 says God "preserves the simplehearted" and "I was helpless, and He saved me." How easy or hard is it for you to admit you are helpless?
In verse 7 the writer tells their own soul, "Return to your rest." After a hard season, what helps you settle back into rest? What makes it difficult?

In verses 10 and 11 the writer admits, "I am greatly afflicted," and in alarm says, "All men are liars!" What do you make of a psalm that keeps these honest, raw words in the middle of a prayer of thanks? Is there something you have felt but hesitated to say to God?

Verse 12 asks, "How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?" The answer is to lift a cup, call on his name, and keep promises "in the presence of all His people" (vv. 13, 14). What might that look like for us today?
Verse 15 says, "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints." How do you hear that when you think of someone you have lost, or of your own fears about death?
116.life: Think of one time God, or another person, came through for you. This week, tell someone about it, in person or in a message, in a sentence or two. Then thank God for it by name.
116.prayer: Thank God that he hears, even when all we have are a few desperate words. Pray for anyone in the group who feels tangled up or worn out right now, and ask for rest for them.
116.tip: Verses 10 and 11 can be confusing, and the translations of verse 10 differ. Don't get stuck on the wording. Point out that the writer is honest about suffering and still keeps praying, and let people who are in a hard place know that honesty is welcome here. Also be gentle with verse 15, since someone in the room may be grieving.

117.open: What is something you love so much that you can't help telling other people about it?
questions: The psalm opens with "Praise the LORD, all you nations!" (v. 1). Why do you think it speaks to every nation and not only to Israel?
Verse 1 also says, "Extol Him, all you peoples!" What do you picture when you imagine people from every nation praising God together?
Verse 2 gives the reason for praise: "great is His loving devotion toward us." What does it mean to you that God's love is loyal and steady, and not just a passing feeling?

Most readers think "us" means Israel, so the nations are invited to celebrate how faithfully God has treated his people. Why might watching God's faithfulness to someone else give you a reason to trust him?
The psalm says "the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever" (v. 2). Think of a time someone's kindness toward you ran out. How does that shape the way you hear this line?

Christians read this psalm in light of Jesus, and Paul quotes it to show that people of every nation are welcome to God. Who might feel like an outsider to God or to church, and how can we help them see they are invited?
If you are in a season where praise feels hard or your trust in God is shaky, what makes it hard? What, if anything, in these two verses still speaks to you?
117.life: Each day this week, name one specific way you have seen God's faithfulness, in your own life or someone else's. Write it down, and bring one to share next time.
117.prayer: Thank God that his love is loyal and his faithfulness never runs out. Pray for people of other nations and cultures, and for anyone in the group who finds it hard to trust right now.
117.tip: The chapter is only two verses, so the group may finish quickly. Slow down, read it aloud twice, and let people sit with the quiet. Question 7 is for honest doubt, so make clear that no one needs a polished answer.

118.open: What is a song, saying or tradition your family always repeats together, and why does it stick?
questions: In verses 1 to 4 a leader calls out and three groups answer with the same line: "His loving devotion endures forever" (v. 1). What does it do for people to say the same words out loud together?
Some days it is hard to say that line and mean it. If that is where you are, what makes it hard? There are no wrong answers here.

The speaker says, "In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free" (v. 5). The Hebrew word for distress pictures a narrow, squeezed place. When have you felt squeezed like that, and what did you do first?
Verse 8 says, "It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man." What do people today lean on for safety? Does the psalm mean people can never be trusted, or something else?
Verses 10 to 12 describe enemies swarming like bees, in blunt battle language. How do you read that kind of language, and what might "surrounded" look like in your own life?

The speaker says, "The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death" (v. 18). He is reading his own story. How do you hear that verse, and what would you want to be careful about when applying it to someone else's pain?

"The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (v. 22). The Gospels show Jesus applying this to himself. Where have you seen someone written off who turned out to matter, and what does it mean to you that Jesus is described this way?

"This is the day that the LORD has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it" (v. 24). The psalm ends with the same line it began with. What gives you a reason to give thanks this week, even a small one?
118.life: Think of one person who helped you through a hard stretch. This week, write them a short note of thanks, and thank God for them in the same sitting.
118.prayer: Thank God that his loving devotion endures forever. Pray for anyone in the group who is in a tight spot right now and is still waiting for room to breathe.
118.tip: Verse 18 can hurt if it is used to suggest that someone's suffering is God's punishment. Say plainly that the psalmist is telling his own story, not giving a rule for everyone, and that Christians also differ on whether this psalm was first about a king or Israel or was written as a direct prophecy of Jesus. Keep the focus on thanks and trust.

119.open: What is something you keep going back to when you need comfort, like a song, a meal, a place or a person?
questions: The writer says, "I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You" (v. 11). What does it look like to carry God's words with you in daily life, and what has helped you do that?
The writer says, "I am a stranger on the earth" (v. 19). When have you felt like an outsider, and what did you lean on then?

In verse 25 the writer says, "My soul cleaves to the dust," and in verse 28, "My soul melts with sorrow." What do these lines show about how the writer feels, and why might it matter that they are in a prayer?

Verse 71 says, "It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes." Some people find comfort in that and others find it painful. How do you hear it, and how should we be careful using it with someone who is hurting?
In verse 82 the writer asks, "When will You comfort me?" and in verse 84, "How many days must Your servant wait?" Have you ever felt like asking God the same thing? What did you do with that feeling?

Verse 105 says, "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." A lamp like this lit only the next few steps. How does that change the way you think about guidance, especially when you can't see the whole road?
The writer calls God's words "sweeter than honey in my mouth" (v. 103). Many of us don't feel that way about the Bible. What gets in the way for you, and what would help?
The psalm ends with "I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek Your servant" (v. 176). Why might the writer end the longest poem about devotion with an admission like that?
119.life: Pick one verse from this chapter that spoke to you tonight, such as verse 105 or verse 114. Write it on a card and read it each morning this week. Notice what it brings to mind during the day.
119.prayer: Thank God for giving guidance and comfort through his word. Ask him to meet each person where they are tonight, whether they feel full of delight, worn out or far away.
119.tip: The chapter is long and repeats itself, so don't try to cover it all. Stay with the three readings and let people pick what stood out to them. Some will wonder about the word "law." Say plainly that Christians understand it differently today: some see it mainly as the commands given through Moses, part of which they see as still binding, while others read it more broadly as God's whole word or will, seen through Jesus. Then bring the group back to the writer's honesty, including the doubts and the waiting.

120.open: Tell about a time you were stuck in a noisy or tense place and just wanted to go home.
questions: The psalm opens with "In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me" (v. 1). When you are in distress, what do you usually do first, and where does prayer land on that list?
The singer asks to be delivered "from lying lips and a deceitful tongue" (v. 2). Why do you think lies and deceit hurt so much, even more than some other kinds of trouble?

Verse 4 pictures "sharp arrows" and "burning coals of the broom tree." Some read this as what God will do to liars, and others as a picture of how sharp and lasting lying words are. How do you hear it, and what in the picture stands out to you?

In verse 5 the singer says, "Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!" Those were distant, hostile places. What places or settings today leave you feeling like a stranger among people who don't share your values?
Verse 6 says, "Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace." Have you ever felt worn down by a situation that just kept going? What did that weariness feel like?

The singer says, "I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war" (v. 7). When someone keeps twisting your words or wants a fight, what does wanting peace look like in practice? Is there a point where something more is needed?

This psalm is honest and a bit raw, and it begins with God having answered but ends with the trouble still there. If you have ever prayed and still felt stuck, or wondered whether God hears, what would you want to say about that here?
120.life: Think of one relationship or setting where words get twisted or conflict keeps flaring up. This week, bring it to God by name each day, as the psalmist does, and ask what one peaceful step you could take.
120.prayer: Thank God for hearing when we cry out. Ask him to protect anyone in the group who is worn down by lies or conflict, and to make each of us a person who brings peace.
120.tip: Verses 3 and 4 can sound harsh, and people may be unsure whether they describe God's punishment or the sting of the words themselves. Say plainly that readers take it both ways, don't push for a single answer, and move on to the singer's honest weariness in verses 5 to 7.

121.open: When you were a kid, who did you call when you were scared or stuck?
questions: The psalm opens, "I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?" (v. 1). Scholars are not sure if the hills stand for danger, other gods or Jerusalem. Which reading helps you most, and why?
The answer is, "My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth" (v. 2). Why might it matter that the one who helps is also the one who made everything?
When you feel unsafe or uncertain, where do you instinctively look for help first? How well has that held up?
Verses 3 and 4 say the LORD "will not slumber" and will "neither slumber nor sleep." What do you picture when you hear that, and why might the psalm say it twice?
Verse 5 says, "the LORD is the shade on your right hand." Shade is close and quiet, not flashy. When have you sensed help that was steady rather than dramatic?

Verse 7 says, "The LORD will guard you from all evil." Christians read this differently: some see a promise of physical safety, others a deeper keeping of a person even when bad things happen. How do you hear it, especially if you or someone you love has been hurt?
If you are in a season where God feels distant or you are not sure anyone is watching, what would you honestly say to him or to this group tonight?
Verse 8 speaks of "your coming and going, both now and forevermore." What coming or going is in front of you this week, and how would it feel to hand it to God?
121.life: Pick one daily moment this week, like leaving the house or turning off the light. Each time, say verse 2 out loud or silently: "My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth."
121.prayer: Thank God that he never sleeps and never looks away. Name one worry or journey you are carrying and ask him to keep you in it. Pray for anyone in the group who feels unprotected right now.
121.tip: Verses 5 to 8 can sting for anyone who has been hurt despite praying for safety. Do not rush to explain it away. Say plainly that Christians read the promise differently, let people voice the tension, and keep returning to the psalm's center: God stays awake and stays near.

122.open: What is a trip or a gathering you looked forward to for weeks, and what made it so good to finally arrive?
questions: The psalm opens, "I was glad" when people said it was time to go to the house of the LORD (v. 1). Why do you think the invitation itself brought gladness, and not only the arrival?
The singer says, "Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem" (v. 2). What do you think it felt like to finally arrive after a long journey on foot?
Jerusalem is called "a city united together" (v. 3). What helps a group of people feel truly joined together, and what pulls them apart?
The tribes came "to give thanks to the name of the LORD" (v. 4). When did you last stop to give thanks with other people, and what was that like?
Verse 5 says the city was also where "the thrones of judgment stand." Why might it matter that worship and fair justice were found in the same place?

The singer says, "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem" (v. 6). Christians differ on whether this points mainly to the actual city today or to God's people everywhere. How do you hear it, and what does it lead you to pray for?
In verse 8 the singer speaks a blessing of peace over his brothers and friends, and does it for their sake. Who in your life or your church could use that kind of blessing from you this week?
Be honest: when you think about gathering with God's people, do you feel glad, tired, unsure, or something else? What do you think is behind that?
122.life: Choose one person from your church, family or friends and bless them by name this week. Pray for their peace each day, and send them a short message letting them know.
122.prayer: Thank God for the people who invited you in and walked beside you. Ask him for peace and gladness in your gatherings, and for the people in this group by name.
122.tip: Someone may feel flat about church, or may be hurt by it, and verse 1 can sting. Say plainly that gladness is not always how it feels, and let people answer the last question honestly without fixing them. If the debate over Jerusalem and politics comes up, name that Christians differ, and bring the group back to praying for peace and for one another.

123.open: When you were a kid, who did you look to when you needed help or wanted to know everything was okay?
questions: The psalm begins, "I lift up my eyes to You, the One enthroned in heaven" (v. 1). What does it say about God that he is pictured sitting on a throne? How does that picture land with you today?
The singer compares the people to servants who watch "the hand of their master" (v. 2). What would a servant be looking for in that hand, and what are you hoping to see from God's hand right now?
Verse 2 says "our eyes are on the LORD our God until He shows us mercy." What is hard about waiting and looking, and what makes it easier?
The psalm says "we" and "our" almost the whole way through. Why might it matter that this is a prayer sung by a whole people and not just one person?
In verse 3 the cry is doubled: "Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy." When have you prayed the same short prayer over and over because you had nothing else left?
Verse 4 speaks of "scorn from the arrogant" and "contempt from the proud." Where do people feel looked down on today, and how does that wear a person out?
The psalm never says who the mockers were or when God answered. If you are honest, what do you do with a prayer that ends while the waiting is still going on?
When you feel looked down on by people who seem to have it easy, where do your eyes tend to go for relief?
123.life: Pick one moment each day this week, even thirty seconds, to stop and literally lift your eyes up. Say a short prayer like "Lord, have mercy," and notice what you are carrying as you say it.
123.prayer: Lift your eyes to God together and ask for mercy for the weary and the mocked. Name before him one thing you are still waiting for, and ask him to help you keep looking to him.
123.tip: The psalm ends with the cry still unanswered, and some people will want to rush to a happy ending. Let the group sit with that honestly, and make room for anyone who says they feel tired or unheard. Waiting while still looking up is the point of the psalm.

124.open: Think of a close call you've had, like a near miss in the car or a narrow escape from a bad situation. What do you remember about the moments right after?
questions: The psalm begins, "If the LORD had not been on our side" (v. 1). Why do you think the writer starts with what could have happened instead of what did happen?
The people are invited to say this together: "let Israel now declare" (v. 1). Why might it matter that this was sung by a whole community and not just one person?
The enemies are described as people whose "anger flared against us" (v. 3). What does it feel like to be on the receiving end of someone else's anger or power, and how does this psalm speak to that?
Verses 4 and 5 use the picture of "floods" and "raging waters." The note says these are like sudden flash floods. What situations in life can feel like a flood that comes without warning?
In verse 7, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler; the net is torn." The bird doesn't free itself. What do you make of that picture of rescue?

Many of us have prayed for rescue and not received it the way this psalm describes. How would you honestly say this psalm lands for you today, whether with gratitude, with questions, or with something in between?

Verse 8 says, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." Why might it matter that the one who helps is also the Maker of everything, and what changes when you say "our" help instead of "my" help?
124.life: Write down one time you were rescued, helped, or protected, whether it was dramatic or small. Share it this week with someone, and say out loud who or what you are thankful to.
124.prayer: Thank God for the ways he has helped you, including the ones you only see looking back. Ask him to be the help of anyone in the group who feels caught in a trap or a flood right now.
124.tip: Some people in the room may be in a hard season where no rescue has come yet, and a psalm of victory can sting. Make space for that honestly. Point out that the psalm looks back after the escape, and let those who are still waiting say so without being hurried toward gratitude.

125.open: What is a place, a person or a routine that helps you feel steady when life feels shaky?
questions: The psalm says those who trust in the LORD are "like Mount Zion" (v. 1). What do you think it means to be steady like a mountain, and does that sound like you right now?
Jerusalem sat among hills that sheltered it. Verse 2 says "the LORD surrounds His people." What does it feel like to be surrounded rather than just watched over?
Pilgrims sang this on the road to Jerusalem, often under foreign rule. Why might a song about steadiness have mattered to people who felt powerless?
Verse 3 says the scepter of the wicked "will not rest upon the land allotted to the righteous." Where do you see unfair power or pressure in the world today, and how does this verse speak to it?
The worry in verse 3 is that the righteous might "put forth their hands to injustice." How can long stretches of unfairness or hardship tempt good people to give up or cut corners?
Verse 4 asks God to do good to "the upright in heart." The note on this psalm suggests this means sincere, not perfect. How does that change the way you hear the word upright?
Verse 5 warns about those who "turn to crooked ways." What does drifting look like in real life, and what helps you notice it early?
If you are honest, do you feel more like the unmovable mountain or like someone who is wobbling? What would you want to say to God about that?
125.life: Pick one thing this week that tends to knock you off balance, like worry, a hard relationship or the news. Each time it comes up, quietly say verse 2 to yourself and remember that God surrounds his people.
125.prayer: Thank God that he surrounds his people like hills around a city. Ask him to steady anyone in the group who feels shaky, and to keep each of you honest at heart.
125.tip: Verses 3 to 5 can sound like a harsh line between good people and bad people, and someone may worry about where they stand. Point the group back to verse 1: the psalm begins with trust in the LORD, not with a record of perfect behavior, and invite honest answers to the last question.

126.open: What is something you waited a long time for that was worth the wait?
questions: The singers say that when the LORD restored the captives of Zion, "we were like dreamers" (v. 1). Can you remember a moment when good news felt too good to be real? What was it like?
Verse 2 says "our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy." Why might joy like that be worth remembering and telling again?

The nations said, "The LORD has done great things for them" (v. 2). Then the singers say it for themselves: "The LORD has done great things for us" (v. 3). What is the difference between hearing that God is good and saying it about your own life?
The psalm moves from celebration to asking: "Restore our captives, O LORD" (v. 4). Why do you think the singers ask for more right after giving thanks? Is that easy or hard for you to do?
The Negev is a dry land where empty streambeds can suddenly fill with water. What dry or empty place in your life, or in the world, would you like to see flooded like that?
Verse 5 says, "Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy." What does it look like to keep doing the next faithful thing when you are sad or tired and can't yet see any harvest?

Verse 6 says the one who goes out weeping "will surely return with shouts of joy." Some of us are still in the weeping part and are not sure we believe that. What would you want to say to God, or to each other, from that place?
Think of a time when something good happened after a hard stretch but some troubles stayed. Did the good news make the remaining troubles easier to carry, or harder? Why?
126.life: Make two short lists this week. On one, write down a few times God has come through for you or your family. On the other, write something you are still waiting on. Read the first list before you pray over the second.
126.prayer: Thank God for one thing he has already restored or done for you. Then ask him honestly for the thing that is still unfinished, and for patience to keep sowing while you wait.
126.tip: Verses 5 and 6 can sound like a promise that every sad season ends quickly and neatly, and that can sting someone who is grieving right now. Say gently that the psalm itself keeps praying in verse 4 for what is still missing. Let people name their waiting without rushing to fix it.

127.open: What is something you worked really hard on that still depended on things outside your control?
questions: Verse 1 says, "Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain." What do you think the psalm is and is not saying about hard work?
Builders and night watchmen were ordinary, respectable jobs. What are the equivalent jobs and duties in your life right now, the things you feel responsible to build or guard?
Verse 2 mentions people who "rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat." What does anxious effort look like in your own life, and what does it cost you?
The psalm says "He gives sleep to His beloved" (v. 2). Some readers think it means God gives rest, and others think it means God provides even while we sleep. Which part speaks to you, and why?
Where do you find it hardest to let go and trust God with the outcome: work, money, family, health or something else? Be as honest as you like, including if trust feels difficult right now.
Verse 3 calls children "a heritage from the LORD." What changes in how we see people when we think of them as gifts received and not something we produce or achieve?
In verses 4 and 5 children are like "arrows in the hand of a warrior." What did that picture of strength and support mean in a world where family stood with you at the city gate?
Whether or not we have children, how can we be a support and a blessing to the families and the younger people around us?
127.life: Pick one thing you have been carrying anxiously. This week, do your part faithfully, then set a time to stop for the day and hand the rest to God in a short prayer. Notice what happens to your rest.
127.prayer: Ask God to be the one who builds and guards what matters most to you. Thank him for rest as a gift, and pray for the families in your group.
127.tip: Verses 3 to 5 can sting for people who are single, struggling to have children, or grieving a loss. Christians also differ on whether these verses encourage large families or simply celebrate children as a gift with no set standard. Say that in one line, keep the focus on gift and trust, and let nobody feel measured by their family.

128.open: What is one meal or table gathering from your life that you still remember fondly?
questions: The psalm opens, "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!" (v. 1). Fearing the LORD here means deep respect, not terror. What does that kind of respect for God look like in an ordinary week?
Verse 2 says, "you eat the fruit of your labor." Why do you think the psalm names honest work and enjoying its results as a blessing? What does that say about everyday jobs, paid or unpaid?
Verse 3 pictures a "fruitful vine" and "olive shoots sitting around your table." What do those images say about the kind of home the writer hopes for? What would your own picture be?
This psalm was sung by pilgrims on the way up to Jerusalem (v. 1, "A song of ascents"). Why might it help a traveling crowd to sing about home and family together?
Verse 5 says, "May the LORD bless you from Zion." The song widens from one house to a whole city and nation. Why might a good home and a peaceful community belong together?

Christians read this psalm differently. Some see a promise of comfort for the faithful, others a general pattern of wisdom, since good people in the Bible, like Job, still suffer. How do you read it, and where does it ring true or hard in your own life?
Not everyone has a full table, steady work or a family nearby. How might someone in that place honestly hear this psalm? What would you want them to know?
The psalm ends with "Peace be upon Israel!" (v. 6). Where do you most long for peace right now: at home, at work, in the world? Say as much or as little as you like.
128.life: Share one meal this week on purpose, with family, friends or a neighbor. Put phones away, thank God for the food and the people, and ask each person to share one good thing from their week.
128.prayer: Thank God for the work, people and meals that are part of your life. Pray for anyone in the group whose home or work feels hard right now, and ask for peace in the places where it is missing.
128.tip: Verses 3 and 4 can sting for people who are single, widowed, childless or estranged from family. Name that gently at the start. Keep the focus on the bigger picture of a life lived with God, and make room for people to say that the psalm feels distant to them without trying to fix it.

129.open: What is something you have been doing for a long time that you are surprised you are still doing?
questions: The psalm opens with "Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth" (v. 1). Why do you think Israel tells its story out loud, and together, before saying anything else?
Verse 2 says "they have not prevailed against me." Notice it does not say they never hurt me. What is the difference between being hurt and being beaten?
Verse 3 says, "The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long." What does this picture tell you about how the writer felt, and why might the Bible include such raw words?
Verse 4 says, "The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked." What do you think it means that God is righteous, and how does that change the way you look at wrongs done to you?
Looking back, where can you see that you were wounded but not finished? If you are not sure you see God in it, you can say that too.
Verses 5 to 7 ask that those who hate Zion be "like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow." How do you react to a prayer this blunt? What do you think it is asking for?
Christians read the wishes in verses 5 to 8 differently, and some weigh them against Jesus' call to pray for enemies. How do you hold honest anger and love for enemies together?
Who around you is in the middle of a long hard stretch right now, and how could this group help them keep going?
129.life: Take ten minutes this week to write down a hard season you came through. Next to it, note one way you were helped, and thank God or that person for it. Share it with someone if you can.
129.prayer: Thank God that he stays with his people through long and painful seasons. Bring to him any hurt or anger you are carrying, and ask for his justice and his peace.
129.tip: Verses 5 to 8 may make some people uneasy and others quietly relieved. Say plainly that Christians disagree about how to read them, let people be honest about their reactions, and gently bring the group back to verses 1 to 4, where the main point is that Israel is still standing.

130.open: Think of a time you waited a long time for something, like a late flight, a phone call or a test result. What was that wait like?
questions: The psalm opens, "Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!" (v. 1). The writer never says what the trouble is. Why might it help that the prayer is so open and raw?
"The depths" is an old picture of deep, overwhelming water. What picture would you use today for a time when you felt in over your head?
Verse 3 asks, "who, O Lord, could stand?" if God kept track of every wrong. What does this tell you about how the writer sees himself, and about how he sees God?

Verse 4 says, "But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared." Readers explain the link between forgiveness and reverence in different ways. How do you understand it? Why might a forgiving God be easier to respect than a harsh one?
The writer says, "my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope" (v. 5). What do you lean on when you are waiting and nothing has changed yet?

Verse 6 repeats the line "more than watchmen wait for the morning." A guard on a wall sat through the dark, sure that dawn would come. If you are in a season where waiting feels more like doubt, what is that like for you? Be as honest as you like.

The psalm moves from one person's cry to a word for everyone: "put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance" (v. 7). Why might it matter that the writer does not keep this hope to himself?
Verse 8 says God "will redeem Israel from all iniquity." Christians have read this in light of Jesus. What does being set free from guilt, and not only from trouble, look like in everyday life?
130.life: Pick one thing you keep carrying, a worry or a wrong you did or one done to you. Each day this week, take two quiet minutes to say Psalm 130:1-2 as your own prayer, then wait in silence like a watchman until you are done.
130.prayer: Thank God that he forgives instead of keeping score. Ask him to meet each person in the group in whatever depths they are in, and for patience to wait for him.
130.tip: Verse 4 can raise a worry about why forgiveness leads to fear, and the psalm does not explain it. Say so plainly, offer that the word is usually understood as reverence and not terror, and move on. Also leave room for people who are still in the dark, since this psalm does not rush to a happy ending.

131.open: When you were a kid, what was the one thing that could calm you down when you were upset?
questions: The singer says, "My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty" (v. 1). Why do you think the psalm begins by saying this to God, and not to other people?

The singer says, "I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me" (v. 1). What kinds of things might that mean: ambition, big questions, things outside our control? What comes to mind for you?
What is one thing right now that you are straining to figure out or control, and how does it feel to carry it?
Verse 2 says, "I have stilled and quieted my soul." The singer talks as if they did this on purpose. What do you think it looks like to quiet your own soul, and what gets in the way?
The picture is of "a weaned child with his mother" (v. 2). A weaned child no longer cries for milk but just rests close. What does that picture say about how this person relates to God?
Some days it is hard to feel calm or close to God at all. If that is where you are, what makes it hard? Be as honest as you like, including if you are unsure about all of this.

The psalm ends by turning outward: "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore" (v. 3). Why might someone who has found quiet want to invite others in? Who around you needs that invitation?
131.life: Set aside five minutes each day this week with no phone and no agenda. Sit quietly, hand God one worry you cannot fix, and then read Psalm 131 slowly out loud.
131.prayer: Ask God to quiet the restless parts of each person's heart. Pray for one worry or question people are carrying that they cannot solve, and ask for hope "both now and forevermore."
131.tip: The psalm can sound like it says never ask hard questions or never try for much. Help the group hear it differently: the singer is describing rest, not giving up. Let people say honestly that calm does not come easily, and avoid hurrying anyone toward peace they do not yet feel.

132.open: Think of a time you worked hard to get a home or a room ready for someone coming to stay. What did you do to make it feel welcoming?
questions: The song begins by asking God to remember "all the hardships he endured" (v. 1). Why might it matter to the singers that someone's sacrifice is remembered?
David vows, "I will not enter my house or get into my bed" until he finds a place for the LORD (vv. 3-5). What does that tell you about how much David cared about God's presence?
The ark stood for God's presence, and it had been tucked away for years before David brought it to Jerusalem. What are some ways God can feel far away or forgotten, even for people who believe?
Verse 7 says, "Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool." This was a song pilgrims sang on the way to Jerusalem. What helps you to travel toward worship, and not just show up?
In verses 11 and 12, God swears an oath back to David, with a condition attached: his sons must keep the covenant. How do you hear that mix of promise and responsibility?
Verse 15 says, "I will satisfy her poor with bread." The poor are named in God's own promise. What might it look like for our group to share in that care?

In verse 14 God says, "This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell." Christians read the promised king in verses 17 and 18 as pointing to Jesus. What does it mean to you that God chooses to live among people?

David would not rest until he had made room for God. If you are honest, where does your own comfort win out right now, and what would it take to change that, or do you find it hard to care about this at all?
132.life: Choose one small way this week to make room for God, such as a set quiet ten minutes, a phone put away at a meal, or a regular time to pray. Keep it modest enough that you will actually do it.
132.prayer: Thank God for promising to dwell with his people and for keeping his word across generations. Ask him to make you more willing to give up comfort for what matters most, and to help you notice the poor around you.
132.tip: Verses 13 to 18 raise a question Christians answer differently: whether God's promises about Zion are fulfilled only spiritually in Jesus and the church, or still include a future role for the physical city of Jerusalem. Say that in a line, do not try to settle it, and bring the group back to what the psalm shows about God's faithfulness and his care for the poor.

133.open: Think of a time when a group you were part of, like a family meal, a team or a church event, just felt good to be in. What made it that way?
questions: The psalm opens with "how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony" (v. 1). Where have you seen that kind of harmony up close, and what did it look like day to day?
This is a song of ascents, which pilgrims sang while traveling up to Jerusalem for the festivals. Why might people from scattered tribes have needed a song about living together as one?
Verse 1 may mean family members sharing a home, or the whole people of Israel gathered to worship. Which one comes to mind first for you, and why?

The psalm compares unity to "fine oil on the head, running down on the beard" (v. 2). The oil is generous and overflowing. What does that picture suggest about what unity is like, compared with just putting up with each other?
Oil like this was used to set Aaron apart for his work as priest. What do you think it means that the psalm links unity with something holy?
Verse 3 compares unity to "the dew of Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion." Dew is quiet and refreshing, and nobody can make it happen. What does that say about where harmony comes from?
The psalm ends with "the LORD has bestowed the blessing of life forevermore" (v. 3). How have you seen a group of people being together bring life to you or someone else?
Harmony can sound easy in a song and feel hard in real life. Where does it feel difficult for you right now, in your family, church or friendships? It is fine to say you are not sure it can happen.
133.life: Pick one person you find it hard to be at peace with, or one person who is on the edge of your group. This week, take one small step toward them, like a message, a meal or an honest and kind conversation.
133.prayer: Thank God for the people he has put around you. Ask him to grow the kind of unity that refreshes, and to show you one step you can take toward it.
133.tip: Some people may carry real hurt from families or churches that were not united, so the psalm can sting. Name that gently, and make clear that the group is not asking anyone to pretend. Let the quiet ones say what is hard before moving on to the hopeful parts.

134.open: Think of someone who works while most of us are asleep, like a nurse, a baker or a night security guard. What do you imagine their night is like?
questions: The psalm opens with a call to "all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD" (v. 1). Who is being spoken to here, and why might a song for them be placed at the very end of the pilgrim songs?
The night workers kept the building safe and the lamps and altar fire burning. What does it say about God that a psalm speaks directly to people doing unseen, ordinary work?
Whose quiet, unseen work keeps your life running? How often does it get noticed, and what could we do to thank them?

Verse 2 says, "Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!" Raised hands were a common way to pray in ancient Israel. What postures or habits help you turn toward God, and which feel awkward to you?
Some readers take raised hands as a sign of a heart turned toward God. How do you think our bodies and our prayers affect each other?
Nights can be hard times: work, worry, loneliness or sleeplessness. What is a night, or a quiet stretch of your life, when praising God felt hard or even impossible? Be as honest as you like.

Verse 3 shifts to a blessing: "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." No one is sure who speaks it, perhaps a priest or one person blessing each listener. How does it feel to be on the receiving end of a blessing instead of having to do something for God?
Why might it matter that the one who blesses is called "the Maker of heaven and earth" (v. 3)? What does that tell us about how big and how close God is?
134.life: Choose one person whose work usually goes unnoticed, such as a night worker, a caregiver or a volunteer. Thank them in person or in a note this week. Then, before bed one evening, say verse 3 aloud as a blessing over your household or yourself.
134.prayer: Thank God for the people who work and keep watch while others sleep. Ask him to bless them, and to bless each person in the group tonight.
134.tip: The psalm is only three verses, so the group may finish fast. Let the quiet stand, and give people time with the question about hard nights. Be ready for someone to name real tiredness or doubt, and receive it without rushing to fix it. Also be upfront that no one knows who speaks verse 3, and that this does not change its meaning.

135.open: What is something you own or use every day that you would be lost without?
questions: The psalm starts with "Hallelujah! Praise the name of the LORD" (v. 1). When you hear a call to praise, what comes up for you: joy, duty, awkwardness, or something else?
Verse 3 says, "the LORD is good; sing praises to His name, for it is lovely." What is one thing in your life right now that makes it easy or hard to believe God is good?
Verse 4 says God chose Israel as "His treasured possession." What do you think it meant for ordinary people then to hear that they were treasured? What does it stir in you to hear it?

In verse 5 the singer says, "I know that the LORD is great." Where did that kind of knowing come from for you, and what has made it stronger or weaker over time? Some scholars read "above all gods" as assuming other gods exist, and others read it as saying none can compare. How does that difference, if at all, change how you hear the line?
Verses 6 and 7 point to clouds, lightning, rain and wind as signs of God's rule. When have you felt small in front of something in nature, and what did it make you think about God?

Verses 8 to 12 celebrate the death of Egypt's firstborn and the defeat of kings as God's acts for Israel. These are hard lines to read. How do you sit with them, and what questions do they raise for you?

Verses 15 to 18 say idols have "mouths, but cannot speak" and that "those who make them become like them" (vv. 16, 18). What do people trust today that cannot answer back, and what might trusting it do to us over time?
The psalm ends by calling everyone to "bless the LORD" (vv. 19, 20). If you are not sure you feel like praising right now, what is an honest thing you could say to God instead?
135.life: Pick one thing you tend to lean on when life feels shaky, like money, work, approval or a screen. This week, each time you reach for it, stop for a moment and say one line of praise from this psalm, such as "the LORD is good" (v. 3).
135.prayer: Thank God that his name "endures forever" (v. 13) and that he is not like silent idols. Ask him to help each person trust him more than the things they usually lean on.
135.tip: Verses 8 to 12 will trouble some people, and it is fine to say so. Don't rush to explain them away or defend them. Name that the psalm tells it from Israel's side as God's rescue, let people voice their unease, and then bring the group back to the main point: God acts, and idols do not.

136.open: What is a song, a phrase or a family saying that gets repeated in your home or friend group, and why does it stick?
questions: The same line closes all 26 verses: "His loving devotion endures forever" (v. 1). Why might the writer repeat it every single time instead of saying it once?
Verse 1 gives a reason to give thanks: "for He is good." What is one thing in your life this week that you could honestly trace back to that goodness, even if it was small?
In verses 7 to 9 the sun, moon and stars are things God made. Many nearby peoples worshiped them as gods. What are some things people today treat as bigger or more powerful than they really are?

Verses 10 to 15 retell the escape from Egypt, and the refrain is sung even after "He struck down the firstborn of Egypt" (v. 10). What was this story to Israel, who had been slaves? What feelings come up for you as you read it?

Christians read verses 10 to 20, with their talk of striking down firstborn and kings, in different ways. Some see faithful truth about God's justice, others see Israel's own limited view of its history. Where do you land right now, and what questions are you still carrying?
In verse 23 the song says "He remembered us in our low estate." Can you think of a low time when you felt forgotten? What, if anything, helped you hold on?

The psalm moves from "Israel" to "us" (v. 23), so a later generation claims the old story as its own. What story of God's help, from the Bible or from someone's life, would you want to pass on to others?
The song ends with God who "gives food to every creature" (v. 25). How does it change the way you see ordinary meals and daily needs to read them as part of this same love?
136.life: Each evening this week, write down one thing from the day and say aloud, "His loving devotion endures forever." If that line feels hard to say on some days, tell God that honestly too.
136.prayer: Thank God for specific things he has done in your own story, one by one. Ask him to help each person in the group trust his faithful love, especially anyone in a low season.
136.tip: Verses 10 to 20 may stir strong feelings about the killing of Egypt's firstborn and other kings. Don't rush to defend or explain it away. Say plainly that Christians read it differently, let people voice discomfort, and bring the group back to the refrain and the story of rescue.

137.open: Is there a song that takes you straight back to a particular place or time in your life? What does it bring back?
questions: The psalm opens with people who "sat and wept when we remembered Zion" (v. 1). Why do you think remembering what we have lost can hurt so much? When have you felt that?
Their captors asked, "Sing us a song of Zion" (v. 3). Most readers hear this as mockery. Have you ever been asked to look cheerful or perform when you were hurting? How did that feel?

The writer asks, "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" (v. 4). Readers differ on whether the reason is grief, a sense that the songs were too holy to perform, or both. Which fits best with how you have felt in hard seasons?
In verses 5 and 6 the singer vows never to forget Jerusalem, even in exile. What do you hold on to, or refuse to let go of, when life feels far from home?
In verse 7 the poet asks the LORD to "remember" what Edom did on the day Jerusalem fell. Why might it matter to someone who has been wronged to know that God sees it?

Verses 8 and 9 are some of the hardest words in the Bible, including "Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks" (v. 9). What is your honest reaction when you read them? It is fine to say you are troubled or unsure.

Christians read the end of this psalm in different ways: as honest anguish handed to God, as a prophecy of Babylon's fall, or as words we would not pray today. What is helpful or difficult about each view?
The psalm is in the Bible, so it seems God lets us bring raw anger and pain into prayer. What do you do with your anger? What might it look like to bring it to God and leave justice with him?
137.life: Think of one hurt or loss you have kept quiet about. This week, tell God about it in plain, honest words, without tidying it up first. If it helps, write it down.
137.prayer: Thank God that we can come to him with grief and anger as we are. Ask him to hold the hurts of the group, and to bring justice and healing where we cannot.
137.tip: Verse 9 will likely dominate the conversation. Don't rush to explain it away or defend it. Name it as a disturbing verse, say plainly that Christians read it differently, and invite honest reactions. Then steer back to the psalm's main movement: grief, memory, and bringing raw pain to God.

138.open: Think of a time someone answered when you really needed help, a phone call, a ride, a kind word. What did it mean to you?
questions: The singer says, "I give You thanks with all my heart" (v. 1). What does it look like to thank God with your whole heart, and what tends to hold you back?
The psalm says God has "exalted Your name and Your word above all else" (v. 2). Why might God's word matter so much to someone in trouble?

Verse 3 says, "On the day I called, You answered me; You emboldened me and strengthened my soul." Notice that the answer is courage and strength. Have you ever received that kind of answer instead of the one you asked for? What was it like?

Verse 1 mentions singing praise "before the gods," and readers understand that phrase in different ways. Whatever it means, the singer praises God openly. Where is it easy or hard for you to be open about your thanks to God?
The singer hopes that "All the kings of the earth will give You thanks" (v. 4). Why would someone who has been helped by God want everyone else to know about it?
Verse 6 says, "Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly." When have you felt small or overlooked? How does this verse sit with you today?
In verse 7 the singer expects to "walk in the midst of trouble" and still trusts God to preserve him. If you are honest, how much do you trust God in your own trouble right now, and what would help?
Verse 8 says, "The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me." What is one area of your life that feels unfinished, and what does it mean to ask God not to abandon it?
138.life: Each day this week, write down one prayer God has answered, big or small, even if the answer was strength to get through rather than a fix. At the end of the week, thank God for them out loud.
138.prayer: Thank God for the times he has answered when you called. Ask him to strengthen anyone in the group who is in the middle of trouble, and to finish what he has started in each of you.
138.tip: Some people will say they have called and not felt answered. Don't rush to fix that. Point out that the psalm describes an answer of inner strength (v. 3), and let people say honestly where they are still waiting.

139.open: Who in your life knows you best, and what is one thing they know about you that most people don't?
questions: The psalm opens, "O LORD, You have searched me and known me" (v. 1). Does being fully known by God feel more like comfort or more like exposure to you right now? Why?
Verse 4 says, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it." What does it mean to you that God understands you even when you can't put things into words?

In verse 5 the poet says, "You hem me in behind and before; You have laid Your hand upon me." That could feel like protection or like being boxed in. Which does it feel like to you, and what shapes that?

The poet asks, "Where can I flee from Your presence?" (v. 7) and then lists the sky, Sheol, the far sea and the dark. Have you ever wanted to get away from God, or felt that God was far away? What was that like?
Verse 14 says, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made." What makes that easy or hard to believe about yourself? What would change if you did believe it?

In verses 19 to 22 the poet suddenly speaks of hatred and enemies. Christians differ on whether this is a fitting stance toward evil or an honest cry that Jesus' call to love enemies later moves beyond. What do you make of an angry prayer like this in the Bible?
The psalm ends, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (v. 23). Why might the poet ask for this right after speaking of enemies? What would you hope God finds, and what would you fear he finds?
139.life: Each day this week, pray verses 23 and 24 slowly in your own words. Then sit quietly for a minute and let God show you one thing, whether a worry to hand over or a habit to bring into the light.
139.prayer: Thank God that he knows you completely and has not turned away. Ask for the courage to be honest with him, including about anger, fear or doubt, and for trust that his hand holds you fast.
139.tip: Verses 19 to 22 will likely stir strong reactions, and some may feel uneasy that a psalm contains hatred. Name the disagreement briefly, point out that the poet brings the anger to God rather than acting on it, and then guide the group to the final prayer in verses 23 and 24 so the discussion ends on honesty and trust.

140.open: When someone has said something unkind about you behind your back, what is your first reaction?
questions: The writer says his enemies "sharpen their tongues like snakes" and that "the venom of vipers is on their lips" (v. 3). Why might words hurt as much as physical attacks?
In verse 5 the proud "hide a snare" and spread a net "along the path." What does it look like today when someone quietly works against a person instead of opposing them openly?
Before asking for anything, the writer says, "You are my God" (v. 6). Why might it matter that he starts there, and what do you tend to say to God first when you are afraid?
Verse 7 calls God the one who will "shield my head in the day of battle." Can you think of a time you felt protected, or a time you felt unprotected? What was that like?
In verses 9 to 11 the writer asks for "burning coals" to fall on his enemies and for calamity to hunt down the violent. What do you make of such a blunt prayer in the Bible?
Some readers see these verses as an honest cry for justice that leaves revenge to God. Others think Jesus' call to love enemies takes us beyond them. How do you hold those two things together?

Verse 12 says, "I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy." If you find that hard to believe right now, what makes it hard? If you do believe it, what has helped?
The psalm ends with the upright dwelling in God's presence (v. 13). What difference could it make to bring your anger to God instead of carrying it alone or aiming it at the person?
140.life: Think of one person or situation that has left you angry or hurt. Once this week, tell God about it in plain words, the way this psalm does, and then ask him to be your shield and to deal with it in his way.
140.prayer: Ask God to help each person speak honestly about their hurt and anger. Pray for anyone in the group who feels targeted or treated unjustly, and thank God that he "defends the cause of the needy" (v. 12).
140.tip: Verses 9 to 11 may make some people uncomfortable, and others may want to use them against someone in their own life. Say plainly that Christians read these verses differently. Point out that the writer brings his anger to God rather than acting on it himself, and let people stay with that without forcing agreement.

141.open: Is there a place where you find it hard to keep your mouth shut, like traffic, family dinners or the comments section?
questions: David asks that his prayer be "set before You like incense" (v. 2). What do you think he hopes God will do with a simple prayer, and what would it mean to you if God received yours that way?
In verse 3 he asks God to "set a guard" over his mouth and "keep watch at the door of my lips." Why might he ask God for help instead of just trying harder himself?
When have words slipped out of your mouth that you later wished you could take back? What helps you pause before speaking?
Verse 4 asks, "Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing." How does a person get pulled toward something wrong a little at a time, through friends, habits or what we watch?
He says, "let me not feast on their delicacies" (v. 4). What do you think are the tempting "delicacies" of our own day, the things that look good but come with strings attached?
In verse 5 he asks for correction from "the righteous man" and calls it "an act of loving devotion." Who in your life can say hard things to you, and what makes it possible to hear them?

Verses 6 and 7 are hard to translate, and the picture of judgment is troubling. How do you feel when the Psalms talk about enemies falling into their own traps (v. 10)? Say it honestly, even if you are unsure what to make of it.
In verse 8 he says, "my eyes are fixed on You." What does it look like for you to turn your eyes back to God on an ordinary, distracted day?
141.life: Choose one situation this week where you tend to say too much or say it too sharply. Before you walk into it, pray verse 3 in your own words. If someone offers you a hard word, try listening first and thanking them before you respond.
141.prayer: Ask God to "set a guard" over your mouth and keep your heart from drifting. Ask for humility to receive correction from people who love you, and for a steady focus on God when you feel pressure.
141.tip: Verses 6 and 7 are unclear even to scholars, so do not let the group get stuck there.
