Say that plainly, then move on to the parts that are clear: his prayer, his mouth, his company and his openness to correction. If someone is uneasy about the wish in verse 10, let them say so without hurrying to fix it.

142.open: When you need to vent about a bad day, who is the first person you call or text?
questions: The heading says David prayed this "when he was in the cave" (v. 1). Why do you think someone in hiding would pray out loud instead of keeping quiet?
David says, "I pour out my complaint before Him; I reveal my trouble to Him" (v. 2). What do you think it looks like to be that honest with God? Is it easy or hard for you?
In verse 3 he says, "my spirit grows faint within me," yet "You know my way." What difference does it make that God knows the path, even when David feels lost?
Verse 4 says, "no one attends to me" and "no one cares for my soul." Why was the empty place at his right side such a painful picture? When have you felt that alone, even in a crowd?
In verse 5 he says, "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living." A refuge is a place to hide, and a portion is what you live on. What would it mean to treat God as both?
Verse 6 says, "I am brought quite low." If you are in a low place right now, or have been, what would you honestly like to say to God about it? You can say it here or keep it to yourself.

David asks to be freed "from prison, that I may praise Your name," and hopes others will "gather around me" (v. 7). The prison may be the cave or a picture of despair. Which reading speaks to you, and how can a group like ours help someone who feels shut in?
142.life: Once this week, set aside five minutes and say your troubles to God out loud, the way David does in verse 2. Don't tidy them up. Then tell one trusted person how you are really doing.
142.prayer: Thank God that he hears us when we are honest and low. Ask for the courage to bring him the real story, and pray for anyone who feels alone or trapped right now.
142.tip: Some people may find David's raw complaint uncomfortable, or may say they feel nothing when they pray. Reassure the group that the psalm shows honest, even bitter words are welcome before God, and don't rush to fix anyone's pain or tie it up with a neat answer.

143.open: When you have had a rough day, what is one small thing that helps you get back on your feet?
questions: The writer asks God to answer "In Your faithfulness" (v. 1), not because he has earned it. Why might he base his request on who God is? What does that tell us about how we can come to God?
Verse 2 says, "no one alive is righteous before You." Does that feel heavy or freeing to you? Why?
He does not hide how low he is: "My spirit grows faint within me" (v. 4). Why do you think a prayer this honest made it into the Bible?
In verse 5 he remembers "the days of old" and what God has done. When you feel worn down, what from your own past do you reach back to? Does it help?

He says, "my soul thirsts for You like a parched land" (v. 6). What does it feel like when you want God but feel dry, distant or unsure? Say it as honestly as you can. Doubts and blank spots are welcome here.
He asks, "Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning" (v. 8). Why might morning matter to someone coming out of a dark night? What would it look like to hear that love today?

In the middle of his trouble he prays, "Teach me the way I should walk" (v. 8). Why would someone who is hurting ask for direction and not only for relief? How do you ask God for guidance when you are struggling?
The psalm ends with a harsh request: "Destroy all who afflict me" (v. 12). How do you react to that? What do you do with anger and hurt when someone has wronged you?
143.life: This week, write down two or three things God has done for you or for people you know. When you feel low, read the list, then pray with your hands open in front of you, the way the psalmist did.
143.prayer: Thank God for being faithful when you have nothing to offer. Ask him to help you hear his steady love in the morning and to show you the way to walk. Pray for anyone in the group who feels crushed right now.
143.tip: Verse 12 may make some people uncomfortable. Don't rush past it or explain it away. Say plainly that the psalm names real anger, and that bringing it to God, instead of acting on it, is part of what the psalm shows. Then move on to the rest of the chapter.

144.open: What is one thing in your home or neighborhood that you would hate to see broken or lost, and why?
questions: David piles up names for God: "my Rock," "my fortress," "my stronghold," "my deliverer," "my shield" (vv. 1-2). Which one speaks to you most right now, and what is going on in your life that makes it stand out?

In verse 1 David says God "trains my hands for war, my fingers for battle." He sees his skill as something God gave him. What strengths or abilities do you have, and how do you think about where they came from?

In verses 3 and 4 David asks, "what is man, that You regard him?" and says "Man is like a breath." When do you feel most small or short-lived, and how does it feel to hear that God still pays attention to us?

Verses 5 to 7 ask God to come down with smoking mountains, lightning and arrows. David is not shy about the size of his request. What have you been hesitant to ask God for, and what makes it hard to ask boldly?
David describes his enemies as people "whose mouths speak falsehood" (v. 8). What does it do to a person or a community when lies and broken promises are common? Where have you seen that?

In verse 9 David says, "I will sing to You a new song." He promises thanks while still asking to be rescued (v. 11). What would it look like for you to thank God while you are still waiting on something? If that feels hard or even false right now, what is getting in the way?

Verses 12 to 14 picture a whole community doing well: children growing strong, full storehouses, "no breach in the walls" and "no cry of lament in our streets." What would a good life together look like for your neighborhood or church, and what part could you play?
The psalm ends with "Blessed are the people whose God is the LORD" (v. 15). Notice it speaks of a people, not just one person. How is being blessed together different from being blessed on your own?
144.life: This week, pick one of David's names for God (rock, fortress, shield, deliverer) and pray it out loud each morning. Then do one practical thing for the peace of someone near you, such as a meal, a visit or a phone call.
144.prayer: Thank God for being your refuge, and admit how short and fragile life is. Ask for rescue where you need it, and for peace and care for your neighborhood and your church.
144.tip: Verses 5 to 8 and 11 use strong language about enemies, and verse 1 talks about war, which can feel out of step with a gentle group. Name it plainly as the honest prayer of a king under threat, and invite people to talk about how they bring real fears and conflicts to God. Verses 12 to 15 may also sting for anyone who is single, childless or struggling financially, so make room for people to say that without hurry or fixing.

145.open: Who is someone who taught you something you still use today, and what did they teach you?
questions: David says, "Every day I will bless You" (v. 2). What would it look like for praise to be part of an ordinary day for you, not only a Sunday?
Verse 4 pictures how "One generation will commend Your works to the next." Who passed their faith, or their view of God, on to you? What did they get right?
Verse 8 says the LORD is "gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion." Which of those words is easiest for you to believe about God, and which is hardest?
Verse 9 says "His compassion rests on all He has made." What does it mean that God's care reaches beyond people who already believe?
Verse 14 says "The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down." When have you felt bowed down? What, if anything, helped you stand again?
Verse 18 says God is near to all who call on him "in truth." What do you think it means to pray honestly? What would you say to God if you did not have to sound polite?
Some days God can feel far away, even when verses like these say he is near. How do you hold the two together, and what would you want someone to say to you on a day like that?
The psalm ends with "let every creature bless His holy name" (v. 21). What is one thing you could say about God this week that someone near you might need to hear?
145.life: Each day this week, name one specific good thing you received and thank God for it out loud or in writing. At the end of the week, tell one person about one of them.
145.prayer: Praise God using the psalm's own words: "Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised" (v. 3). Then bring one honest need to the God who is near to those who call.
145.tip: Verse 20 says God will destroy the wicked, and it can feel jarring right after so much kindness. Don't skip it or rush to explain it away. Notice that the psalm sets it beside God's patience and nearness, and let the group say honestly how it sits with them. Verse 13 may also look different in your Bible, since its last line is missing from most Hebrew copies. A short mention is enough if someone asks.

146.open: Who is someone you have counted on for years, and what made them so dependable?
questions: The singer says, "I will praise the LORD all my life" (v. 2). What would it look like for praise to be a long habit and not just a good mood?
Verse 3 says, "Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save." Who or what do people around us put their hope in, like leaders, money, experts or a good plan?
Verse 4 says that when a person's spirit departs, "on that very day his plans perish." Why might the psalmist want us to remember this about even the most powerful people?
Verse 5 calls the person "blessed" whose "hope is in the LORD his God." What does it mean to hope in God, and how is that different from hoping God will give us what we want?

Verses 7 to 9 list people God cares for: the oppressed, the hungry, prisoners, the blind, foreigners, the fatherless and the widow. Which of these do you see in your own community, and what would it look like to care about them too?

The psalm says God "lifts those who are weighed down" (v. 8). Is there a weight you are carrying right now that you would be willing to name, or would rather just sit with quietly? Where do you find it hard to feel that God is near?
The psalm ends with "The LORD reigns forever" (v. 10). How does it feel to remember that every leader and every season of life is temporary, but God is not?
146.life: Pick one thing you tend to lean on more than God, such as a person, a paycheck or a plan. Each time it comes to mind this week, say a short line of praise from this psalm and ask God to help you trust him with it.
146.prayer: Praise God as the one who "remains faithful forever." Ask him to hold the people and worries you are leaning on too heavily, and to lift anyone in the group who feels weighed down.
146.tip: Verse 3 can slide into talk about politics, and the room may split fast. Steer back to the psalm's point: it is not about which leader is right, but that no human can carry our deepest hope. Invite everyone to answer about their own trust, not about someone else's.

147.open: What kind of weather do you enjoy most, and what does it remind you of?
questions: The psalm begins, "How good it is to sing praises to our God" (v. 1). When has praising God, in song or otherwise, felt natural to you? When has it felt like hard work?
Verse 3 says, "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds." What picture comes to mind when you read that? What does it say about how God treats hurting people?
The writer says God "calls them each by name" when it comes to the stars (v. 4). Why might the psalm put the huge and the tender side by side?
Verse 9 mentions "the young ravens when they call." What does it tell us that God notices creatures that nobody else looks after?

Verse 10 says God does not delight in "the strength of the horse." What do people today lean on for security, like money, skill, status or being in control? How does verse 11 offer a different kind of security?
In verses 16 to 18 God sends snow, frost and hail, and then his word melts them. What do you make of a God who is in charge of both the cold and the thaw? Is that comforting, puzzling or both?
Be honest here: is there a hurt in your life or the world that this psalm's picture of God healing and sustaining is hard to square with? What would you want to say to God about it?
147.life: Spend five minutes outside this week, at night if you can, looking at the sky. Then tell God one thing that is weighing on you, as someone who knows you by name.
147.prayer: Praise God for being both great in power and close to the brokenhearted. Pray for anyone in the group or in your life who is hurting right now.
147.tip: Verse 3 can sound too neat to someone who is still hurting. Make room for people to say that healing feels slow or absent, and let the group simply listen rather than rush to fix it. The psalm itself was sung by people still rebuilding.

148.open: What is one place in nature where you feel most at ease, and what is it about that place?
questions: The psalm begins with "Hallelujah!" and calls on the angels, sun, moon and stars to "praise Him" (vv. 1-3). Why do you think the poet starts at the very top, with the heavens, before coming down to earth?

Verse 5 gives the reason the heavens praise: "He gave the command and they were created." In a world where many people worshiped the sun and stars, what would it have meant to call them God's creations who join in worship?

Verse 8 lists "lightning and hail, snow and clouds, powerful wind fulfilling His word." Storms can feel frightening or out of control. How does it change things to picture even the weather as part of God's praise?
Verses 7 to 10 name sea creatures, mountains, trees, wild animals and birds. Which part of creation do you tend to overlook, and what might it teach you about God?
Verses 11 and 12 include "kings of the earth" and "young men and maidens, old and young together." Who in your own life is easy to leave out of the picture when you think of people who worship God?
Some days praise comes easily and some days it does not. What is it like for you right now, and what makes it easier or harder to join in?

Verse 13 says "His name alone is exalted; His splendor is above the earth and the heavens." When you look at the night sky, a storm or a crowd of very different people, does it point you to something beyond itself, or does it feel complete just as it is? Be honest.
Verse 14 says God "has raised up a horn for His people," a picture of strength given back to them. Where do you most need God to give you strength right now?
148.life: Spend ten minutes this week outside, at dawn, at night or in the rain. Leave your phone in your pocket, look closely at one thing God made, and thank him for it in your own words.
148.prayer: Thank God that he made everything and that nothing he made is too small or too big to matter to him. Ask him to help each person in the group notice his work this week and to give strength to anyone who feels worn down.
148.tip: Verse 4 mentions "waters above the skies," and someone may ask whether this is science or poetry. Say simply that the poet is using the language of his day, that some readers see an ancient picture of the sky and others see the clouds, and that the main point is that all of it praises God. Then move on.

149.open: What song, dance or kind of music makes you feel happiest, and where were you the last time you enjoyed it?
questions: The psalm opens with "Sing to the LORD a new song" (v. 1). What would a fresh song of thanks from your own life sound like right now?
Verse 2 calls God both "their Maker" and "their King." Which of those two feels closer to you today, and why?
Verse 3 pictures worship with "dancing" and "tambourine and harp." What does your own worship look like, and what makes it easy or hard to be expressive with others?
Verse 4 says "the LORD takes pleasure in His people." Is it easy or hard for you to believe that about yourself? Say honestly where you land, even if it is somewhere in the middle.
God "adorns the afflicted with salvation" (v. 4). Why might the psalm say this about the afflicted rather than the strong? What does that tell us about who God notices?

Verse 5 speaks of shouting for joy "upon their beds," a place where many people lie awake worried. What would it look like to bring praise, or even just an honest word to God, into those private hours?

In verses 6 to 8 the singers hold "a double-edged sword" to punish nations and bind their kings. The psalm puts joyful worship and judgment side by side. What do you make of that, and what questions does it raise for you?

Verse 9 speaks of carrying out the judgment written against the nations and calls it an honor for all God's saints. Many Christians read the sword as spiritual struggle or God's final judgment rather than a call to violence. How does that shape the way you hear this psalm, and what do you want to be careful about?
149.life: Each day this week, give God one minute of praise at a private moment, such as when you wake up or when you lie down. Sing, speak or sit quietly, and say one thing you are thankful for.
149.prayer: Thank God that he takes pleasure in his people and rescues the afflicted. Ask him to put real joy in your hearts, and to help you bring honest questions about hard passages to him.
149.tip: Verses 6 to 9 are the likely hard spot, and someone may worry the psalm blesses violence. Say plainly that Christians read it differently: as ancient Israel's wars, as later revolts, or as a picture of spiritual struggle and final judgment. Don't force agreement. Keep the group steady by returning to the joy and rescue in verses 1 to 5, and invite anyone who is uneasy to say so.

150.open: What is a song that you can't help singing along to, even if you sing badly?
questions: The psalm opens with "Hallelujah!" and tells us to praise God "in His sanctuary" and "in His mighty heavens" (v. 1). Where do you feel most aware of God: in a church building, outdoors, or somewhere else? Why?
Verse 2 gives two reasons to praise: "His mighty acts" and "His excellent greatness." What is the difference between praising God for what he has done and praising him for who he is?
Think of a time you saw God act in your life or in someone else's. What happened, and how did you respond?

Verses 3 to 5 pile up instruments: horn, harp, lyre, tambourine, strings, flute and cymbals, plus dancing. What does it tell you that worship here is loud, physical and joyful, not only quiet and careful?
Different people worship in different ways, from still and quiet to loud and moving. What helps you connect with God, and what leaves you feeling distant?

This is the last psalm, and the book before it holds many cries of pain, anger and doubt. If you are in a season when praise feels hard, what is that like for you? What might it mean that the book ends on praise?
Verse 6 says, "Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!" What does it mean to you that every breath is a reason to praise, and who would you want to invite into that?
150.life: Once a day this week, stop for the length of a few breaths and thank God for something specific. Let each breath be a small "Hallelujah." Try it with music at least once.
150.prayer: Thank God for what he has done and for who he is. Ask him to help each person in the group praise him honestly, whether they feel joyful or weary tonight.
150.tip: Some people will be uncomfortable with the loud, physical picture of worship, and others may feel they can't praise right now. Make clear that the psalm is an invitation and not a test. Let people name what worship looks like for them without comparing styles.
